metadata.title: How Loan Brokers Can Earn $200K+ From Just 2 Deals
metadata.author: Commercial Loan Broker Institute
metadata.shortDescription:
How many deals does a commercial loan broker actually need to close to make six figures—or even $500,000+ per year?

Most people assume loan brokers need hundreds of clients to earn serious income. The reality is very different.

In this video, Shane Walton breaks down the real math behind commercial loan broker commissions, business loan broker income, commercial real estate financing fees, SBA loan commissions, equipment financing commissions, bridge loan compensation, and private credit opportunities.

You'll learn:
• How commercial loan brokers get paid
• Typical commission percentages by loan type
• Commercial real estate commission examples
• SBA loan commission ranges
• Equipment financing and working capital commissions
• How many funded deals it takes to reach $200K, $500K, and beyond
• Why deal quality matters more than deal quantity
• The difference between small-ticket and large-ticket finance businesses

0:00 Introduction
1:08 Real Economics Inside Active Brokerages
1:51 Why the Math Becomes Inspiring
2:00 How a Commercial Loan Broker Works Around Capital
5:00 Commission Structures Overview
5:05 Small Working Capital & Equipment vs. Large CRE and M&A Deals
6:55 Interest-Only Lines of Credit and Private Lenders
7:02 Higher-Risk Lenders and 10% Broker Fees
7:24 Deal Volume Scenarios
9:00 Realistic Income Projections
10:30 Key Takeaways
11:30 Conclusion

Want to read the full breakdown? Check out the article over on: https://commercialloanbrokerinstitute.com/how-many-deals-does-a-business-loan-broker-need-to-close/

Watch Next: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s12jRSIozKA
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FnBYMtrQW9M&t=2s

If you're exploring a career as a commercial loan broker, business finance consultant, commercial real estate finance professional, or business funding specialist, this video will help you understand the income potential and economics of the industry.

Subscribe for more videos on commercial lending, business funding, commercial real estate finance, loan brokering, lender relationships, SBA lending, and business capital solutions.

metadata.title: What is a Commercial Loan Broker? What do they do?
metadata.author: Commercial Loan Broker Institute
metadata.shortDescription:
What does a commercial loan broker actually do, and how do they get their clients financed?

In this video, CLBI breaks down the real job of a commercial loan broker (sometimes called a business loan broker, capital consultant, loan advisor, or capital advisor). 

A broker is not a direct lender. They work as a consultant who helps clients access and use capital to grow their businesses and investment portfolios. You'll see the full process: understanding a client's goals and financial position, deciding whether capital is the right tool, preparing a strong financing package, and matching the client to best-fit lenders. 

Watch next: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=n_b4Wz6CGJQ

Want to see if brokering fits you?  Take the free personality quiz:
https://commercialloanbrokerinstitute.com/loan-broker-personality-test/

CLBI creates educational content for people who want to start, operate, and grow a commercial loan brokerage. Subscribe for weekly training on the business.

#CommercialLoanBroker #CommercialLending #BusinessFinance

metadata.title: How to Become a Business Loan Broker in 2026
metadata.author: Commercial Loan Broker Institute
metadata.shortDescription:
How do you become a business loan broker in 2026, with no license, finance degree, or bank experience?  This video walks through the full six-step path to becoming a business loan broker: learning the craft (not just memorizing loan products), standing up your business entity and brand, getting access to lenders, building a deal-flow system, generating your first borrowers, and placing your first deal to get paid. 

Shane also covers why 2026 is a real moment to start, with roughly $875 billion in commercial and multifamily mortgage debt maturing and banks lending more narrowly. If you're weighing commercial finance as a business, this is the practical roadmap.

Chapters:
0:00 So You Want to Become a Loan Broker
0:38 Why 2026 Is the Moment to Start
2:20 Step 1: Learn the Craft of Brokering
3:43 Step 2: Stand Up Your Business and Brand
5:35 Step 3: Getting Access to Lenders
6:58 Step 4: Build Your Deal Flow System
8:14 Step 5: Generate Your First Borrowers
10:03 Step 6: Place Your First Deal and Get Paid
10:41 What the Commission Math Actually Looks Like
12:31 Your Free Brokerage Launch Checklist

Want to read the full breakdown? Check out the article over on: https://commercialloanbrokerinstitute.com/how-to-become-a-business-loan-broker-in-2026-6-steps-to-your-first-funded-deal/

Watch next: See what a day is like in the life of a business loan broker:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WUTiN5zYjnU&t

Take a free personality quiz to see how you fit the broker industry:  https://commercialloanbrokerinstitute.com/loan-broker-personality-test/

Want the six steps expanded into a granular action list? Grab the free step-by-step brokerage launch checklist, over 100 steps pulled from launching hundreds of brokerages: https://commercialloanbrokerinstitute.com/brokerage-start-checklist/

CLBI has launched and supports more than 500 commercial loan brokerages nationwide, and our brokers have placed well over $2 billion in funding. We create educational content for people who want to start, operate, and grow a commercial loan brokerage. Subscribe for weekly training on the business.

Disclosure: This video is for educational and informational purposes only and is not financial, legal, or investment advice. It does not guarantee or imply any specific earnings or results; individual outcomes depend on effort, experience, market conditions, and other factors, and many participants earn less or nothing at all.

metadata.title: What Does a Commercial Loan Broker REALLY Do?
metadata.author: Commercial Loan Broker Institute
metadata.shortDescription:
A commercial loan broker connects a business that needs financing to the right lender and gets paid points when the deal funds - often $30,000+ on a single commercial loan, without lending a dollar of their own money.

Watch next: The Business Loan Broker Model — Steps, Pay & Career Fit → https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8074K4dLOrQ

Free: The 100+ step broker launch checklist — the same sequence we run with new brokers → https://commercialloanbrokerinstitute.com/brokerage-start-checklist/

So what does a commercial loan broker actually do? A broker matches a business that needs capital with the right lender, structures the deal, and guides it through to funding — the same way a real estate broker connects a buyer and seller, or an insurance broker matches a client to the right insurer. The broker isn't the bank and never lends their own money. They get paid only when the deal closes, in points: a percentage of the funded loan amount, usually somewhere between one and six percent, and very often paid by the lender rather than the borrower.

That's why one deal can pay so well. Place a $2,000,000 commercial loan at 1.5 points and that's $30,000 on a single funded deal. Because your fee scales with the size of the loan and commercial loans are large, this is per-deal income — not per-hour, not salaried. The comparison to a residential mortgage broker is stark: the same percentage on a $400,000 home loan is roughly $4,000.

The biggest misconception is that a commercial loan broker only does commercial real estate. Real estate is one slice of the pie. A broker also places equipment financing, working capital and business lines of credit, SBA loans, bridge and asset-based financing, business acquisition loans, inventory financing, and more — across many lenders, not just one. That breadth is the broker's real power: because they aren't tied to a single product or bank, they can find a yes where one lender says no.

And this is a real, durable business, not a fad. According to the Mortgage Bankers Association, U.S. commercial and multifamily real estate debt alone stands at roughly $4.8 trillion, with over a trillion in commercial real estate loans maturing in 2025 — and that's only the real estate slice. What makes it accessible: you don't need your own capital, you don't need to have been a banker, and most business-purpose commercial brokering doesn't require the NMLS/SAFE Act license residential mortgage officers carry (confirm the rules for your state — this isn't legal advice). What you do need is the skill to package and place deals well, and that's learnable.

metadata.title: The Broker Business Explained: Low Risk, Big Commissions
metadata.author: Commercial Loan Broker Institute
metadata.shortDescription:
There are businesses that need money. There are lenders with money to lend. But they don't connect as easily as you'd think. A business loan broker is the bridge, and gets paid when a deal funds.

This video breaks down the broker business model in plain English: what you actually do as a broker, how and how much you get paid (points, and real commission examples), why it's a low-risk model compared to most startups, and a realistic beginner path from referral all the way to funding your own deals. If you're weighing commercial finance as a business, this is the honest overview of the real job.

Wonderfing if you're a fit for the broker industry? Take this free quiz to identify your personality fit:  https://commercialloanbrokerinstitute.com/loan-broker-personality-test/

What You'll Learn:
- What a business loan broker actually does and how commissions are calculated
- Why this is a low-overhead, low-risk business model compared to traditional startups
- Real commission examples from working capital, equipment, and commercial real estate deals
- The four-stage beginner's ladder from referring deals to full brokerage
- A practical 30-day starter plan you can follow even with a small existing network

Chapters:
00:00 The gap between borrowers and lenders
01:16 What a business loan broker actually does
04:06 How brokers get paid and what points are
07:08 The beginner ladder: refer, team up, broker, fund
11:36 The income math that makes it predictable
15:06 A 30-day starter plan
18:38 Why this is one of the cleanest models in finance

Watch Next:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8074K4dLOrQ&t=334s

CLBI publishes educational content about becoming, operating, and growing a commercial loan brokerage. Subscribe for weekly videos on building the business.

Disclosure: 
This video is for educational and informational purposes only and is not financial, legal, or investment advice. It does not guarantee or imply any specific earnings or results; individual outcomes depend on effort, experience, market conditions, and other factors, and many participants earn less or nothing at all.

But your commission will usually be somewhere in the 1% to 10% range and will be calculated based on the amount of funding that you provide or you're sourcing for your client. And your income grows as you close more deals and close larger deals. But the key is always to just start on your first deal. And most brokers seem to really remember their first check, right? Sometimes it's just a few thousand dollars, a $4,000 or $5,000 commission, but it flips a switch in their head and they realize this is real. And yes, there's going to be much bigger commission checks down the road for them, but there's some magic in that that first one that lets you know, oh, this is a process I can repeat again and again here. How do you get to that first commission, especially when you're new in the industry? So, let's cover the beginner safe ladder for entering this business so you can start earning as a business loan broker without pretending that you're an expert in the field already and without risking your reputation. Because too many beginners fail because they are trying to jump to the highest rung of the ladder immediately. And they try to be a full broker without getting the full system in place first. And a smarter approach is to pick the right entry stage for your vision. Think of it like a ladder. Stage one is refer and earn. And this is really the simplest way to start. You identify a business with a real need and you connect them to a trusted broker and you get paid for the referral when the deal funds. It's fast, it's low friction, and it teaches you the first step in the game while you're earning along the way. You're developing your ability to speak with business owners and real estate investors. You're building trust, you're building your network. And you're getting leads in play along the way and you're also earning some money. And at our institute, we support numerous brokerages. So, we have a program where you can apply to do exactly this. Refer opportunities to brokerages and they'll be placed with an experienced brokerage and then you get paid as soon as that deal funds. Stage two is where you team up to earn more. And this is where you're working closely with an established brokerage. You become a part of their team, typically as a 1099 contractor. You get support and you're practicing, learning the ropes, and you're doing more front-end work with lead generation still, but you're moving into loan assessment. You're running the initial discovery conversations, you're gathering key info, you're often working on collecting docs for the package, and you help to shape the request, but you have that more experienced partner that places it with the lender and closes it, and that's often one of the best models for beginners because you're learning and earning simultaneously, but you're earning more than if you just refer it out, but you're doing a bit more work, right? You're also building that competence, but you don't have to carry the deal entirely on your own from day one. And if you're already in this place and generating opportunities and looking for a good home for them, and you're looking for that team to work with, again, connect with our institute. We are always happy to make introductions and to support collaborations, and we know hundreds of brokerages, and we'd be happy to connect you with a reputable brokerage. And that brings us to stage three, which is where you broker and earn. And this is the full model, right? You do the lead sourcing, the discovery, you package the deal, you place it with lenders, you manage it to close. And here you have a much higher upside. You also have much higher responsibility. There's no commission splits, so unlike the other models, you're going to keep 100% of the commissions. But you are also responsible for 100% of the work. So when you're ready for this stage, our institute has a broad variety of launch programs. For new brokerages, they include full education, ongoing support and mentoring, the tools you need to run your brokerage, the branding and marketing, the entire lender network to support your deals, and a whole lot more. It's really a brokerage incubator or brokerage sandbox platform to help you get out into the market quickly and more profitable. Stage four is fund and earn. And this is typically later in the brokerage life cycle, but over time, some brokers are going to move into participating in capital, either syndicating, lending out their own money, or taking yield positions. It's not typically a beginner step, but it's part of why this industry can be such a massive wealth engine as you grow into it. Because as you start placing enough money, you start to say to yourself, "Well, I know how to find the deals, I know what a good deal looks like, I know what looks risky and what isn't risky. So why don't I just put this all together and become the lender myself and keep all of the profit in the deal." But you don't need to start at the top of the ladder. but you need is to start at the right rung for you. And now that you see that ladder, I'm going to go ahead and talk a bit about how to make this a predictable process with predictable income. And here's your income math. Your monthly income equals your qualified conversations times your close rate times your average commission per close. That's it. Conversations multiplied by your close rate multiplied by your average commission. And here's the beginner mistake. Many new brokers try to scale the first variable, their conversations, before they can reliably and consistently close. They chase leads, they chase traffic, they chase volume. But early on, your fastest path to income is usually going to be improving your close rate. Because if you can close more of the conversations that you are already having, if you're closing more of what you already touch, then you don't need massive lead volume. You don't have to work lead your way through a lot of junk to get commissions. And of course, you need to have conversations. Without those, you're not in touch with anyone who needs your help, but the place to focus your energy and your hustle isn't just in having more conversations. The big idea is that you focus that energy and hustle in having more quality conversations, investing in relationship building with qualified borrowers, investing in creating outstanding packages, and placing them with well-targeted lenders, and using all of your hustle and your energy to keep the good deals moving quickly and efficiently. And after you've mastered that, the next lever that you need to pull is increasing your average commission amount. That's the next step at not going back to more conversations because at the Institute, we spend a lifetime coaching brokers on how to deal with their capacity constraints. Once you're out and into the market and you have established a few good referral partnerships, it's quite common to have more deal opportunities coming in than you have time in your day to work. So, if you go back to our money-making equation, income equals conversations multiplied by closing rate multiplied by average commission, at this point, you don't want to focus on increasing conversations. You already have those flowing in and you often are overwhelmed by them. So, if you're feeling stuck on time, more of the same type of opportunities isn't going to help. Instead, you focus on increasing your average commission per deal. If you increase deal size, deal amount, the size of the loan that you're willing to work on, you will be working your way steadily upstream in the market. And with larger loans come larger commissions. And this is how brokers go from sporadic income into reliable income and to massive income. So, next, let's talk through the three different skill blocks that you need in order to start making money as a beginner so that you know what to learn, what to ignore, and how you can avoid the I'm busy but broke trap in this industry. So, let's make it practical. We're going to walk through a 30-day starter plan that gets deals moving even if your network is small so that you can start creating momentum without a whole lot of chaos. In week one, you want to choose your entry stage and pick a lane. Decide which rung on that ladder you're going to start on. Is it going to be referral only? That's the low-touch model where you do an initial discovery and then connect that borrower with a trusted capital provider, or is it going to be model two, rung two, where you're teaming up with a brokerage, you're working with them more closely, you're doing more of the work, but you've more support and more of the commission is coming to you? Or is it rung three, where you're the full broker? You steer the ship and you don't give away any of your earned commission to anyone else, there's no hands in your pie. But pick a rung and then pick a simple lane or a niche to start. Working capital and equipment is often a starting beginner lane because the deals are easier to understand and there's always constant demand. Or maybe you have a network of connections, a particular industry that points you there. But either way, identify where you're going to start working your niche because that's going to influence your subsequent steps. Week two, you want to build your partner ecosystem and then your intake checklist. So if you're at the referral or partner stage, you identify who you're going to work with to close deals where it's those referrals are going. And if you're at the broker stage, you're going to need some lenders. And then you create that simple intake process or checklist to use with your clients. So you're going to be collecting the business basics and the use of funds and the timeline and the revenue and the cash flow snapshots and any collateral information, any credit issues, so that you're identifying the right things and you're not trying to be perfect. Your goal here in this first month is to build a consistent system that you can refine week after week. Start using it, refine, use and refine. And week three, you want to talk to 20 prospects from your existing network, right? Start warm. Business owners that you already know, real estate investors you know, people in your community. And along the way, don't pitch, right? Come in and ask questions. Get curious. Authentically look to understand what people are working on, what their projects are, what their challenges are. You'll be shocked by how many businesses have capital needs once you start the conversations. And week four is submitting, following up, and refining. Your first deals aren't going to be perfect, and that's fine. Your goal is to start the cycle because that's the fastest way to improve. You're moving from discovery to matching to packaging, submitting, you're following up, you're funding, and this is how you make money as a business loan broker. It's not by watching more videos, though we do have lots of great training videos. Please do like and subscribe, but even more important than subscribing is doing your reps out in the real world, seeking out those conversations so that you can learn about what others are working on. If you do that, you're going to find opportunities. And when they come up, just let them know that you'd be happy to help out. So if you've been looking for a business model with real upside, low overhead, high demand, this is one of the cleanest opportunities in the finance sector. You're not taking any balance sheet risk or big investments. You're creating outcomes. You're helping businesses to survive, to grow. You're helping them to expand by getting them the right capital at the right time. And along the way, you're getting paid when each deal funds. Commercial loan brokering offers serious income potential, but you need the right foundation to win. In this video, Shane Walton of CLBI breaks down 11 key concepts that successful brokers build on in the real world.

What You'll Learn:
- Who needs a commercial loan broker and why
- How to speak the language lenders use to approve deals
- Why deal quality matters more than volume
- How lender matching determines whether deals close or die
- Why trust and process are what separate funded brokers from frustrated ones

1:15 Know Who Needs Your Help 
2:33 Why Borrowers Need Capital and Struggle to Get It 
4:44 Solve Capital Problems, Not Just Sell Money

8:08 Deal Quality Matters More Than Quantity 
9:23 Lender Matching Is Your Core Skill 
10:31 Storytelling with Documentation Unlocks Capital 
12:17 The Income Potential and How It Is Earned 
13:46 Brokering Is a Relationship Business 
15:35 Build a Process, Not Just Motivation 
17:23 Training and Infrastructure Compress Your Learning Curve

should blindly jump into just because

to understand what brokers actually do,
why borrowers need help, how lenders
think, and what separates a great
opportunity from wasted time. So, in
this video, I'm going to break down what
you need to know before becoming a

I'm Shane Walton, co-founder of the

growth nationwide. And we work with an
active lender network that's used by
brokers placing deals with hundreds of
lenders across the country. So, this
video is not just about theory. It's
about the key concepts that we see
successful brokers building on in the
real world. So, let's jump in. First, as
a commercial loan broker, you really
need to understand who needs your help.
Commercial loan brokers help people who
need capital to move their business
ventures forward. That can include
business owners, real estate investors,
developers, entrepreneurs, acquisition
buyers, and any other commercial
borrower. These are the people who are
trying to do something meaningful in the
world. They may be buying real estate or
equipment. They're purchasing inventory
for their stores or businesses. They're
acquiring another business. They're
refinancing existing debt or stabilizing
their cash flow month to month. But, in
most cases, the borrower is very clear.
They know the destination. In other
words, they know what they want to
accomplish, but they might not know the
financing path to get there. They may
not know which lender is right or which
products fit or how to present the
opportunity in a way that a lender can
understand and feels comfortable
approving. And this gap between their
goal and the knowledge of how to achieve
that goal, that is where a broker comes
in and creates huge value. You're not
simply helping someone to get money.
You're helping them to navigate a
complex capital market so they can move
from where they are to where they are
trying to go. Second, to be a successful
commercial loan broker, you need to
really understand why borrowers need
your help. Businesses need capital
because growth usually requires money
before the payoff arrives. A company may
need to buy equipment before it can
increase its production. A developer
might need financing before a project
can be built. A store owner may need
some working capital to purchase more
inventory before they can sell it. Or a
doctor's office might need to pay their
staff and their monthly lease before the
insurance company pays them for all the
services that they provided to their
patients. A real estate investor will
need financing to purchase and to rehab
a property before that property can be
leased out and start producing income.
So capital becomes the bridge in all of
these scenarios. It's what enables the
entrepreneur or investor to walk from
opportunity through execution in the
business to payout. And getting capital
now allows you to seize the opportunity
today to build the business tomorrow and
keep it going without running out of
cash until you ultimately get the big
payout of the profit at the end. But
getting that capital is not always
simple. All right, banks are
conservative by design. That's no insult
to banks. That's their role. Banks
protect depositors. They follow credit
policy and they answer to regulators in
a way that provides safety for their
depositories, their clients. And private
lenders don't need to play by those same
rules because they have a different role
in the market. The banks will reject
deals that are too complex or too small
or too risky or the businesses are too
young or they're simply outside their
credit box. So, a business can be solid
and still get declined by a bank. A
project can make sense and still not fit
the first lender that's put in front. A
borrower can be fundable but not
fundable at the first bank that they
call. And that is one of the biggest
opportunities for a commercial loan
broker. A bank decline does not
necessarily mean that a deal is
impossible. Sometimes it just means that
that deal is in the wrong room. The
third thing that you need to know to be
successful as a commercial loan broker
is to internalize this lesson. Your job
is to solve capital problems, not to
sell money. If you think your job is
just selling money, you immediately
become a commodity because money is
available from so many different places.
Banks have money, private lenders have
money, credit funds, fintech platforms
have money, equipment lenders and
factoring companies have money. So, the
question is not who has money to sell
but the question is what capital
solution actually fits this specific
borrower, this deal, this timeline, this
risk profile and today's lender market.
And that is a much more valuable
question. The broker's value comes from
the process that they run through, the
diagnosis, assessment, structuring,
packaging, lender matching, facilitating
the conversations and helping move the
deal toward closing. And there's a big
difference between saying, "I'm a
broker, I've got money for sale." and
saying, let's figure out together what
capital structure actually fits your
business, fits you as a borrower, fits
this project in this lender market.
Because the first approach, I've got
money for sale, sounds like a sales
person. But the second sounds like a
true business advisor. And the broker
who solves problems for businesses is
much more valuable than the broker who
simply says they have lenders and money
for sale. And the fourth big idea you
need to understand when starting out as
a commercial loan broker is this. You
don't need to be a banker, but you do
need to learn their language. And that's
really good news for beginners. You
don't have to come from banking to
become a commercial loan broker. You
don't need to have spent 20 years
underwriting loans or to have worked
inside a credit department, but you do
need to learn how lenders think.
Borrowers and lenders think very
differently, and consequently talk
differently. Borrowers usually talk in
terms of goals, pressure, opportunity,
problems, urgency. We need it now. A
borrower might say, I need money to
expand. I need to buy this property. I
need to refinance this debt today. I
need working capital to keep operations
going. I need to close quickly to seize
this opportunity. But lenders think
differently. They want to know, how will
the loan be repaid? What collateral
supports it to keep me safe? What is the
borrower's cash flow month after month
after month? What is the use of funds
when I give it out? How will it be used?
What's the loan to value? How much am I
loaning out compared to how much the
client has for skin in the game? What's
the debt service coverage? What happens
if things don't go to plan? What What's
the exit strategy if things go south?
The broker becomes the The then between
these two worlds, the borrower and the
lender, you listen to the borrower's
problem and then you translate that
problem into the language that a lender
is going to use to make a credit
decision. All right, you're not just
passing messages back and forth, you're
translating between two worlds where
people speak different languages and
think in fundamentally different ways.
And when you can do that well, you
become extremely valuable to both sides.
The fifth big idea that successful
brokers universally understand is this.
Deal quality matters more than quantity.
New brokers often think that they need a
huge number of deals to be successful.
They think that success is about more
calls, more submissions, more names in
my pipeline. But commercial finance
actually rewards quality more than
quantity because the loan sizes are
larger and the commissions are so
meaningful. And one strong funded deal
can create a significant payout
depending on the deal size and
compensation. Two good deals can easily
create 10x more revenue than a dozen
weak files ever will. And the goal is
not frantically chasing. The goal is to
find good opportunities that can
actually close. This business rewards
judgment, not just activity. And this is
one of the most important lessons for
any new broker. Busy does not mean
productive in our industry. Submissions
do not mean income. Funded deals are
what matter. And once you understand
lender matching, you're going to start
seeing why some deals get declined
repeatedly while other deals are moving
forward quickly and easily with the
right lender. So, we'll get to that. But
the sixth big idea that you need to
understand to become a successful loan
broker is that lender matching is your
real skill. A good loan can still get
declined, get a big no stamped on it if
it goes to the wrong lender. The same
deal that looks weak to one lender may
look like a great opportunity to another

metadata.title: A Day in the Life of a Commercial Loan Broker (The Real Version)
metadata.author: Commercial Loan Broker Institute
metadata.shortDescription:
What does a day in the life of a commercial loan broker actually look like, minus the highlight reel?

This is the real version, hour by hour. CLBI walks through how a strong broker actually runs a day: the 6 a.m. start, morning business development and prospecting, midday client consultations built on the right questions, afternoon deal work when problems hit, and the evening networking that fills the pipeline. It also lays out who this career fits, and who it doesn't, so you can decide honestly whether it's for you.

Want to hear how an actual broker describes a day in their life:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gclRu25te-Q

Want to go deeper? The guide to the life of a loan broker:
https://commercialloanbrokerinstitute.com/day-life-commercial-loan-broker/

Chapters:
00:00 What commercial loan brokers actually do
01:42 Why every day is different
02:07 The morning routine that makes the money
03:26 Business development and client consultations
07:42 When deals go wrong: problem-solving under pressure
10:10 The rewards: income and lifestyle flexibility
10:45 Is this career right for you, and how to start

CLBI creates educational content for people who want to start, operate, and grow a commercial loan brokerage. Subscribe and hit the bell for weekly training on the business.

Disclosure: This video is for educational and informational purposes only and is not financial, legal, or investment advice. It does not guarantee or imply any specific earnings or results; individual outcomes depend on effort, experience, market conditions, and other factors, and many participants earn less or nothing at all.

metadata.title: 4 Foundations for New Commercial Loan Officers
metadata.author: Loan Officer Training | Zevi Shafran
metadata.shortDescription:
What helps new commercial loan officers bring in business? Drawing on my experience overseeing a team of commercial originators, I explain four foundations: relationships, lending skills, consistent marketing, and a focused brand.

Interested in becoming a commercial loan officer? Sign up for the free first module of the Part-Time Commercial Lender Academy (name and email required):
https://www.loanmastermind.com/free

In this lesson:
- Building referral relationships with brokers, CPAs, and attorneys
- Understanding an initial property loan package: rent roll, profit and loss statement, and personal financial statement
- Staying in touch through calls, networking, and useful content
- Choosing a commercial lending niche, such as multifamily, and becoming known for it

I also share a story about an originator who focused his outreach on a specific multifamily financing program. The emphasis is on developing skills and relationships over time, not a promised income level or timeline. Documentation and underwriting requirements vary by property, borrower, and lender.

All submissions are subject to credit and underwriting review. The receipt of a loan application does not constitute loan approval. Any content featured on this channel is strictly for informational use and should not constitute legal or financial advice.

Zevi Shafran | NMLS# 1067721 | DRE# 01259491

Whether you’re tired of working at a dead-end job, your company is facing lay-offs, or you just want to be your own boss, the opportunity to become a loan broker might be a perfect fit.


This article gives you an in-depth look at how to become a loan broker, how to start a loan broker business, how to make money in the world of commercial capital, and how to be a commercial loan broker that is recognized and trusted in the industry.


Learn More: https://commercialloanbrokerinstitute.com/start-loan-broker-business/

metadata.title: Why 1 Loan Deal Pays More than 100 B2B Sales
metadata.author: Commercial Loan Broker Institute
metadata.shortDescription:
One commercial loan deal can pay more than a hundred small B2B sales. This video puts the actual math on the table.

Shane Walton, co-founder of the Commercial Loan Broker Institute, walks through why a single commercial real estate loan (a roughly three million dollar strip mall) can pay a broker around sixty thousand dollars, and how that stacks up against roughly a hundred and twenty smaller sales for the same paycheck. This is for anyone exploring commercial finance as a business and trying to understand the real income model: how broker fees work, why a three million dollar deal is the average one and not an exotic one, why one deal is not a hundred times harder to land than one small sale, and what you actually need to do the work (no finance degree and none of your own capital).

It's an honest look at the leverage behind the business, including the catch: commercial deals take weeks or months to close, not every file funds, and this is a pipeline you build and tend rather than a button you press.

Chapters:
0:00 One Deal vs 100 Small Sales
0:47 How the $60,000 Actually Adds Up
1:37 The Other Side: 120 Website Sales
2:30 Is a $3 Million Deal Really Realistic?
3:44 The Catch (It's Not What You Think)
5:46 Treadmill vs Pipeline: The Income Shift
7:04 What You Actually Need to Start
8:50 Your Next Step

Watch next: Eleven Things to Know Before Becoming a Commercial Loan Broker
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=svRIdayYOLo&t=5s

Subscribe for weekly videos on becoming, operating, and growing a commercial loan brokerage.

Want CLBI's program details? Start here:
https://commercialloanbrokerinstitute.com/

CLBI publishes educational content about starting, running, and growing a commercial loan brokerage.

Disclosure: This video is for educational and informational purposes only and is not financial, legal, or investment advice. It does not guarantee or imply any specific earnings or results; individual outcomes depend on effort, experience, market conditions, and other factors, and many participants earn less or nothing at all.

#CommercialLoanBroker #CommercialLending #BusinessFinance

On a $3 million deal, a 2% fee comes out to $60,000. And that's the whole engine. And before anyone says 2% is made up, it isn't. 2% sits at the low end for a bridge loan and the high end for a conventional real estate loan. >> [music] >> Fees move around by deal and by lender, and I'm using 2% because it's in the normal range, not because it makes the numbers look good. If I was trying to make the numbers look good, I'd talk about equipment financing where you can earn 3% [music] or MCAs where you earn 10% or more. But I'm using 2% because it's realistic. Let's take the middle of that and call it 10%. That's $500 for a sale. $60,000 divided by $500 is 120 sales. 120 websites sold to match the commission that would be one strip mall that you find. And both of these people are doing the same thing. Both are earning a percentage of [music] what they close. The web rep is working off of a $5,000 number. I picked a strip mall on purpose, too, because the $3 million isn't a fantasy thing. $3 million is quite reasonable, and there's strip malls all around the country. So, let's look at what these centers >> [music] >> actually cost on average. Exceed Insurance put the average strip mall build around $3.7 [music] million. RealMo, which is a national real estate marketplace, it lists the average sale price of just over $3 million for a strip center. $3 million [music] and $48,000. It's the average one around the country. So, why am I walking you through this? I'm Shane Walton, co-founder of the Commercial Loan Broker Institute. And we've helped launch and support over 400 brokerages around the country with brokers who have placed well over $2 billion in financing. So, when I tell you that a single commercial deal can out-earn a year of small ticket sales, that's not a theory that I'm floating, it's something that we watch happen across real funded deals every single week. [music] You source the deal, you package it, and you place it with the right lender, and you guide the borrower through the funding. And that's genuine work. But, it's the same kind of work [music] as running one good consultative B2B sale. There's a discovery [music] conversation, a proposal, replying to objections, closing. The mechanics are all the same. And I also own a marketing agency [music] that's been running for 15 years now, Green By Marketing. I've done a hundreds of website sales [music] myself, and I've managed the sales teams in this industry. segments.text: You do not need years of finance
experience to start a brokerage, but you
do need to understand how the business
works, where deals come from, how
lenders evaluate applications, and how
to [music] guide a customer from I need
equipment to a completed transaction.
In this video, I'll walk you through the
beginner [music] road map for starting a
brokerage, from choosing your market to
finding your first deal.
And stay [music] until the end because
I'll give you a simple first 30-day
action plan.
A broker [music] connects a business
that needs financing with a lender that
can provide it.
The customer may need [music] a truck,
trailer, excavator, medical equipment,
manufacturing machinery, or another
business asset.
The broker [music] usually does not
provide the money personally. Instead,
the broker helps organize the request,
[music] collect information, identify
potential lenders, and move the
application through the process.
Think of the broker as a guide [music]
and matchmaker.
The customer may not know which
financing option fits. The lender may
not want to spend [music] time sorting
through incomplete applications.
A good broker helps both sides
communicate [music]
clearly. That is the value you bring.
The first mistake beginners make is
trying to finance [music] everything for
everyone.
A better approach is to start with one
customer type or equipment category.
For example, transportation companies
needing trucks or trailers,
contractors needing construction
equipment, medical practices [music]
needing specialized equipment,
manufacturers upgrading machinery,
>> [music]
>> or new businesses purchasing their first
major asset. Why choose a market?
Because specialization makes your
marketing clearer. It also helps [music]
you learn the equipment, the customers,
the common documents, and the lenders
[music] understand that industry. You do
not need to stay in one category
forever. But, when you are starting,
focus gives you credibility faster.
Choose a market where businesses
regularly need expensive equipment, and
where you can consistently reach [music]
potential customers.
Before you approach customers, learn the
basic financing structures. [music]
A customer may be considering a loan, a
lease, or another [music] commercial
financing option.
You should understand the approximate
cost of the equipment, the customer's
business history, revenue, and cash
flow, credit profile, down payment
expectations, the useful life [music] of
the equipment, whether the equipment is
new or used, and how the financing
payment fits the business.
You do not need to become [music] an
attorney, accountant, or underwriter.
But, you do need to know enough to ask
good questions and avoid making promises
you cannot guarantee.
Also, remember licensing, registration,
disclosures, and compliance requirements
can vary by location and business model.
Get professional guidance before making
claims about what is legally required in
your area.
Your lender network is one of the most
important assets in this business.
Different lenders have different
preferences.
One may prefer established companies.
Another may work with newer businesses.
Some may focus on specific equipment
types, industries, credit profiles, or
transaction sizes.
Your goal is not to collect the largest
possible list of lenders.
Your goal is to understand which lender
is a good fit for which type of
customer.
Create a simple tracking sheet with
information such as industries accepted,
equipment types accepted, minimum time
in business, credit preferences,
typical transaction size,
required documents,
application process, and communication
expectations.
Start with quality relationships.
Ask lenders what makes an application
strong, what causes delays, and what
types of deals they do not want.
That information will save you time and
improve your submissions.
A professional process makes you easier
to trust.
Your process can be simple. First, have
a discovery conversation.
Ask what equipment the customer wants,
why they need it, how soon they need it,
and whether they already have a purchase
quote.
Next, collect the basic information
needed to understand the opportunity.
Then, review the request and explain the
next step clearly.
After that, submit the application to an
appropriate lender and keep the customer
updated.
Finally, help coordinate communication
between the customer, lender, and
equipment seller until the transaction
is completed.
Do not disappear after submitting an
application.
Customers remember communication.
Even if the lender has not made a
decision yet, a quick update can prevent
confusion and build trust.
If you are learning how to become a loan
broker, subscribe to Equipment Finance
Academy.
This channel is designed to help
beginners understand the business, find
opportunities, communicate with
customers, and build a repeatable
brokerage process.
Now, let's talk about the part most
beginners struggle with. Finding
customers.
You do not need a massive audience to
find your first opportunity. Start with
people and businesses already connected
to equipment purchases.
Potential referral sources include
equipment dealers, equipment
manufacturers,
contractors,
truck and trailer dealers, accountants,
insurance agents, business consultants,
commercial real estate professionals,
and industry associations.
Your message should be simple. Do not
begin with a complicated sales pitch.
Explain who you help, what type of
equipment you focus on, and how you make
the financing process easier.
For example, I help construction
companies explore financing options when
they are purchasing equipment.
If one of your customers needs help
understanding the next step, I can help
organize the request.
That is clearer than saying, "I can get
anyone approved."
Never promise approval, a specific rate,
or a guaranteed funding result.
Your job is to guide the process
professionally.
Your first few applications are learning
opportunities.
Track what happened with each one.
Where did the customer come from?
What equipment were they buying?
Which documents were missing?
Which lender reviewed the request?
What questions caused confusion?
What caused the deal to move forward or
stop?
Over time, these notes become your
operating system.
You will start recognizing stronger
opportunities earlier.
You will know which customers need more
preparation.
You will also learn which referral
sources send serious prospects.
That is how a beginner develops
judgment, not by trying to sound
experienced, but by paying attention to
every transaction.
Here is a practical first 30-day plan.
Days 1 through 7,
choose your target market and study the
basic financing terms.
Create a list of common equipment and
customer questions.
Days 8 through 14,
research potential lenders and build
your lender tracking sheet.
Learn their application requirements.
Days 15 through 21,
create your basic customer intake
process, email templates, follow-up
messages, and document checklist.
Days 22 through 30,
contact referral partners every day.
Have real conversations.
Ask what equipment their customers are
buying and where financing questions
come up. Your goal in the first month is
not to look like a giant company.
Your goal is to become useful,
organized, and consistent.
Avoid these common mistakes.
First, trying to serve every industry
immediately.
Second, sending incomplete applications
to lenders.
Third, promising approval before a
lender has reviewed the request.
Fourth, failing to follow up with
customers.
Fifth, focusing only on getting leads
instead of building referral
relationships.
And finally, believing that one course,
one lender, or one marketing method will
build the entire business for you.
Training gives you a foundation. Results
come from applying what you learn
repeatedly. Starting a brokerage with no
experience is possible, but it is not
automatic.
You need a clear market, basic financing
knowledge,
strong lender relationships,
an organized customer process, and
consistent outreach.
Start small.
Learn one market. Complete one process
correctly. Then, improve it.
If this video helped you understand the
road map, subscribe to Equipment Finance
Academy and comment with the industry
you want to serve first.
Your next step is simple.
Choose your market and begin building
your first referral list today.

metadata.shortDescription:
Equipment financing masterclass for better business finance management. Before signing an equipment loan or lease agreement, you need to understand the real costs, risks, and financial impact.

In this complete Equipment Financing Masterclass, you will learn how business equipment financing works. 

The differences between equipment loans and leasing, and how to choose the right financing option without damaging your business cash flow.

#businessfinance #equipmentleasing #businessloans #smallbusinessfinance 

Whether you operate a small business, manufacturing company, construction business, restaurant, or growing startup, understanding equipment financing can help you make better financial decisions.

Video chapters

Intro - 00:00
Understand Equipment Financing - 00:35
Equipment Loans vs Leasing - 03:49
True cost of Equipment Financing - 07:06
Actually Pay for Itself? - 11:01
Protecting CASH Flow - 14:50
Hidden Financing Traps - 18:14
Financing Like CFO - 21:30
Long Term Equipment Financing - 24:54

How to Track Business Finance Step by step - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fH9C_piY2eo
How to Avoid Bad Debt in Your Small Business - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YINjuEmAeos

Equipment financing is not simply about getting approved for a loan. It is about understanding whether the equipment will generate enough financial value to justify its total cost.

This masterclass uses practical business examples and straightforward financial explanations to help entrepreneurs and small business owners understand equipment financing.

Subscribe for more business finance masterclasses, cash flow management strategies, financial planning tutorials, and practical business education.

segments.text: Imagine spending $50,000
on a new machine only to discover 3
months later that your business cannot
afford to pay its employees.
The machine works perfectly, customers
are satisfied, and sales are increasing.
Yet the business is running out of cash.
How can buying something that improves
productivity create such a serious
financial problem?
>> [music]
>> In this masterclass, you will learn how
equipment financing works, compare loans
and leases, avoid costly mistakes, and
make smarter financing decisions.
Step one, understand why equipment
financing can make or break your
business.
Imagine a small bakery producing 500
loaves of bread every day. The owner
discovers a commercial oven that could
double production.
The oven costs $40,000,
and the business currently has $50,000
in its bank account.
>> [music]
>> Buying the oven with cash seems
attractive because the owner would avoid
interest payments.
But after spending $40,000,
only $10,000 would remain available for
ingredients, employee salaries,
electricity, rent, and unexpected
repairs.
Now consider financing the oven with a
loan. The business makes an initial
payment of $8,000 and finances the
remaining $32,000.
Although the loan creates interest
expenses, the bakery keeps significantly
more cash available for daily
operations.
This example reveals the first important
principle of equipment financing. The
objective is not simply to purchase
equipment at the lowest possible price.
The objective is to acquire productive
assets while protecting the financial
health of the business.
Equipment financing allows companies to
obtain machinery, vehicles, computers,
manufacturing systems, medical devices,
restaurant equipment, and other business
assets without necessarily paying their
entire purchase price immediately.
However, financing does not
automatically make equipment affordable.
A business can borrow money to purchase
an asset and still experience serious
financial problems if the equipment
fails to generate enough economic value.
Consider a construction company
financing an expensive excavator.
If the excavator remains unused for
several weeks every month, the company
must continue making loan payments even
though the machine generates little or
no revenue during those periods.
This creates a dangerous mismatch
between financial obligations and actual
business activity.
Equipment payments are usually
predictable, but the revenue generated
by that equipment may fluctuate because
of seasonal demand, customer
cancellations, or unexpected market
conditions.
Successful equipment financing therefore
requires understanding three separate
questions. Can the business obtain
financing? Can the business afford the
payments?
And will the equipment generate enough
value to justify the entire investment?
These questions may sound similar, but
they produce very different answers. A
lender might approve a large equipment
loan based on financial history,
collateral, and creditworthiness.
That approval does not guarantee that
borrowing the money represents a good
business decision.
The smartest business owners treat
equipment financing as a capital
allocation decision.
They compare the expected benefits of
the equipment against its complete
financial cost while considering what
other opportunities might exist for the
same money.
Step two, equipment loans versus
leasing. Choose the right financing
structure.
Suppose a delivery company needs five
new vehicles. Purchasing them outright
would consume most of its available
cash.
The owner approaches two financing
providers and receives two different
proposals, an equipment loan and an
equipment lease.
An equipment loan generally allows the
business to purchase the vehicles using
borrowed money. The company makes
scheduled payments consisting of
principal and interest. Depending on the
agreement, the lender may hold a
security interest in the vehicles until
the loan is repaid. A lease works
differently. Instead of purchasing the
equipment through a traditional loan,
the business obtains the right to use it
for an agreed period. Ownership,
purchase options, maintenance
responsibilities, and end-of-term
obligations depend on the specific lease
contract. Imagine the company expects to
use its delivery vehicles for 8 years.
Purchasing through a loan could make
financial sense because the business
intends to retain the vehicles long
after the financing period ends.
Now, imagine a technology company that
replaces its computers every 3 years.
Leasing might be attractive because the
business wants regular access to updated
equipment without managing the long-term
ownership of rapidly aging technology.
However, leasing is not always cheaper.
A lease with low monthly payments can
become expensive when additional fees,
mandatory services, purchase options, or
end-of-term charges are included.
Some leases also contain strict rules
about equipment usage, physical
condition, mileage, maintenance, or
early termination. These restrictions
can create costs that business owners
overlook when comparing advertised
monthly payments.
Another important consideration is the
difference between equipment ownership
and equipment usage.
A company may need a machine to generate
revenue, but that does not necessarily
mean owning the machine provides the
greatest financial benefit.
For example, a landscaping company might
need specialized equipment only during
certain months.
Renting that equipment for specific
projects could cost less than
maintaining year-round financing
payments, insurance, storage, and
repairs.
Business owners should compare
purchasing, financing, leasing, and
renting before committing to any
agreement. Each option changes the
timing of cash payments, the allocation
of risk, and the company's financial
flexibility.
Tax and accounting treatment also
matters.
Loan interest, depreciation, lease
expenses, and recognized lease
liabilities may be treated differently
depending on local tax laws, accounting
standards, and contract terms.
The important lesson is simple. Never
select a financing arrangement only
because its monthly payment appears
affordable.
Evaluate the complete agreement,
including ownership rights, long-term
costs, contractual restrictions, and the
expected useful life of the equipment.
Step three, calculate the true cost of
equipment financing.
Imagine a manufacturing company
purchasing a machine advertised for
The lender offers financing with
manageable monthly payments, and the
owner immediately assumes the machine
will cost approximately $60,000.
But the purchase price is only the
beginning.
The business must also pay for
transportation, installation, employee
training, insurance, maintenance,
electricity, and possibly modifications
to its production facility.
Suppose transportation costs $2,000,
installation costs $3,000,
and employee training costs another
Before considering financing expenses,
the business has already committed
to bringing the machine into operation.
Now, assume the business finances
$50,000 over 5 years at a fixed annual
interest rate of 10% with monthly
payments and no additional financing
fees.
Under these assumptions, the monthly
payment would be approximately $1,062.
Over 60 payments, the business would
repay approximately $63,700,
including roughly $13,700
in interest.
Because the company financed $50,000 of
the purchase, the remaining $16,000
of initial equipment and setup costs
must come from another source.
Combined with loan repayments, the
overall cash outflow would approach
And that amount still excludes ongoing
maintenance, insurance, utilities,
taxes, and unexpected repairs.
The real economic cost of using
equipment can therefore be substantially
higher than its advertised selling
price.
This is why experienced financial
managers calculate the total cost of
ownership. They examine every
significant expense associated with
acquiring, operating, maintaining, and
eventually replacing or disposing of an
asset. A simple framework begins with
the purchase price. Add transportation,
installation, financing expenses,
insurance, maintenance, operating costs,
and expected disposal expenses.
Then subtract any estimated resale or
salvage value.
However, timing matters. Spending
$10,000 today is financially different
from spending $10,000
5 years from now.
A more advanced comparison uses
discounted cash flow to convert future
costs and benefits into present values.
Businesses should also compare financing
offers using the effective borrowing
cost, not simply the advertised interest
rate.
Origination fees, documentation charges,
payment frequency, and other financing
expenses can increase the actual cost of
borrowing.
>> [music]
>> For example, two lenders might advertise
the same interest rate, but one charges
a substantial upfront fee. The second
lender could offer a lower total
financing cost despite displaying an
identical interest rate.
A longer repayment term creates another
trade-off. It generally reduces the
monthly payment, making cash flow easier
to manage.
But when other terms remain comparable,
extending the loan can increase total
interest expenses. The objective is not
always to minimize monthly payments or
total interest individually.
The objective is to choose a financing
structure that balances overall cost,
cash flow protection, equipment
usefulness, and financial risk.
Step four, find out whether equipment
will actually pay for itself.
>> [music]
>> Imagine a printing company considering a
new automated printing machine. The
salesperson promises faster production,
fewer mistakes, and improved
profitability.
The owner feels excited because the
machine appears capable of transforming
the business.
But excitement is not a financial
calculation. Before signing the
financing agreement, the owner must
determine whether the machine will
generate enough additional cash flow to
justify its cost. Suppose the new
machine allows the company to accept
additional customer orders worth $8,000
per month. At first glance, that sounds
like a strong reason to purchase the
equipment. However, the company must pay
for additional materials, packaging,
delivery, electricity, and other
variable expenses.
If those costs total $5,000, the
additional contribution toward fixed
costs and profit is only $3,000.
Now, suppose the machine requires $500
per month in additional maintenance and
operating expenses.
That reduces the estimated incremental
monthly operating cash benefit to
approximately $2,500,
assuming no other changes.
If monthly loan payments are $1,500,
the machine could generate approximately
$1,000 of additional monthly cash after
debt service under these simplified
assumptions.
But this calculation depends on the
company actually receiving enough
orders.
The equipment's theoretical production
capacity does not guarantee customer
demand, timely customer payments, or
uninterrupted operation.
A more reliable financial analysis
examines three possible outcomes: strong
demand, normal demand, and weak demand.
This approach helps the business
understand how financing payments would
affect cash flow under different
operating conditions.
Imagine that weak demand reduces the
machine's incremental operating cash
benefit to only $900 per month.
The business would then face a $600
monthly shortfall against its $1,500
loan payment. This shortfall must be
covered by cash generated elsewhere in
the business or by existing reserves.
>> [music]
>> If the situation continues, the
equipment could gradually weaken the
company's financial position despite
improving production capacity.
>> [music]
>> Another useful calculation is the
payback period. Suppose a machine
requires an initial investment of
and generates $6,000 in annual
incremental net operating cash inflows.
Under these simplified assumptions, the
investment has a five-year payback
period, but payback alone ignores the
time value of money and cash flows
occurring after the payback date.
For major purchases, net present value
provides a stronger analytical
framework.
It compares the present value of
expected future incremental cash flows
against the initial investment using a
discount rate that reflects the
investment's risk and cost of capital.
When evaluating the equipment itself,
calculate project cash flows separately
from financing payments.
Then analyze the proposed loan or lease
to determine whether the business can
meet its contractual obligations without
creating excessive financial pressure.
This distinction helps prevent
misleading conclusions. A machine might
be an economically attractive
investment, but become dangerous when
financed with an overly aggressive
repayment schedule. Step five, protect
cash flow before signing any equipment
loan.
Consider a profitable restaurant
purchasing a new commercial
refrigeration system. The equipment
should reduce food waste and improve
kitchen efficiency.
The owner calculates the expected
savings and concludes that the purchase
makes financial sense.
But there is a hidden problem.
The restaurant receives most of its
revenue during weekends, while employee
wages, supplier invoices, rent, and
equipment payments must be paid on
specific dates throughout the month.
Even a profitable business can
experience cash shortages when money
arrives later than its financial
obligations.
Adding equipment debt increases the
number of payments the company must make
regardless of short-term sales
performance.
This is why equipment financing
decisions should begin with a cash flow
forecast.
A forecast estimates when cash will
enter the business and when it must
leave, helping owners identify periods
of potential financial pressure.
>> [music]
>> Start with the expected opening cash
balance. Add anticipated customer
collections and other cash receipts.
Then subtract supplier payments,
payroll, rent, taxes, existing debt
payments, and other operating
obligations. Next, include the proposed
equipment down payment, financing fees,
and scheduled repayments. The resulting
forecast shows how the purchase could
affect the company's cash position over
the coming months.
A 12-month forecast can reveal seasonal
pressure that a simple monthly
affordability calculation misses.
A business might comfortably afford
equipment payments during its strongest
season, but struggle when customer
demand declines.
Financial managers also examine debt
service coverage. This compares cash
flow available for debt payments against
required principal and interest payments
over a specified period.
For example, if a business generates
in annual cash flow available for debt
service and must pay $100,000
in annual debt service, its coverage
ratio is 1.5.
That means the business generates $1.50
of available cash for every dollar of
required debt service.
>> [music]
>> However, the appropriate calculation and
acceptable coverage level depend on the
lender, industry, and business
circumstances.
A coverage ratio above one indicates
that measured cash flow exceeds required
payments, but it does not guarantee
financial safety.
Businesses still need sufficient
liquidity for working capital,
unexpected expenses, and periods of weak
demand.
Before financing equipment, establish a
minimum cash reserve based on operating
expenses, revenue volatility, and the
consequences of unexpected
interruptions.
There is no universal reserve amount
suitable for every business.
The strongest financing decision is one
that remains manageable even when
business conditions become less
favorable than expected. Equipment
should support growth without forcing
the company to operate dangerously close
to an empty bank account.
Step six, avoid the hidden equipment
financing traps.
Imagine a business owner comparing two
equipment financing offers. The first
lender charges a lower interest rate,
but requires a substantial down payment.
The second offers almost no down
payment, but charges more interest and
additional fees.
The owner selects the second offer
because it requires less money
immediately. Six months later,
unexpected charges and restrictive
contract terms reveal that the agreement
is significantly more expensive than
anticipated.
This situation illustrates a common
financing mistake, focusing on the
easiest way to obtain equipment instead
of evaluating the complete financial
commitment. One major trap involves
personal guarantees. Some lenders
require business owners to accept
personal responsibility for repayment if
if business fails to meet its
obligations.
This can expose personal finances to
risks beyond the company's equipment
investment. Owners should understand the
scope of any guarantee, the events that
trigger liability, and the legal
consequences before signing.
Another trap involves blanket liens or
additional collateral requirements. A
financing agreement may give the lender
rights over assets beyond the specific
equipment being purchased.
Such provisions can restrict future
borrowing opportunities or complicate
refinancing.
A business planning additional
investments should carefully examine
whether the financing arrangement limits
its ability to obtain new capital.
Early repayment penalties deserve
attention as well. An owner might expect
to save interest by repaying a loan
ahead of schedule, only to discover that
the contract includes prepayment charges
or other restrictions.
Equipment obsolescence creates a
different problem. A company might
finance technology over 7 years, even
though the equipment is likely to become
commercially outdated after 4 years.
The business could then face several
years of payments on equipment that no
longer provides competitive value.
Financing terms should therefore reflect
the asset's realistic economic useful
life.
Maintenance responsibility is another
overlooked risk. A business owner may
assume that a leasing provider will
handle equipment repairs, even though
the contract places maintenance
obligations entirely on the business.

Borrowing capacity is not the same as
investment opportunity.

defensible financial objective. Step

like a CFO.
Imagine two companies purchasing

the same supplier.
Both receive similar financing offers,

advertised terms, while the other
carefully negotiates the agreement.
The second owner asks about alternative

assumptions.

>> For equipment that requires several

strength to survive uncertainty and
