videos.full_text: Imagine spending $50,000 on a new machine only to discover 3 months later that your business cannot afford to pay its employees. The machine works perfectly, customers are satisfied, and sales are increasing. Yet the business is running out of cash. How can buying something that improves productivity create such a serious financial problem? >> [music] >> In this masterclass, you will learn how equipment financing works, compare loans and leases, avoid costly mistakes, and make smarter financing decisions. Step one, understand why equipment financing can make or break your business. Imagine a small bakery producing 500 loaves of bread every day. The owner discovers a commercial oven that could double production. The oven costs $40,000, and the business currently has $50,000 in its bank account. >> [music] >> Buying the oven with cash seems attractive because the owner would avoid interest payments. But after spending $40,000, only $10,000 would remain available for ingredients, employee salaries, electricity, rent, and unexpected repairs. Now consider financing the oven with a loan. The business makes an initial payment of $8,000 and finances the remaining $32,000. Although the loan creates interest expenses, the bakery keeps significantly more cash available for daily operations. This example reveals the first important principle of equipment financing. The objective is not simply to purchase equipment at the lowest possible price. The objective is to acquire productive assets while protecting the financial health of the business. Equipment financing allows companies to obtain machinery, vehicles, computers, manufacturing systems, medical devices, restaurant equipment, and other business assets without necessarily paying their entire purchase price immediately. However, financing does not automatically make equipment affordable. A business can borrow money to purchase an asset and still experience serious financial problems if the equipment fails to generate enough economic value. Consider a construction company financing an expensive excavator. If the excavator remains unused for several weeks every month, the company must continue making loan payments even though the machine generates little or no revenue during those periods. This creates a dangerous mismatch between financial obligations and actual business activity. Equipment payments are usually predictable, but the revenue generated by that equipment may fluctuate because of seasonal demand, customer cancellations, or unexpected market conditions. Successful equipment financing therefore requires understanding three separate questions. Can the business obtain financing? Can the business afford the payments? And will the equipment generate enough value to justify the entire investment? These questions may sound similar, but they produce very different answers. A lender might approve a large equipment loan based on financial history, collateral, and creditworthiness. That approval does not guarantee that borrowing the money represents a good business decision. The smartest business owners treat equipment financing as a capital allocation decision. They compare the expected benefits of the equipment against its complete financial cost while considering what other opportunities might exist for the same money. Step two, equipment loans versus leasing. Choose the right financing structure. Suppose a delivery company needs five new vehicles. Purchasing them outright would consume most of its available cash. The owner approaches two financing providers and receives two different proposals, an equipment loan and an equipment lease. An equipment loan generally allows the business to purchase the vehicles using borrowed money. The company makes scheduled payments consisting of principal and interest. Depending on the agreement, the lender may hold a security interest in the vehicles until the loan is repaid. A lease works differently. Instead of purchasing the equipment through a traditional loan, the business obtains the right to use it for an agreed period. Ownership, purchase options, maintenance responsibilities, and end-of-term obligations depend on the specific lease contract. Imagine the company expects to use its delivery vehicles for 8 years. Purchasing through a loan could make financial sense because the business intends to retain the vehicles long after the financing period ends. Now, imagine a technology company that replaces its computers every 3 years. Leasing might be attractive because the business wants regular access to updated equipment without managing the long-term ownership of rapidly aging technology. However, leasing is not always cheaper. A lease with low monthly payments can become expensive when additional fees, mandatory services, purchase options, or end-of-term charges are included. Some leases also contain strict rules about equipment usage, physical condition, mileage, maintenance, or early termination. These restrictions can create costs that business owners overlook when comparing advertised monthly payments. Another important consideration is the difference between equipment ownership and equipment usage. A company may need a machine to generate revenue, but that does not necessarily mean owning the machine provides the greatest financial benefit. For example, a landscaping company might need specialized equipment only during certain months. Renting that equipment for specific projects could cost less than maintaining year-round financing payments, insurance, storage, and repairs. Business owners should compare purchasing, financing, leasing, and renting before committing to any agreement. Each option changes the timing of cash payments, the allocation of risk, and the company's financial flexibility. Tax and accounting treatment also matters. Loan interest, depreciation, lease expenses, and recognized lease liabilities may be treated differently depending on local tax laws, accounting standards, and contract terms. The important lesson is simple. Never select a financing arrangement only because its monthly payment appears affordable. Evaluate the complete agreement, including ownership rights, long-term costs, contractual restrictions, and the expected useful life of the equipment. Step three, calculate the true cost of equipment financing. Imagine a manufacturing company purchasing a machine advertised for $60,000. The lender offers financing with manageable monthly payments, and the owner immediately assumes the machine will cost approximately $60,000. But the purchase price is only the beginning. The business must also pay for transportation, installation, employee training, insurance, maintenance, electricity, and possibly modifications to its production facility. Suppose transportation costs $2,000, installation costs $3,000, and employee training costs another $1,000. Before considering financing expenses, the business has already committed $66,000 to bringing the machine into operation. Now, assume the business finances $50,000 over 5 years at a fixed annual interest rate of 10% with monthly payments and no additional financing fees. Under these assumptions, the monthly payment would be approximately $1,062. Over 60 payments, the business would repay approximately $63,700, including roughly $13,700 in interest. Because the company financed $50,000 of the purchase, the remaining $16,000 of initial equipment and setup costs must come from another source. Combined with loan repayments, the overall cash outflow would approach $80,000. And that amount still excludes ongoing maintenance, insurance, utilities, taxes, and unexpected repairs. The real economic cost of using equipment can therefore be substantially higher than its advertised selling price. This is why experienced financial managers calculate the total cost of ownership. They examine every significant expense associated with acquiring, operating, maintaining, and eventually replacing or disposing of an asset. A simple framework begins with the purchase price. Add transportation, installation, financing expenses, insurance, maintenance, operating costs, and expected disposal expenses. Then subtract any estimated resale or salvage value. However, timing matters. Spending $10,000 today is financially different from spending $10,000 5 years from now. A more advanced comparison uses discounted cash flow to convert future costs and benefits into present values. Businesses should also compare financing offers using the effective borrowing cost, not simply the advertised interest rate. Origination fees, documentation charges, payment frequency, and other financing expenses can increase the actual cost of borrowing. >> [music] >> For example, two lenders might advertise the same interest rate, but one charges a substantial upfront fee. The second lender could offer a lower total financing cost despite displaying an identical interest rate. A longer repayment term creates another trade-off. It generally reduces the monthly payment, making cash flow easier to manage. But when other terms remain comparable, extending the loan can increase total interest expenses. The objective is not always to minimize monthly payments or total interest individually. The objective is to choose a financing structure that balances overall cost, cash flow protection, equipment usefulness, and financial risk. Step four, find out whether equipment will actually pay for itself. >> [music] >> Imagine a printing company considering a new automated printing machine. The salesperson promises faster production, fewer mistakes, and improved profitability. The owner feels excited because the machine appears capable of transforming the business. But excitement is not a financial calculation. Before signing the financing agreement, the owner must determine whether the machine will generate enough additional cash flow to justify its cost. Suppose the new machine allows the company to accept additional customer orders worth $8,000 per month. At first glance, that sounds like a strong reason to purchase the equipment. However, the company must pay for additional materials, packaging, delivery, electricity, and other variable expenses. If those costs total $5,000, the additional contribution toward fixed costs and profit is only $3,000. Now, suppose the machine requires $500 per month in additional maintenance and operating expenses. That reduces the estimated incremental monthly operating cash benefit to approximately $2,500, assuming no other changes. If monthly loan payments are $1,500, the machine could generate approximately $1,000 of additional monthly cash after debt service under these simplified assumptions. But this calculation depends on the company actually receiving enough orders. The equipment's theoretical production capacity does not guarantee customer demand, timely customer payments, or uninterrupted operation. A more reliable financial analysis examines three possible outcomes: strong demand, normal demand, and weak demand. This approach helps the business understand how financing payments would affect cash flow under different operating conditions. Imagine that weak demand reduces the machine's incremental operating cash benefit to only $900 per month. The business would then face a $600 monthly shortfall against its $1,500 loan payment. This shortfall must be covered by cash generated elsewhere in the business or by existing reserves. >> [music] >> If the situation continues, the equipment could gradually weaken the company's financial position despite improving production capacity. >> [music] >> Another useful calculation is the payback period. Suppose a machine requires an initial investment of $30,000 and generates $6,000 in annual incremental net operating cash inflows. Under these simplified assumptions, the investment has a five-year payback period, but payback alone ignores the time value of money and cash flows occurring after the payback date. For major purchases, net present value provides a stronger analytical framework. It compares the present value of expected future incremental cash flows against the initial investment using a discount rate that reflects the investment's risk and cost of capital. When evaluating the equipment itself, calculate project cash flows separately from financing payments. Then analyze the proposed loan or lease to determine whether the business can meet its contractual obligations without creating excessive financial pressure. This distinction helps prevent misleading conclusions. A machine might be an economically attractive investment, but become dangerous when financed with an overly aggressive repayment schedule. Step five, protect cash flow before signing any equipment loan. Consider a profitable restaurant purchasing a new commercial refrigeration system. The equipment should reduce food waste and improve kitchen efficiency. The owner calculates the expected savings and concludes that the purchase makes financial sense. But there is a hidden problem. The restaurant receives most of its revenue during weekends, while employee wages, supplier invoices, rent, and equipment payments must be paid on specific dates throughout the month. Even a profitable business can experience cash shortages when money arrives later than its financial obligations. Adding equipment debt increases the number of payments the company must make regardless of short-term sales performance. This is why equipment financing decisions should begin with a cash flow forecast. A forecast estimates when cash will enter the business and when it must leave, helping owners identify periods of potential financial pressure. >> [music] >> Start with the expected opening cash balance. Add anticipated customer collections and other cash receipts. Then subtract supplier payments, payroll, rent, taxes, existing debt payments, and other operating obligations. Next, include the proposed equipment down payment, financing fees, and scheduled repayments. The resulting forecast shows how the purchase could affect the company's cash position over the coming months. A 12-month forecast can reveal seasonal pressure that a simple monthly affordability calculation misses. A business might comfortably afford equipment payments during its strongest season, but struggle when customer demand declines. Financial managers also examine debt service coverage. This compares cash flow available for debt payments against required principal and interest payments over a specified period. For example, if a business generates $150,000 in annual cash flow available for debt service and must pay $100,000 in annual debt service, its coverage ratio is 1.5. That means the business generates $1.50 of available cash for every dollar of required debt service. >> [music] >> However, the appropriate calculation and acceptable coverage level depend on the lender, industry, and business circumstances. A coverage ratio above one indicates that measured cash flow exceeds required payments, but it does not guarantee financial safety. Businesses still need sufficient liquidity for working capital, unexpected expenses, and periods of weak demand. Before financing equipment, establish a minimum cash reserve based on operating expenses, revenue volatility, and the consequences of unexpected interruptions. There is no universal reserve amount suitable for every business. The strongest financing decision is one that remains manageable even when business conditions become less favorable than expected. Equipment should support growth without forcing the company to operate dangerously close to an empty bank account. Step six, avoid the hidden equipment financing traps. Imagine a business owner comparing two equipment financing offers. The first lender charges a lower interest rate, but requires a substantial down payment. The second offers almost no down payment, but charges more interest and additional fees. The owner selects the second offer because it requires less money immediately. Six months later, unexpected charges and restrictive contract terms reveal that the agreement is significantly more expensive than anticipated. This situation illustrates a common financing mistake, focusing on the easiest way to obtain equipment instead of evaluating the complete financial commitment. One major trap involves personal guarantees. Some lenders require business owners to accept personal responsibility for repayment if if business fails to meet its obligations. This can expose personal finances to risks beyond the company's equipment investment. Owners should understand the scope of any guarantee, the events that trigger liability, and the legal consequences before signing. Another trap involves blanket liens or additional collateral requirements. A financing agreement may give the lender rights over assets beyond the specific equipment being purchased. Such provisions can restrict future borrowing opportunities or complicate refinancing. A business planning additional investments should carefully examine whether the financing arrangement limits its ability to obtain new capital. Early repayment penalties deserve attention as well. An owner might expect to save interest by repaying a loan ahead of schedule, only to discover that the contract includes prepayment charges or other restrictions. Equipment obsolescence creates a different problem. A company might finance technology over 7 years, even though the equipment is likely to become commercially outdated after 4 years. The business could then face several years of payments on equipment that no longer provides competitive value. Financing terms should therefore reflect the asset's realistic economic useful life. Maintenance responsibility is another overlooked risk. A business owner may assume that a leasing provider will handle equipment repairs, even though the contract places maintenance obligations entirely on the business. Insurance requirements can also increase expenses. Some financing agreements require specific coverage levels, approved insurers, or additional protection for the lender's financial interest. Currency exposure matters for international businesses. Financing equipment in a foreign currency can become expensive when exchange rates move unfavorably, especially when business revenue is earned in a different currency. Avoid financing unnecessary equipment simply because credit is available. Borrowing capacity is not the same as investment opportunity. Every financing agreement should support a clear operational need and a defensible financial objective. Step seven, negotiate equipment financing like a CFO. Imagine two companies purchasing identical manufacturing machines from the same supplier. Both receive similar financing offers, but one owner immediately accepts the advertised terms, while the other carefully negotiates the agreement. The second owner asks about alternative repayment periods, down payment requirements, interest rates, financing fees, and the possibility of aligning payments with seasonal business revenue. Even modest improvements in these terms can influence total borrowing costs and monthly cash flow. Negotiation should therefore focus on the complete financing structure, rather than only the interest rate. Begin by requesting detailed proposals from multiple qualified financing providers. Compare loan amounts, repayment schedules, fees, collateral requirements, guarantees, and total expected payments using consistent assumptions. A lower interest rate does not automatically produce the best agreement. A larger down payment reduces the amount financed and can lower interest expenses, but it also removes cash that could support inventory, payroll, marketing, or emergency reserves. A smaller down payment preserves liquidity, but increases the outstanding financing balance. However, avoid allowing a supplier's financing promotion to distract from the equipment's actual price. The most effective negotiation begins before the business urgently needs equipment. Owners with sufficient cash reserves and multiple financing options are often better positioned to reject unfavorable terms. Step eight. Build a long-term equipment financing strategy. Imagine a manufacturing business that purchases equipment whenever production becomes difficult. Every year, the owner reacts to urgent problems by borrowing money for another machine. Eventually, the company operates several expensive machines with different repayment schedules. Some equipment is highly productive, while other assets remain underused. Management identifies which machines are essential, which assets are approaching replacement, and which purchases could deliver measurable financial benefits. Instead of making isolated purchasing decisions, the business ranks equipment investments according to expected returns, operational importance, urgency, risk, and the cash required. This approach turns equipment financing into a structured capital budgeting process. These reviews improve future decisions because they replace assumptions with real operating evidence. metadata.author: Neil.Finance
metadata.shortDescription:
Learn Equipment Finance Brokering
If you're serious about learning how equipment finance actually works from the lender side, watch the free breakdown:

https://equipmentfinancemastery.com/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=equipment_finance

Most people think banks are in the business of lending money.
The reality is they're in the business of managing risk.
Every day, thousands of small business owners apply for financing and get declined—not because they're bad business owners, but because they don't fit the bank's lending criteria.
That's where equipment finance brokers come in.

In this video, I explain:
✅ Why equipment finance brokering exists
✅ The hidden gap between lenders and business owners
✅ Why demand for alternative financing continues to grow
✅ How brokers create value without lending their own money
✅ Why equipment finance is one of the most overlooked industries today✅ The skill that can create opportunities for years to come
If you've ever wondered how equipment finance works or why brokers play such an important role in the lending ecosystem, this video will give you a completely different perspective.

About Neil Chohan
Neil Chohan is a Chartered Accountant with over a decade of experience in equipment finance. Unlike most educators in the industry, Neil teaches from the lender side of the desk—showing brokers what actually happens behind the scenes when deals are reviewed, approved, or declined.

metadata.title: How Brokers Get Paid Points, Fees & Splits
metadata.author: Commercial Loan Broker Institute
metadata.shortDescription:
How do commercial loan brokers actually get paid, and what does a "point" on a loan really mean?

This video breaks down the full stack of broker compensation: points (1 point = 1% of the loan amount), the packaging or processing fees you can charge, referral splits you control, correspondent yield you can earn once a lender trusts you, and how one client can pay you multiple times across a capital stack.

Using a standard million-dollar commercial loan as the example, it walks through why 2 points is $20,000 at closing, why the biggest point number isn't always the biggest check, and why your income scales with deal size instead of hours worked. If you already know brokering can pay well and want to understand exactly how the money works, this is the breakdown.

Chapters:
00:00 Layer 1: How Points Really Work
02:19 Why the Biggest Point Number Can Lose
04:54 The Fee That Screens Out Tire Kickers
07:08 What You Keep When You Own the Brokerage
08:34 The Backend Payday: Becoming a Correspondent
10:17 Broker Compensation is Determined by This
12:02 The Full Earnings Stack

Watch next - 12 Cheat Codes for Business Loan Brokers: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4a-yaXaypD0&t=5s

Want to see how CLBI trains brokers to build this kind of income? Start here:https://commercialloanbrokerinstitute.com/

The Commercial Loan Broker Institute has launched and supports more than 500 commercial loan brokerages nationwide, and the brokers it has trained have placed well over $2 billion in funding. CLBI publishes educational content for people who want to start, operate, and grow a commercial loan brokerage. Subscribe for weekly training on the business.

Disclosure: This video is for educational and informational purposes only and is not financial, legal, or investment advice. It does not guarantee or imply any specific earnings or results; individual outcomes depend on effort, experience, market conditions, and other factors, and many participants earn less or nothing at all.

#CommercialLoanBroker #CommercialLending #LoanBrokerIncome

At COBI, [music] we built and we run our own active lender network. Hundreds of lenders our brokers are using to place deals, and those are the kind of relationships you step into and can grow into a correspondent relationship over time. And correspondent pricing, of course, it varies by lender and program, but it's a real upgrade, a real upside in how much a single deal is going to pay. And broker compensation is also determined by this fact. A single client almost never needs just one loan. Take a real estate investor who's buying a property to fix, to rent out, to hold as part of their portfolio. First, you have acquisition financing to buy it. Then, you have a rehab or construction facility for renovating [music] the property. Then, you have permanent financing that refinances and pays off the short-term debt once the building has been stabilized and rented out. That's three financing events, three paydays, all on one property. Or you have a business owner who's opening a second location. They need a real estate loan for the space, equipment financing for the build-out, say it's a restaurant, a commercial kitchen. They need the furniture and fixtures, and they have working capital to carry that location >> [music] >> through its first few months until it stabilizes and is cash flowing well. And on a more complex play, a deal might stack senior [music] debt with a layer of mezzanine financing, or even bring in a second lender who's comfortable [music] taking a higher risk position behind the first. And then you have clients that pay you again and again and again as they grow. So, this is a stack of earnings that you build out and it compounds over time, over deals. Learn Equipment Finance Brokering From The Lender Side

Watch the free Equipment Finance Mastery breakdown:👉 

https://equipmentfinancemastery.com/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=equipment_finance

Most brokers think lenders approve deals based on credit scores alone.
They're wrong.

After spending over 10 years on the lender side of equipment finance, I've reviewed thousands of submissions and seen firsthand why some deals get approved quickly while others get declined.

In this video, I break down exactly what lenders are looking for when evaluating an equipment finance deal, including:

✔️ How lenders assess risk
✔️ Why some deals get approved faster than others
✔️ The biggest mistake brokers make when submitting deals
✔️ How lender selection impacts approvals
✔️ What new brokers should focus on first
✔️ What happens behind the scenes after a deal is submitted

If you're an equipment finance broker—or thinking about becoming one—understanding how lenders think can dramatically improve your results.

videos.full_text: asset-based Lending asset-based lending abl originated in the U.S it is a system of financing that uses assets such as equipment or company inventory also known as stock as security against the loan whereas factoring uses unpaid invoices as collateral against prepayments on money due from invoices asset-based lending spreads its net wider to secure collateral often big operations will use a factoring facility in conjunction with asset-based Lending difference between invoice factoring and asset-based lending the key difference between these two forms of financing Arrangements is that an invoice financier involved in factoring will buy unpaid invoices in the case of abl the assets are not bought instead security is taken against the assets in the event of bad debt a company will be obliged to sell the asset to cover the debt the asset will be insured and the benefits of the insurance policy assigned to the lender inventory or stock a company's inventory consists of items that are ready for sale it also covers materials that can be turned into inventory stock financing One stock is used as Surety against the loan it is called stock financing in order to qualify for this type of financing a company will have to produce detailed and up-to-date stock reports it is not just the amount of stock that needs to be considered but also the quality of the stock the financier will assess how easy it is to sell stock high-tech seasonal and bespoke products might not be easy to sell to protect the assets used in asset-based lending a financier can either take legal charge of the asset or just floating charge of the asset the first means the financier has control of the asset the second means a company can still use and sell the asset as in normal trading conditions if the company stops trading a financier will move from floating charge of an asset to legal charge of an asset how much can be raised against stock this is the key question for the company offering asset based Lending an expert will assess how easy it would be to sell the stock if the borrower defaults included in these calculations are storage and transport costs these types of stock evaluations are made annually to dig deeper the financier will place retentions against stock based on a number of criteria retentions refers to money withheld and not available for financing purposes here is a list detailing these retentions one damage stock no funding will be available against damaged stock in the event that the stock is badly damaged an insurance claim will be made with the funds going to the lender two work in progress unfinished inventory still counts as stock but a financier will place a retention on these items free slow moving stock a financier will usually Place retentions against slow moving stock 4. short shelf life items with a short shelf life are not suitable for asset based Lending five obsolete aged and out of date stock obsolete could refer to stock that is no longer relevant age refers to items that have been in the warehouse for a long time that are not looking likely to be sold any item that is labeled out of date is also subject to retentions six selling costs the annual evaluations of stock will assess the overheads involved in selling stocks such as bills for warehousing transporting and electricity these costs will be accounted for in retentions seven retention of title this refers to a situation where the supplier maintains legal ownership of the parts for materials it is supplied until its client has made a sale and paid off its supplier this type of stock is subject to retention eight unsecured creditors in the UK If a company goes into liquidation then the administrators will have to set aside stock that can be used to pay off unsecured creditors this can be up to six hundred thousand pounds retention will be made to cover this possibility costs of stock Finance when a financier sets up a stock facility he or she will set out a number of fees administration fee this will be the cost for administering the finance facility and may include the costs of the stock audits interest on the amount borrowed the interest rate will be higher than the central bank's interest rates it will also be higher than the discount charge that features in factoring costs valuation fees this is the cost of assessing the value of the stock and assessments over things such as how easy it would be to sell stock in the event there was a default in loan repayments availability as with invoice finance a calculation is made to show the amount of money that is available to be borrowed firstly the total stock value is assessed and then deductions are made for out of date damaged and obsolete stock deductions are made for the costs of selling stock and deductions are made for unsecured creditors after deductions a stock financier will set a percentage for how much he or she will lend against the remaining stock value it is typically between 50 and 80 percent this final figure is the availability stock Finance is invoice Finance the availability percentage is normally higher for invoice Finance than for stock Finance collecting debt from unpaid invoices is considered less expensive and less risky than selling stock moreover evaluations are more accurate with invoice finance a stock financier will be basing their decisions on monthly stock reports it can be up to four weeks out of date another worry for a stock financier will be the quality of the remaining stock for sale a failing company will quite often sell their best stock first to deal with shortfalls in cash flow borrowing against machinery and property asset-based lending is also possible using plant machinery and commercial property normally loans against Machinery are repaid over three years loans against property are repaid over 7 to 15 years

Growing your business means taking advantage of every opportunity, but you can’t always do that if you don’t have the cash flow to support your growth. By forming a relationship with an asset-based lender or factoring organization, you gain a financial partner that can leverage your receivables to provide you with the cash to reach your full potential.

metadata.title: Asset-Based Lending and Borrowing Base Facilities
metadata.author: Financely Group
metadata.shortDescription:
Asset-based lending uses eligible accounts receivable, inventory, equipment and other collateral to support a revolving credit facility. This video covers borrowing-base calculations, advance rates, collateral monitoring, covenants and lender underwriting.

Financely structures asset-based lending and working capital facilities for established companies with bankable collateral and recurring financing requirements.

https://financely.io

#AssetBasedLending #ABL #BorrowingBase #WorkingCapital #CorporateFinance #PrivateCredit

segments.text: Welcome to this video on asset-based
lending.
>> [music]
>> We will explore how balance sheet assets
like receivables and inventory are
converted into a collateral base [music]
to determine revolving cash
availability. Profitable companies often
face liquidity gaps [music] due to
timing. Cash is paid upfront for
operations, while revenue is trapped in
receivables. Asset-based [music] lending
offers a solution by monetizing these
assets before collections are finalized,
supporting growth and seasonal needs. An
asset-based [music] revolver focuses on
collateral quality with availability
that fluctuates based on a formula. In
contrast, a cash flow loan is typically
based on enterprise value [music] and
EBITDA with a fixed commitment and
periodic compliance testing. The
borrowing base calculation [music]
involves multiplying eligible
receivables and inventory by their
respective advance rates, then
subtracting specific reserves. The final
net availability [music] is determined
by the lesser of the borrowing base or
total commitments. Not all invoices are
[music] eligible collateral. To be
included, an invoice must be legally
valid, creditworthy, within aging

segments.text: [Music]
Hi, I'm Elliot McKillrath, product
strategist for Alternative Credit and
PIMCO's UK team. You may have heard
about assetbased finance and wondered
what it's all about. Let me help
demystify the exciting evolution in
private
credit.
Assetbased finance or ABF for short
refers to any kind of private lending
that occurs outside of traditional
corporate lending or commercial real
estate markets. It's also referred to as
assetbacked finance or specialty
finance. ABF provides critical funding
across the global real economy and
categories you interact with daily. In
fact, it's what enables us to finance a
car purchase or obtain a home mortgage,
take a flight on holiday, attend
university, or purchase goods on a
credit card. From an investing
perspective, ABF loans are often secured
by hard assets as collateral, which
typically support the cash flows of the
investment itself. This could be a
house, a car, a plane, or financial
guarantees like business receivables and
intellectual property rights such as
royalties, just to name a
few. At PIMCO, we estimate the ABF
market to be over 20
trillion. Much of this fixed income-like
universe is held by banks or pulled into
securitizations.
But a major shift towards private
markets is underway, which we believe is
creating a multi- trillion opportunity
set for alternative lenders in the
coming
years. PIMCO has been actively investing
in various forms of ABF for decades.
With our fixed income DNA crucial in
making us one of the largest and most
experienced investors in this
space, diverse and growing, we consider
assetbased finance to be the next
frontier of private credit. We've
mentioned some examples already, but at
a high level, the ABF universe can be
broken down into three main categories.
Consumer, non-consumer, and mortgages.
The consumer category includes consumer
orientated credit such as auto loans,
credit card receivables, student loans,
or other types of personal loans.
Non-consumer areas are more business

Let me help demystify the exciting evolution in private credit. Assetbased finance or ABF for short refers to any kind of private lending that occurs outside of traditional corporate lending or commercial real estate markets. It's also referred to as assetbacked finance or specialty finance. ABF provides critical funding across the global real economy and categories you interact with daily. In fact, it's what enables us to finance a car purchase or obtain a home mortgage, take a flight on holiday, attend university, or purchase goods on a credit card. From an investing perspective, ABF loans are often secured by hard assets as collateral, which typically support the cash flows of the investment itself. This could be a house, a car, a plane, or financial guarantees like business receivables and intellectual property rights such as royalties, just to name a few. At PIMCO, we estimate the ABF market to be over 20 trillion. Much of this fixed income-like universe is held by banks or pulled into securitizations. But a major shift towards private markets is underway, which we believe is creating a multi- trillion opportunity set for alternative lenders in the coming years. PIMCO has been actively investing in various forms of ABF for decades. With our fixed income DNA crucial in making us one of the largest and most experienced investors in this space, diverse and growing, we consider assetbased finance to be the next frontier of private credit. We've mentioned some examples already, but at a high level, the ABF universe can be broken down into three main categories. Consumer, non-consumer, and mortgages. The consumer category includes consumer orientated credit such as auto loans, credit card receivables, student loans, or other types of personal loans. Non-consumer areas are more business related, including aircraft leasing, royalty streams such as music, or heavy equipment finance such as manufacturing equipment. Finally, the mortgage category includes residential mortgages in the UK, Europe, and the US, as well as home improvement loans. As you can see, ABF is a highly diverse credit market. However, most investors remain underexposed to this asset class, particularly in private markets. We think ABF is attractive for investors today for three key reasons. First and foremost, ABF has a target-rich, rapidly expanding opportunity set that we believe offers a compelling risk return profile. Relatively high barriers to entry mean valuations today are attractive relative to historical levels. At the same time, ABF's defensive qualities offer potential downside mitigation as ABF loans are usually secured by physical assets, providing an often senior secured investment profile. The second key advantage is a portfolio diversification. Private credit has matured in recent years and in particular corporate direct lending has seen elevated competition with most private credit investors heavily allocated in this area. Adding private ABF to a portfolio could potentially be highly complimentary to investors credit allocation given the idiosyncratic lowcorrelated nature to other parts of private credit. ABF loans also tend to be paid back more quickly due to amatizing payment schedules, meaning there is less guesswork on whether you will be repaid. This adds yet another dimension of diversification relative to corporate direct lending where coupon payments are interest only and a loan is only repaid at the end of term, meaning investors often have to guess how well a company will be doing several years in the future. Lastly, ABF has a very compelling entry point today. Stress in the US banking sector and tighter regulations have created large liquidity gaps left by banks pulling back. Private lenders like PIMCO are stepping in to fill that gap. Partnering with banks looking to optimize their balance sheets by selling assets or seeking other partnerships. metadata.title: Who Is the SBA 504 Loan For?
metadata.author: CDC Small Business Finance
metadata.shortDescription:
🏢 The SBA 504 loan is designed for for-profit, owner-occupied businesses that want to invest in commercial real estate or large equipment. If your business will occupy at least 51% of the property, this loan could be the perfect fit for you!

The SBA 504 loan is all about:
 ✅ Supporting business growth
 ✅ Creating jobs in the community
 ✅ Helping businesses in underestimated markets
 ✅ Providing long-term rate protection
 ✅ Building equity and long-term wealth through property ownership

⏱️ Take two minutes to learn how the SBA 504 loan helps business owners secure the space they need—and how we guide you every step of the way.

Don’t qualify for an SBA 504 loan? No problem. As part of the Momentus Capital-branded family, we have other financing options to help you grow:
➡️Impower(504 Alternative Commercial Real Estate Loan) : https://momentusdirectcapital.com/impower/
➡️SBA Community Advantage loan program: https://cdcloans.com/small-business-loans/ 

✉️ Still need help? Talk to one of our loan experts and take the next step toward growth! https://cdcloans.com/contact/

VIDEOS TO WATCH NEXT:
 👉 What Can I Use an SBA 504 Loan For? https://youtu.be/hK_Qb2vkxp8?si=hJ9v__LrvzrKAPNy
 👉 Buying a commercial property vs leasing - benefits of an SBA 504 loan - https://youtu.be/EHqsNDzicIo?si=7DtUbRZKFcl0Euhb

VISIT OUR SBA 504 PAGE FOR THESE FEATURES:
 🔢 SBA 504 Rates (updated daily)
 ❓ SBA 504 FAQ
 ⚖️ Compare the SBA 504 vs. SBA 7(a)
 🌐 https://cdcloans.com/commercial-real-estate-loan/

The Momentus Capital branded family of organizations is transforming how capital and investments flow into communities to provide people access to the capital and opportunities they deserve. We are working to reinvent traditional financial systems by offering a continuum of financial, knowledge, and social capital to help local leaders build strong communities and create generational wealth. This includes a comprehensive package of loan products, impact investment opportunities, training and business advising programs, and technology services that advance locally-led solutions.

The Momentus Capital branded family of organizations includes Capital Impact Partners and CDC Small Business Finance, as well as their affiliates, Momentus Direct Capital, and Momentus Securities (an SEC-registered broker-dealer and FINRA/MSRB/SIPC member).

Our Continuum of Capital provides a variety of loans and services that can support your organization or business to grow:

•Commercial Real Estate
•SBA-Alternative Commercial Real Estate (Impower)
•Impact Investments
•Community Development Real Estate
•Community Development Working Capital
•Small Business Community Advantage
•Small Business Microloans
•Training and Business Advising 

Leveraging more than 80 years of combined experience, more than $3 billion in assets under management, and strong community engagement, we have delivered $24 billion in financing, created and preserved 293,000 jobs, and served 13,800 small businesses and 5.5 million people across their history.

With headquarters in Arlington, Virginia, and San Diego, California, Momentus Capital operates nationally with a focus on larger urban areas and cities in Arizona, California, Georgia, Michigan, Nevada, New York, Texas, and the Washington D.C. metro area.

Learn More:

•        Momentus Capital - https://momentuscap.org/

•        Capital Impact - https://www.capitalimpact.org/

•        CDC Small Business - https://cdcloans.com/

You can use an SBA 504 loan for more than buying existing real estate:

This loan works for a wide range of property types, including:
 🏭 Industrial & manufacturing buildings
 🏪 Retail spaces & restaurants

videos.full_text: So today we're going to be talking about how to unlock capital that entrepreneurs can use to purchase and to grow strong businesses. And when most people hear SBA 7A, they think about the standard governmentbacked small business loan. But in the hands of the right buyer, the right bank, the right broker, 7A can become one of the most powerful tools in the acquisition market. It can help take a letter of intent and turn it into a real closing and create a completely new future for an entrepreneur. My guest today is Ryan Collins from Trillant Bank. Ryan specializes in helping buyers and advisors navigate SBA 7A loans in the M&A space. And that makes him exactly the kind of guest that we love talking with on this show because this is where theory meets reality with a real practitioner. Ryan is the 2025 Coleman SBA BDO of the year, 2025 Nagle Top Originator, and the number one top producing M&A lending or loan originator for the highest volume SBA credit union in the entire country. Ryan, it's great to have you today. >> Yeah, thank you, Shane. I I very much appreciate that uh that introduction. >> Yeah. Yeah, it's wonderful to be chatting. And for somebody listening who knows the SBA loan environment at a high level, but they're not deeply knowledgeable of how to use it in the M&A space. Can you give us some quick context? Why does a 7A work so well for acquisitions? >> Yeah, so I think to start with, you kind of alluded to it in your introduction, but these SBA loans [clears throat] Uh there's a lot of there can be a lot of misconception around them in that they're difficult, they take forever, there's a million hoops to jump through. And the short answer is it doesn't have to be when you're working with the right partners. That can be a very sync and and very clear process. But, you know, if you have a lender that doesn't quite know what they're doing or maybe an attorney that doesn't specialize in M&A um or there's some hiccup in financial due diligence, that's where you can start to see roadblocks. But when working with the correct partners all throughout, that's where you can have a very clean and clean and sync process. And so um the other thing I want to kind of lead with is that further alluding to some misconception within the program is that the SBA like any government program and like most institutions have a standard operating procedure. The SOP that is the minimum requirement that is that is needed for an SBA loan. Every lender has discretion on top of that. So while the SOP may say minimum debt service of 1.15 times, for example, a lot of lenders are not going to be at that minimum. And so as you're navigating a a um acquisition opportunity, if you're being met with resistance, I always recommend to buyers um and ask the question of is this your institution's policy or is this an SBA procedure or requirement? Um I think a lot of times the SBA can get a bad rap and be used as a scapegoat. Truthfully, I I did it early in my career because nobody likes telling people no. It's just we're humans. So, it's a lot easier to say, "Ah, well, that's not SBA eligible or whatever." But it might not be the case. They just don't want to. A lender just may not want to elude to our bank doesn't do that because another bank might. So, um if you I like to be very clear when working with partners both on buyer and sell um sales side in saying look this is SBA eligible but we wouldn't do this because of 123 or something to that nature. >> And you've worked with other SBA lenders prior to Trillant. How much variation do you really see between one SBA lender and another? >> So, surprisingly a lot. Um, which is funny because it's still the same governing body. It's still the same loan program. Um, but, uh, different institutions just have different flavor. Um, and it can be industry based, it can be locationbased. Um, it can even be use of proceeds based. You know, some some institutions like construction loans where it's, you know, you're constructing a new facility or whatever. Some do not. Some don't like debt refinances. Some are like, "Yep, let's clean up that balance sheet." So, it's uh there there can be a lot of variety in uh in lender appetite, which is good. I mean, it's necessary because kind of back to what I was saying before with the SOP being the bare minimum and every lender differing from there. If we all liked million-doll M&A transactions that had 1.4 times cash flow, well, everybody's doing those deals. So, we need somebody that's going to do, you know, your groundup construction or your non-franchise startup. Um, it, you said it in the intro, but the SBA 7A loan can be, you know, really is a multi-tool for business funding. And so while I am focused in on, you know, financing changes of ownership from from $1 to $5 million doesn't mean that it can't be used for, you know, buying equipment for $100,000 or refinancing your debt or, you know, all the other use of proceeds. And so um it is is to a borrower's benefit to have many institutions within the environment because everybody's going to have a little bit different flare on on an opportunity. >> Wonderful. So, let's start at the beginning here and look at it through the lens of a potential buyer who's getting a look first look at a target business. What are and they're thinking about leveraging a 7A for the financing? What are their first go or no go questions that they should be thinking about right up front? >> Yeah. So, something that I talk with buyers a lot about just from the jump is if you anybody that's read a SIM or an offering memo or whatever, there typically is a lot of detail and a lot of description about growth opportunities. So I always raise my hand at that and say that's great but why are you paying for the growth opportunity that you are going to have to do? And two, why didn't they do it? And there's maybe reasonable answers to both. But just take a step back and pause and say, well, it's got all this growth potential. Why are you going to pay for the potential that you're going to do? So, um I like to from the jump just push pause there and have them think about that because, um sometimes it's easy like, well, they're going to add another sales individual. And you are the one to How about disqualifiers? So, it's a fine balance of putting enough in there to make it palatable to both a seller and a lender, but you're not leaving a lot of ambiguity up there for the same parties to infer what it is. And maybe they end up looking the same, but it's like, why did it take us four weeks and six other versions to get here when this buyer was like, here we are. So there's definitely there's definitely a trick to that. Part of that is use utilizing good partners, good parties, so a good M&A attorney to help you.
