The other two would be um like in a licensed or home services business. If the buyer is not an individual that can uh facilitate licensing, I always ask people if not you then who? And then whoever that person is, make a plan around them. Is it the seller? Okay, they need to carry equity. Is it an existing GM? Okay. Are you going to do a rev share or equity or profit share or anniversary bonuses, employment contract? There's a lot that you can do. Is it a outside third party that's coming in? Okay, maybe that's fine, but what state are you in? Because that might might mean they need ownership. So, there can be a lot there can be a lot there, but it's just thinking through the specifics of the opportunity to kind of try and forecast of like, all right, well, we're going to have to get a license prior to close, so how are we doing that? >> So, you're really thinking of how the structure can be set up in the LOI, whether it's going to be the seller notes, earnouts, whatever it might be, in order to uh set the entire transaction up as a win from day one. And how do you think about seller transition support? Is that something that you're regularly looking for? Is it really on a case-byase basis that is primarily determined by the level of experience of the buyer? How do you think about that as part of the deal structure? >> Yeah. So, I'd say I mean generally yes. I'm looking for some level of seller transition. Um now obviously if you have like somebody that owns and operates an HVAC and they have the license and can facilitate themselves that transition period can be much shorter you know maybe it's 30 days in office and then another 60 days over phone that can be that can be short but uh in general though that is something that that we look at um in that in that transition and consulting period to bring a buyer up to speed um on not only the, you know, maybe it's their first time owning a business. So, not only business ownership, but business ownership in whatever given industry they have and managing a P&L and people associate to that P&L. Maybe they've managed people in the past, but it hasn't been their P&L. They're not the one writing on the check. So, that can just be a little bit different than how than how a [clears throat] buyer's maybe managed a business unit in the past if they have that type of experience. And so having the seller around to just ease that out to say like, "Hey, everybody likes to be paid on Friday and they like checks." It can be something that simple. I've had that before. People that where we worked on a transaction that was a business acquisition and they paid weekly on Friday and nobody wanted direct deposit because they walked to the bank across the street. They got off at three. They ran shifts. So the first shift got off at three. They walked across the street. They cashed a check and then they all went to the bar next to the bank. >> It's a lifestyle. >> It's right. It can be a detail that's that easy. But had they switched to direct deposit now people are grumpy and then maybe, you know, I'm pulling the straws here, but maybe it leads to one or two of them leaving. >> Yeah. It's amazing the things that you might not think about that have a big impact in the real world of day-to-day business. >> Right. Right. >> So, let's shift from the buyer's deal structuring mindset over to the banker's mindset. What are some of the core pillars that you underwrite on when you're looking at an acquisition deal? >> Yeah. So, I kind of hit it again uh or hit it earlier, but uh going off to the tax returns. So, we've got to use that as our as our un as our basis. And then if we're do if there's levels of financial due diligence that are occurring such as a quality of earnings or an audit or something to that nature, um I'm not saying don't get those things because you should. Um they're important. Um but they are going to be layered onto our analysis of the tax return. And so um kind of again similar I take the same approach to every stage and to every opportunity but when it comes to the financials make it make sense to me. What are these adjustments? Why are we adjusting it? Why is this uh uh change to the cash flow? How are we going to verify it? you know, your $800 of meals and entertainment that is broken up into 75 receipts. Are we really going to validate that? Do we really know it wasn't for the business? No, we don't. But the 1099 that you paid your son to not show up at all or the W2 that you paid your daughter while she's in college, yeah, those are valid. give us some tax proof of it and we'll use those. So on the on the adjustment vein, it's number one, it's got it has to have been expensed. If they never expensed it, you can't add back the expense. Believe it or not, I know that sounds so simple. We see it all the time. They never expensed the expense that they want to add back. So number one, you got to start there. Number two, it has to have hit the tax return. So, a lot of times it'll be buried in the statements after like your K1s, well, in an [clears throat] escort. Sometimes it'll funnel up into one of the broader categories, but it's still there. So, it's really just point blank provide context to what those adjustments are, but then as a buyer, think about what think about what you're going to have. So, are are you going to run your cell phone through the business? probably. Are you going to run your life insurance through the business? Probably. I mean, an SBA lender is going to require you to get it financing, so that would make sense. You going to run your mileage through the company? Probably. Um, are you going to use the business to improve your house? Probably not. So, it's it's kind of finding that balance of like what's valid and what is going forward. Now, I understand when looking at a historical basis, it may be a different cost structure, but you still need to think about those things because part of the lure of entrepreneurship and a and a business ownership is the freedom that that offers. You can do those things as a business owner. And so to say that going into this business you're not going to funnel any personal expenses through it um is probably not true. Um and that's okay. That's okay. >> That's really practical and realistic real world. >> Yeah. >> Perspective because that's how it works. And let's talk a bit about their cash flow. when you look at DSCR, what is bankable in your mind versus something that's immediately going to raise a concern? >> Yeah. So, um it would depend upon the opportunity. So, I referenced a high growth company before. We may have a little different metrics on those. So, I'm going to I'm going to leave that out the time being. But in your standard business acquisition, stable company, stable business and industry, um we this is true requirements by the way. This is not SBA. So, we're a little bit above it. So, we're looking for 1.25 times at least 1.25 times in uh 2024. Well, let me say it this way. At least 1.25 times in the most recent tax return and year-to- date. And how do you view those year-to- date financials compared to tax returns? Because you focused on tax returns. they are the gold standard for SBA lending. Are you just looking for pretty much consistency or are you expecting them to be wildly divergent? >> Ideally, they're they're consistent. Um, one thing too that I recommend to buyers or I ask of buyers and brokers truthfully is when switching between financial statements, so you're going from a tax return to a P&L, always, always, always use the same accounting basis. So, a lot of times we'll get they file on a cash basis accounting tax return and then they're providing us with an acrruel basis P&L probably because it looks better. Um, and so if they're going to be using a cash basis return, we need to see a cash basis P&L. That's where you'll see a lot of big swings in specifically margins, gross profit margins and net profit margins is just purely in the accounting type and something many would overlook. So how do you think about the management role? So what are you looking for when you evaluate the management depth, the u strength of the buyer operator and their level of experience? What happens if they're a newbie? How do you view in that particular industry? How do you view this? >> It's it's right sizing their experience to the business and to the size of the business. Um, and so, you know, if somebody historically has managed, let's just say it's like an IT, they worked in IT and they managed a team of five. Are they cut out to take over a $5 million IT business that has 60 employees? Maybe, but maybe not. Like that's a huge jump. So is it So from an experience standpoint, is it right size to them? In that case, yes. But is it right sized from a scope of it? Maybe not. And so it's it's again you you'll see or you've seen in this conversation. I'm very point blank. I'm very blunt and just make it real life for me because this is going to be your life. So, we don't need to be, you know, up here in the stars when looking at this acquisition opportunity from the nuts and bolts level. Let's get it get to the foundation of it and then we can start to build from there. >> And let's say that you're getting a package from a commercial loan broker and you're looking it over. What makes you think this person really understands their job and how lenders think? And then on the flip side, what's going to just eliminate their credibility with >> um something that that really is frustrating for me um is not having a complete package and then pressing for answers. So if I ask for things um I I don't want to collect all the documentation in the world either. If I'm asking for things, it's because I need it and I need it to get you to the next stage, whatever we're trying to do, whether it be a term sheet, um, or a commitment letter or to closing. Um, I don't want any [clears throat] more paperwork than we have to get. If we're asking for it, it's cuz we need it. And so, if you if a broker has an incomplete package, is continuously pressing for an answer, then I'll give you the answer. And it's no, because I don't have enough information to make a decision. So, no. And then also too is just consideration to timing. You know, I sent out a request for documents, it takes a week and a half to get to me. It's not reasonable to expect an answer that day or even the next day because, you know, any top producing um SBA lender has other deals. And it's it's it's the hard truth. But if I'm looking at your deal and I identify that I need these four things and I request those four things, guess what? File goes to the side. You open up the next one and if that one's complete, you run it. You press it and then you come back um now and it's like, okay, well, I've got to relearn this file quick and complete the the items that that were requested. So, I'm not saying don't follow up and be conscious of time, but like think about how that process went. Did it take a week and a half to get for you to get the items? Then do you should give that lender if you want to have a good relationship, you know, at least 24 hours. But depending upon what that information is, it may be something that takes more time than that. Um, just keeping in mind of uh, you know, the when you're working with an SBA or or at least a high performing one, they want to deal, they want to do the deal just as much as the broker does, just as much as the borrower does. We're all on the same team here. So there's no reason to press somebody that's on your team ultimately to make a decision that they're not comfortable with or that they don't want to if they don't have enough information or haven't had enough time or whatever. >> So I'm really hearing there number one complete package that when you see that right out of the gate, you know that the broker is doing their job and there's somebody you want to work with. And then number two, having the perspective that is a partnership because it truly is. It's you and the broker working together to get the client what they need in order to take the next step with their acquisition. And they need to recognize that and treat you and any other lender as a partner rather than just somebody who's there to take their orders. >> Right? So, let's talk about some other things that impact the momentum of a deal along the way. Let's talk about We haven't touched on equity. So, what sources of equity are usually acceptable? What are equity pitfalls that you've seen historically? Um, where have things gone off the rails? So part of it is with the changes um that they made to the SOP. I think it was last August, but a couple years ago they allowed partial changes of ownership and then I think it was last August, but they changed it to where the seller has to personally guarantee for two years at any percentage of ownership 20 or le or less than 20. So, if a seller was retaining 1%, they still had a 2-year personal guarantee. So, when structure that changed a lot of the structuring structure of opportunities that we were looking at, specifically with licensed businesses, um that was for like a year. That was a really really good tool to transition a home service business for example because a seller could stay on they could facilitate the license until the buyer either had enough time or experience to get it themselves or to identify somebody within the business that was willing and able to step up. Um and so then other than that uh um it'd be it'd be that 20% threshold that you want to keep in mind. And so if you're involving friends or family um or investors then uh 20% or more um indicates the need for a personal guarantee. So a lot of times from an investor standpoint that's not the intent of the investment. And so if they uh from a from a group standpoint are wanting more equity keeping that in mind. So let's talk about liquidity as well. So we talked about equity. What about liquidity? What are the most what are your expectations for them in working capital reserves? Um where do you need to see that liquidity and how much are they going to need to bring to the table and how much wiggle room is there? And the easy answer here is it depends because depending upon the purchase transaction, it could be zero, it could be 10. And so your typical business acquisition though is going to be 10% of total project injection requirement. And so I want to emphasize total project that includes your guarantee fee that includes your includes your closing cost that includes your working capital. than anything other that there might be that you're trying to finance. It is not 10% of purchase price. So keep in mind it is total project. >> How much additional percentage-wise is that likely to add up to on average above the purchase price? >> Um again it's opportunity specific. So the guarantee fee is a percentage basis of the loan. Closing cost would be, you know, standard is is 15 to 20,000 for just business acquisition. And then if a buyer wants to do financial due diligence or legal due diligence or maybe there's an LOI, assignment fee, reassignment fee, you can kind of go down a rabbit hole there. Um, but from a bank side, it's usually 15 to 20,000. And then, uh, working capital would be opportunity specific, too. So um is there is there working capital being left in the business? If yes then of course you know we would finance less or have that ability to finance less lowering your total project lowering the leverage lower the loan in turn. So, um, when when thinking about the the 10% of total project, how we're applying that or sources of capital that that would come from that. Of course, cash liquidation of stocks or bonds. Just quick note on that, most most buyer, excuse me, most lenders are going to discount that though. So, like if you need $100,000 to um uh for your 10% of total project and you have $100,000 in stocks, most likely that's going to be discounted because you've got to pay um well, it's it's market based. So, today it's worth $100,000. Tomorrow might be 90, tomorrow might be 120. Like, it's totally market based. Um but then you're most likely going to have to pay tax on that, too. And then access access to capital would be another one. So think of like a heliloc. That's probably your most common when looking at debt um to facilitate equity injection. Um that is eligible. So you can use a debt facility um to finance your injection, but that debt needs to be have the ability to be repaid with sources of cash flow outside of the business. So, think like a spouse salary, maybe affiliate income, rental property income or what have you. Um, gifts from family members or um or uh maybe friends would be an eligible source of equity. Um and then of course investor funds. And so they're, you know, in they're maybe going to be getting some in exchange for um for equity or something of a um some other type of a agreement in place. I think that discussion of [sighs] liquidity sources really goes back to emphasizing that this is a product for small business acquisition, right? that when you get into a space where you're using a heliloc or you're getting gifts from friends or family, these really are local entrepreneurs who are going ahead acquiring and growing businesses and it's not as much an institutional play where you're bringing on investors for millions here to the left and to the right. And it's really powerful what this loan can do for helping entrepreneurs to take the next step in their journey. >> Right. Yep. >> So, what are some of the most common surprises, the surprise headaches that people didn't see coming, the buyers didn't expect, that throws a wrench in the works, and you were seeing it coming miles away? Um, well, I'd say the one we probably see most often or or often isn't one that we see coming, and this happens more than you think, but the seller never never having filed tax returns. And so, part of a part of underwriting for an SBA lender, they have to reconcile the tax returns provided to the tax transcripts that the IRS has recognized. And so more often than you think, those tax returns never got actually filed with the IRS or at least were not recognized by the IRS. And so that can be that can kill the deal if they never did it or at the very least create a delay because they then have to go do that. Um, and so, uh, um, I'd say that's that's that's definitely one that is not, uh, that we don't usually see coming. Wise things are a little bit more predictable, are leaving things, um, up for open or up for discretion. um early on in your LOI or in discussion, it's been discussed that you're going to be leaving a normalized level of networking capital, for example, from the moment that LOI is signed, you need to be working towards narrowing in on that. If you're waiting until the closing table to say, "Well, we thought networking capital was 500,000." And the seller said, "Well, we thought it was 100,000." We have a huge rift there. But you have time in the SBA loan process and closing process to start to narrow in on that and shrink that gap. And that can that can be um something that pops up late where they never reconcile the networking capital and it can really put a put a transaction at leverage. >> And what is a reasonable timeline for a buyer to expect on 7A? Uh generally about uh generally about 45 to 60 days. Um there is um I referenced before not wanting to collect paperwork or any more than we have to. It's true. It is still a government loan. So there is paperwork. Um so I don't want to be um you know sorry to be the bearer of bad news here but there's going to be paperwork. You know at True Liant we give you templates for everything. We docu sign as much as we can coordinate position coaches of that buyer through through that process. So try to make it as clean and easy as possible. Um but um I say that here because there is a lot of um work that a buyer and early on is going to have to do and then ultimately a buyer, seller and representation is going to have to do in the closing process. And so if we're asking for something and then in turn getting it in a couple of hours or maybe within the within a day, that can keep things moving. But if we are delayed on receiving of the information that we need, um, of course the whole thing is going to be delayed. And so I think SBA lenders get a lot of bad rap there in that. Um, can it take forever? Yes, it can. But for um you a top like industry producer like True Lion is doesn't have to. Um so it's all in how quickly can we get the information in order to pro in order to process and make decisions. >> So let's make that a bit more concrete. Can you walk me through a deal that just made sense right from the start? It really worked. It was a slam dunk. How did that flow? what made it such a great fit for you? Walk me through a real world example. >> Yeah, for sure. Actually, it's fairly recent. We closed early in February. Um, but had a a CPA that wanted to buy a CPA firm in her area and so we were time conscious for tax season. Um, and long story short, from the first time I talked to her to Money in the Bank was 35 days. Now, that's not normal, but that's what can happen. Um, that also occurred over the holidays. So, Christmas and New Year's were crammed in the middle there. Um, but we would ask for something and we'd have it in three or four hours. um we would ask something of her attorney, we'd have it in, you know, three or four hours. And so there was never a lapse and so nobody had to go back and you know you know where where are we at with this or what you know what was our last conversation again because it's been two weeks. Everything was fresh in mind and so it keeps everything going and it closed in 35 days. she took over the business first week of February. She's capturing pretty much all of tax season um and then can focus on the business uh and the amendments or changes that she wants to make within it here come next month or uh uh in May when when they have a little bit uh little bit more time. >> Wonderful. So in that I'm hearing that there was already buyer experience, right? It was a CPA buy into CPA firm. So that eliminates that as an issue for you. You had strong financial organization, the CPA buyer and CPA seller. I'm assuming their taxes were filed in a timely manner. Everything was easy to access. They had their year-to-ates >> and then there was a partnership just like you were talking about with brokers. They recognized that you're working together towards a common goal. They were responsive and cooperative and that allowed you to do your job so much better, quicker, faster. >> That's right. Yep. >> How about the converse, Ryan? What's a deal that just failed? It went up in smoke. And what are the lessons learned that a buyer could take away from that? >> Yeah. So, it's honestly just the flip side of the same on how it goes well. Um, but if you're if you're making or if you're seeking to buy a business, you and your finances need to be prepared to do so. If you're taking on investors, identify them. Have your capital stack. It doesn't have to be, you know, in pen, but you know, I I expect to use these three or four parties. They're investing via this vehicle. I'm buying the business via this vehicle, being an entity structure, and having a strong understanding of of that. >> Those are great principles. Is there a deal that you've worked that came in and in the end just didn't make sense, didn't get funded, and what did that look like in those specific mistakes? >> Yeah. So in this in this example, a changed just changes throughout um changing the purchase type, changing the purchase price, changing the seller note, um changing the the terms of it and then financials start to expire and then the financial performance of the company starts to lag. Now it no longer cash flows the proposed purchase price. So we try to shift course. financials continue to lag and so it can just start to snowball. Um, and so I think a lot of times, truthfully, I think a lot of times the seller gets a bad rap in those final weeks of selling the business because most of the time they're full-time running a business and it's kind of a full-time job to try and sell that business. So they have to be very very organized and very conscious of keeping business performance as it was or better because they're going to be analyzed on their most recent period. So, I'm sure there's seasonality to businesses and we can look at that in a little bit different scope, but let's say it's a regular stable business and Q4 they just like plummeted. That's going to be very hard for a lender to get comfortable with because we're now buying the business at its worst at the same price. Maybe at the same price, but is there broader issues with the business? These are broader economic um implications that are causing this. Um tariffs was a big one last year, Q1 of last year. Um businesses were impacted significantly by those. And so a lot of sellers, you know, took that time to um bring things uh through um different channels, whether it be reshoring or or through other countries that had a lower tax rate or excuse me, a um a lower effective rate. But um I think for a buyer keeping that in mind and and is it can can help with uh that relationship with the seller going forward so that should something like that happen that is able to be overcome. You've built up rapport and you now have the ability to renegotiate that. So you know in the same example yet Q4 Q4 was down a little bit. This is why we don't think it's a broader economic um implication. I think we need 5% more sell or not. It's a much easier conversation um when those seeds have been planted um uh kind of throughout the throughout the process. And it sounds like a key lesson there is to not look to sell in the valley to but rather to sell at the peak of the business just as you want to do with any good investment but sell when things are going well because it has a distinct impact on the ability for the buyer to get the financing which means it's impacting the your price at which you can sell in many real world scenarios. and that in that example there was a lack of strong structure from day one. You were mentioning how they were shifting everything from equity to pricing to the actual entity being sold throughout the deal and that things were not planned and structured properly from the beginning which led to headache after headache that eventually torpedoed the deal. >> That's right. So, what's something that a seller or a buyer could do if they're looking at an acquisition and they've got 30, 60 days before they're ready to pull the trigger and approach you? What are the things that they should be focused on in order to make sure it's looking really good when it gets in front of your eyes? >> Yeah. So, um, gather your documents, tax returns, resumes, personal financial statement, um, and then credit scores. So, if you're have lesser credit, begin to repair those things. Um, and then on the personal financial statement side, uh, acrew cash or acrew cash as best as you can if that's going to be one of your capital sources. [clears throat] um so that uh you're presenting yourself as be with your best foot forward when it comes to um when it comes to buying the business. Then have have clear I I prefer working with with a buyer um that has clear identified metrics on what they're searching for. You know, if somebody just says, "Well, I want a business that is a million in IBIDA." Okay. Well, that's like that could be anything. So, having clear metrics for for what it is that you're you're looking for can help to again makes it very point blank when talking to a lender. I don't have to infer anything or or jump to conclusions when you have somebody that, you know, maybe they've never been an owner, but they have they have some level of experience in in management in in a given industry, they've got the cash to do it. Uh, and you know, it makes sense. Um, that that uh preparing yourself best there can really lead to a clean to [clears throat] a clean loan process. And we've talked a lot about from the buyers perspective. To sum up, if you were talking to the loan broker community, the capital consultants out there, and from your position as a banker, there was one thing you could really get across for them to remember about what they should be doing to help people looking at acquisitions, help their clients. What's that key most important lesson? >> Yeah. So, for a broker, um I would say a complete package. So, um when you're working with a with a top producing lender, um you know, if you're consistently getting files from various sources, you know, a good a good one is maybe getting seven or eight new opportunities a day that they've got to sift through. So, typically it goes into an A, B, or C bucket. A, this is a good relationship or I feel confident about this transaction or I know we can get this done. B, I think we can do this. It's going to take a little work. C, I'll get to it, which you never do. So, how do you go from the C bucket to the B bucket to the A bucket if it's consistently a full package? For me, that's moving you up the ranks because I don't have to ask for things. I can pick it up. I can digest the whole thing at once and tell you yes or no or I have these questions. I feel good about it. Let's proceed. >> And what are you looking for in that full package? >> Yeah. So, generally um generally it's on the on the business side. three years of taxes, most recent financial statements in the same accounting basis as the tax returns, similar website, the LOI, um, and then it depends on the business, but like ARAP aging might be something that we're looking for. And then if not in the sim, a description of the non-ordinary adjustments on the buy side, buyer side, three years taxes, PFS, resume, credit score, and then if they have affiliates, it kind of depends on there. So I won't go down that rabbit hole. Um, with that information set, typically I've got enough to write it up and and seek for for an approved term sheet for approved loan proposal. Um, if we can knock that out in once or at once, that is going to lead to your cleanest cleanest process. And um uh working with a broker, uh a lender will be excited to open and work on that file because they know we've got a live one here. Let's do it. Let's hit the gas. I'm not going to have to back and forth this thing because that that back and forth bad mitten is a lot of times where deals are lost. Um, and so if you can just avoid that by having a complete package, maybe it means holding on to it for another day or two before you're sending it out, that might be in your client's best interest. Um, then do that. Well, Ryan, this was excellent. What really stands out to me is that the SBA 7A acquisition lending field is not just about the loan product, but it's for brokers and buyers thinking about thinking about the deal and structuring it from the banker's perspective from the very first screen all the way through underwriting and closing. And that's really kind of our mission at our institute, unlocking capital for entrepreneurs. It not only impacts our businesses, but that impacts our communities and the American economy. And the more clearly that brokers, buyers, and lenders understand how to structure and position these deals and do it from day one, the more likely that strong businesses are going to get the capital they need to succeed. And Ryan, I appreciate you sharing both the tactical details and the bigger picture. Thank you for being here and all you do to help American businesses. How can people follow up with you and connect? Yeah. So, easiest place is probably LinkedIn. So, search my name, Ryan Collins, and you'll be able to find it there. Otherwise, email. It's probably best, which again, you'll find it on my LinkedIn. So, that's probably the best. And >> we'll include that social link. So, check in the show notes. And again, Ryan, thank you so much for taking the time. >> Awesome. Thank you, Shane. [music]

Comparing SBA 7A vs 504 Loans for Business Acquisitions w/ Real Estate

Welcome to another insightful episode where we delve into the nuances of business acquisitions with real estate! Join us as we compare SBA 7A versus 504 loans and dissect the ideal structures for your next venture. From understanding purchase price dynamics to navigating prepayment penalties, we've got you covered. 

Are you an entrepreneur or business owner looking to buy or expand a business? Book a discovery call with Beau to learn all the ways he can help you - http://bookwithbeau.com/
Join my new Business Ownership Academy community on Skool - http://businessownershipacademy.com/

0:10 - Assessing Purchase Price Allocation
0:37 - Exploring Loan Options: SBA 7A vs. 504
1:11 - Advantages of SBA 7A vs. 504
1:58 - Refinancing Considerations and Opportunities
2:20 - Leveraging SBA Financing: Tips & Strategies

💥 Thanks for watching 💥
#SBAloans #BusinessAcquisitions #RealEstateInvesting #SmallBusinessFinance #LoanStructures #SBA504 #SBA7A #Entrepreneurship #FinanceTips #BusinessStrategy

About Beau: Beau Eckstein is a franchise consultant, commercial mortgage advisor, and business ownership coach who helps entrepreneurs buy, build, and expand their businesses. He assists aspiring entrepreneurs in finding their ideal franchise or business opportunity. Beau's expertise as an investor and business owner allows him to guide clients through the entire process of acquiring, funding, and growing their ventures.

🎥 The video interviews we do on IFP will help you scale your real estate business and learn how to finance all your projects.

Learn great insights and make the right decisions through the Investor Financing Podcast hosted by Beau Eckstein.

metadata.title: How to Buy Commercial Real Estate (100% Financing Explained!) | SBA Loans
metadata.author: SBA University
metadata.shortDescription:
Welcome to SBA University! 🎓 I’m Glenn Giro, and in this episode, I’m diving into how to purchase commercial real estate using the SBA 7A Loan program—including how you can qualify for 100% financing with no money down.

If you’ve ever wondered:

Can I use an SBA loan to buy my own commercial property?
How do eligibility rules for mixed-use properties work?
What are the benefits of 100% financing, and how do I qualify?
This video is for YOU.

Here’s what we’ll cover:
1️⃣ Eligibility – What makes a property eligible, including mixed-use requirements.
2️⃣ Down Payment Benefits – How to qualify for 100% financing with no money down.
3️⃣ Term – Why the 25-year, fully amortized structure with no balloon payments is a game-changer.
4️⃣ Qualification – How existing rent expenses and cash flow impact your approval.
5️⃣ Projections – How to use future revenue estimates to strengthen your loan application.
6️⃣ Due Diligence – Appraisals, environmental surveys, and contractor bids you’ll need before closing.

I’ll guide you step-by-step through these concepts so you can make informed decisions and take your business to the next level.

💡 Got questions? Drop them in the comments—I’d love to help!

📝 Be sure to subscribe to SBA University for weekly lessons that simplify the SBA loan process. From eligibility to closing, I’m here to guide you every step of the way.

👉 Contact me directly: ggiro@tbank.com
👉 Subscribe for more insights!

metadata.title: New SBA Rule Unlocks $10M: Who Actually Benefits | Shane Walton ft. Jeff Hildebrandt
metadata.author: Commercial Loan Broker Institute
metadata.shortDescription:
The SBA loan changes 2026 headline sounds huge: combine 7(a) and 504 loans for up to $10M in SBA-backed financing. But who actually benefits?

Shane Walton sits down with Jeff Hildebrandt of Bankc of California, an SBA lender and trainer with 15+ years on both the broker and banking side, to break down what the announcement really means for borrowers and brokers.What You'll Learn:

  •  What the July 2026 7(a) + 504 rule change actually does, and the narrow group it helps
  •  Eligible vs bankable: why SBA approval rules and lender appetite are two different tests
  •  How to find lenders that actually fund your deal type
  •  Down payment structures, seller notes on standby, and the cash flow test
  •  Why the money comes from the bank, not the government

Learn commercial loan brokering at https://www.commercialloanbrokerinstitute.com

The Commercial Loan Broker Institute has helped launch and support hundreds of brokers with training, mentorship, and an active lender network.

#sbaloanchanges2026 #sbaloans #sba7a #sba504 #commercialloanbroker

metadata.title: SBA 504 vs. 7(a) Loans for Commercial Real Estate
metadata.author: Community Business Finance
metadata.shortDescription:
Bill Ebersole explains the differences between the SBA 504 and 7(a) lending programs in regard to commercial real estate financing. The 504 Loan Program was designed specifically for real estate and equipment purchases. It offers a fixed interest rate for 20 years. While the 7(a) Loan Program usually has a variable interest rate, Bill offers insight as to why 7(a) loans are sometimes used for real estate financing.

Community CDC specializes in 504 fixed-rate loans in Texas and Louisiana, but we are experts in all SBA lending programs. Contact Community CDC to learn more about all the lending options that are available before you sign on the dotted line.

Call Bill Ebersole at 713-457-1650, ext. 201, or email him at bill.ebersole@communitycdc.com.

MCA or Merchant Cash Advance loans look at either your past 3 to 6 months business merchant statements or checking statements to offer loans with daily or weekly payments. metadata.title: 4 Ways to Get Out of Merchant Cash Advance Debt
metadata.author: Zach Siegel
metadata.shortDescription:
WATCH NEXT:
▶️ The Truth About Merchant Cash Advances (How They Really Work):
https://youtu.be/g3DWsqTZDbE?si=aF1kMKFcPQXhEsQA

If you've got multiple merchant cash advances pulling money out of your account every day... second, third, fourth position stacked on top of each other, there is a way out. It's not magic, and it's not painless, but it's real.

I am not against MCAs. But I am against owners getting stuck in too many to where they have no cash flow anymore. In this video, I break down every realistic route out: the conventional financing that buys them out, the asset-backed options 95% of brokers never mention (business-use HELOC, receivables facilities, invoice factoring, equipment sale leasebacks, stacked term loans), how to negotiate directly with your funder, and the "MCA relief" companies you need to be extremely careful with.

I also cover the trap most owners fall into. Reverse consolidation: and how to tell real help from an expensive advance wearing a rescue costume.

📞 Stacked in advances? Get an honest look at your options and book a free call:
http://www.bit.ly/applyforaloanwithsbh

📕 Get Zach's book, The Hero's Journey to Capital:
https://www.bit.ly/journeytocapital

📲 Or call the team directly: (888) 859-8408
─────────────────────
CHAPTERS:
0:00 Stacked in MCAs? There Is a Way Out
1:15 How Most Owners End Up Here (The Broker Pitch to Watch For)
3:01 Step 1: Stop the Bleeding
3:56 Know Your Real Numbers (Build a Debt Schedule)
4:34 Route 1: Buy the MCAs Out With One Product
5:18 Best Case: Conventional Line of Credit or Term Loan
6:08 Asset-Backed Option: Business-Use HELOC
6:30 Asset-Backed Option: Receivables & Invoice Factoring
7:15 Asset-Backed Option: Equipment Sale Leaseback
7:38 Stacked Term Loans (and Using a Co-Signer)
7:55 Route 2: Consolidation vs. the Reverse Consolidation Trap
9:28 Route 3: Negotiating Directly With Your Funder
11:35 Route 4: The Truth About MCA Relief Companies
13:16 The Hard Questions to Ask Before You Sign
14:50 The Long Game: Getting Bank-Ready
16:02 The 4-Step Recap
─────────────────────

At Small Biz Heroes, we work with more than 20 funding programs and we're trying to raise the standard in alternative finance. No judgment, no pressure, and no shoving you into something you don't fully understand. Thanks for watching and I look forward to seeing you in my next Friday video!

metadata.title: What Really Happens When You Default on an MCA? (Warning)
metadata.author: Rise Alliance
metadata.shortDescription:
Thinking about missing a merchant cash advance (MCA) payment? If you carry one or multiple stacked MCAs, default isn't a slow burn—it's an immediate trigger for operational collapse.

Because MCA companies buy the right to a percentage of your future sales rather than issuing traditional loans, their contracts give them extraordinary collection rights. As soon as you miss a payment, an MCA can issue a UCC 9-406 notice that tells your customers to pay the MCA directly, sweep your operating accounts to drain the cash you need for payroll and rent, and file lawsuits to lock down your accounts. It only takes one aggressive MCA lender to pull the trigger and collapse your entire revenue system.

Most debt relief firms completely miss this danger. They either tell you to stop paying and save up for a settlement, or they promise to negotiate reductions—which only works if every single MCA agrees. Without structural defenses, your business is fully exposed when creditors make a move.

See how Rise Alliance approaches this differently by stabilizing your business first. We leverage tools most won't—from your contractual right to reconciliation to a full Article 9 restructuring alongside our parent company, Second Wind—to protect your cash flow, preserve business value, and resolve debt.

metadata.title: Merchant Cash Advances and Bankruptcy: What Business Owners Need to Know
metadata.author: Parkins & Rubio LLP
metadata.shortDescription:
Episode Summary: 
In this episode of the Business Restructuring Podcast, hosts Lenard Parkins and Charles Rubio, experienced corporate bankruptcy and financial restructuring attorneys, delve into the intricacies of merchant cash advances (MCAs) and their impact on businesses. Joined by Lisa Mosbey, they explore why business owners often turn to MCAs for quick cash flow solutions and the potential pitfalls of MCA stacking, which can signal financial distress. The discussion highlights the differences between MCAs and traditional factoring, the warning signs of MCA debt threatening long-term viability, and how bankruptcy, particularly Chapter 11, can offer a lifeline by restructuring these obligations into more manageable repayment plans. This episode is essential for business owners facing cash flow challenges, offering insights into how legal strategies can transform financial burdens into sustainable solutions.

Key Timestamps:
00:02 – Introduction
00:49 – Understanding Merchant Cash Advances
02:43 – Differences Between MCAs and Factoring
05:11 – MCA Stacking and Financial Distress
08:08 – Recognizing MCA Debt Warning Signs
10:07 – Dealing with Multiple Creditors
11:38 – Bankruptcy's Impact on MCA Obligations
13:13 – Chapter 11 and Managing Debt
16:03 – Legal Challenges to MCA Agreements
17:44 – Evaluating Bankruptcy Options for MCA Pressure
19:13 – Chapter 11 as a Long-term Solution

About the Show: 
The Business Restructuring Podcast with Parkins Rubio offers insightful discussions for business owners, financial professionals, and legal practitioners navigating complex financial challenges. Hosted by Lenard Parkins and Charles Rubio, the show provides expert analysis on corporate bankruptcy and financial restructuring, focusing on strategic decision-making where financial pressure and litigation intersect. With a commitment to clarity and actionable advice, the podcast aims to empower listeners with the knowledge to make informed decisions about business restructuring and financial health.

#BusinessRestructuring #MerchantCashAdvance #Bankruptcy #Chapter11 #FinancialDistress #ParkinsRubio

if an entity wanted to attack this as a

reading through the documents and

they're usurious loans and they're
subjecting the FC lenders to serious
consequences because of that.
And it gives you as bankrupt you the
form to challenge that
very vigorously.
>> And another means of challenging it,
which is
um
separate and apart from being a usurious
loan and trying to recognize it as a
loan, is that there's there's an action
that's very common in bankruptcy called

Uh and the specific one called a

reasonably equivalent value.

a relative of an owner, that might be
clawed back as a transfer for no value

these facilities have been challenged on

reasonably equivalent value, that
they're giving too much value away and
there's a possibility of clawing some of
that amount back into the bankruptcy

uh
attacking these facilities after you're
in a bankruptcy case either by trying to
characterize it as a loan that's a
usurious loan or alternatively, you
know, clawing back some of the funds as
being less than reasonably equivalent
value.

owners be evaluating if MCA obligations
are creating significant financial
pressure for them?

evaluating,
you know, your your bankruptcy options
and you know, chapter 11 you you don't
have to be insolvent to use chapter 11.
That's incredibly important. You just
have to have a financial issue that
chapter 11 can solve. So, you know, that

started to see million-dollar,
two-million-dollar MCAs that are going

draw on cash flow.

That's the difference. A factor buys receivables that exist, a merchant cash advance lender quotes will buy future receivables, not present receivables. >> Another key difference in that this touches on something that Lenny was talking about before is the interrelationship between an MCA and the bank account is that how a merchant cash advance facility is always set up is that it directly takes ACH transactions from the entities for lack of a better borrower's bank account. It takes those either on a daily or weekly basis. It directly draws from the bank account through an ACH transaction. So, that's Lenny also was describing a traditional factor which buys a created accounts receivable at a discount. Here, the structures are really fundamentally different in that they buy future accounts receivable, but how they pay themselves back is through taking direct transfers out of the borrower's bank account on a daily or weekly basis. >> What's also interesting is if you look at the documents that do these MCAs, okay? They will say, "I am not a lender. I'm a buyer. I'm a buyer of future accounts receivable. This is not a loan. This is a purchase of future accounts receivable." And we'll talk a little bit more about why that's important in the context of bankruptcy strategy. >> What is MCA stacking and why is it often a sign that a business is heading toward financial distress? >> So, the nature of the MCA itself is intended to be a short-term liquidity boost. You you get it one time often to navigate some pick up that you have in the road or maybe you got a big project that you need to fund it and you need quick financing in order to fund a big project that came in, but stacking is essentially where you use a new MCA, a new merchant cash advance facility to pay off an old merchant cash advance facility. And so, why that's an indicator that the the entity may be approaching financial distress is that it really shouldn't be used that way. It really shouldn't be used where you're constantly rotating these merchant cash advance facilities because at the end of the day, these are very high interest financing instruments, much higher than traditional financing. So, if you find yourself stacking, which is replacing a new MCA to pay off an old set MCA, um you're you're kind of in this loop of essentially needing these payday loans all the time. That's that's the troubling part of stacking MCAs. >> And what it indicates is that it isn't just a single short-term cash need. You have a repeated problem with cash flow, and therefore you're seeking another lender now to take out the first lender's cash flow, incurring a very high interest rate loans in order to do that. And uh it indicates there's a more maybe a more fundamental problem with a business than a short-term cash need because of a short-term hiccup in the business. >> Another thing about stacking that's that's worth raising now is that, you know, stacking is also a controversial thing in the law and that these MCAs don't want to be loans because if they were loans, they would often be exceed the amount of the usury interest rate. So, what a stacking is is essentially a refinancing. There's a remaining amount of the old MCA that is being paid off from the proceeds of a new MCA so that it is a refinancing and if there is a dispute between, you know, the borrower and the MCA, then that backed the existence that there was stacking is a factor that would be indicative of this being more of a loan than a real purchase of future receivables. So, if there was if an entity wanted to attack this as a usurious loan, that is a fact that would uh lean towards that end result of it actually being a loan and not a purchase of future receivables. >> Sure. And then, how can business owners recognize the warning signs that MCA debt is beginning to threaten the company's long-term viability? >> Well, the most the most easy signal is they look at their bank account every day and they see how much money is being drawn out by the MCA lender from their bank account and they realize that they are running short of cash and they cannot subsidize with their own operations the payback at the huge interest rates these lenders have from the cash flow that's coming in. Or they may have a slowdown in cash flow. They may need to renegotiate the percentage. So, this is these are signs that that the owner of the company sees that basically the the drawdown of cash, which is automatic from the bank account under the MCA loans, okay, is impairing their business and they just don't have the liquidity anymore to run their business. >> Yeah, I I I wholeheartedly agree with Lenny. I I The The key sign that an MCA is >> So, >> getting problematic is that usually you do have stacking, you have entities that have multiple MCAs sometimes, and they look at their bank account and they say "Oh my goodness, all my money is getting drafted out of this account every day or every week from from these MCAs." >> And then, why do businesses with MCA obligations often find themselves dealing with multiple creditors at the same time? >> It's the same reality. It's this, you know, you're you find yourself in a liquidity crunch, you turn to the MCAs in order to solve you to ideally solve the short-term liquidity crunch, but you know, these MCAs often become liquidity traps where while they were there to solve the short-term liquidity problem, just by the nature of how they're structured in their so short-term in their repayment, they often create liquidity constraints and then you know, often times these owners are faced confronting a situation where they have to decide, you know, which creditors they're paying cuz the money's being taken out of their accounts. >> Yeah, the MCA lenders are not generally the only creditors of a company. A company will have a lot of other creditors that need to be paid either on 30-day 60-day intervals normally and uh with the MCA loan and the drawdowns of cash are so extreme, especially if you have stacking may have two of them drawing down cash from the bank account, it just says to the company, wow, um I'm running out of cash and you I'm only going to pay this creditor this month and that creditor next month and because I just don't have the cash now and I have you have to decide who to pay rather than be able to pay your creditors in normal course and that creates an accelerated pressure on the company. >> And Lenny, isn't it true that you you have to pay the MCAs? They're automatically taking that money out, so it's the other creditors that suffer in these cases, correct? >> The MCAs automatically take their money at the way the MCA is structured is they give access the borrower gives access to the bank account that the MCA lender has studied to say how much money comes in and you give access to that bank account to take out the contractual amount of money every week or every month from the bank account automatically versus writing a check to creditors to pay their debt, the MCAs take their money first. Before I before when I wake up, I'll see how much they took. versus I'm going to pay the bill. That's a big difference. >> How can bankruptcy immediately change the situation for a business struggling with MCA obligations? >> Yeah, the The immediate One of the immediate advantages of bankruptcy is the automatic stay. So, you That's a an injunction on creditors from taking actions against a debtor in bankruptcy. So, what that practically means is that that ACH that was occurring every week or every day, which they're often structured every day they actually take out money out of the account, that immediately stops upon the filing. Another huge advantage from a bankruptcy perspective is that the the future work that that entity does, the the future work that creates post-petition accounts receivable, those post-petition accounts receivable are not subject to the liens of the MCA lenders pre-petition liens or at least they shouldn't. So, that's another advantage there is that you immediately have a partition in time where a debtor in possession in bankruptcy can start doing work, start generating post-petition accounts receivable that are outside of the liens of the MCA lenders. So, those are two immediate advantages that you get as an entity filing for Chapter 11 when you have MCA debt. >> This This is It is important to understand just to clar- clarify something Charles said. There's pre-bankruptcy, and then you draw a big line when you file Chapter 11, for example, bankruptcy. That demarcation is very significant. By statute, for example, as Charles said, newly created receivables would not be subject to a pre-bankruptcy lien or security interest, nor would nor would newly created receivables be subject necessarily to their claim that they're purchasing those receivables. That demarcation of filing bankruptcy is critical in order to cut off rights that a MCA lender might assert pre-bankruptcy. They're They're slowed down or impossible to assert on newly created receivables post-bankruptcy. And that's why the cut the consequence of filing bankruptcy has to be considered when dealing with an MCA loan. If If things get so tight you cash flow is just not enough to run the business. >> So, Charles, how can Chapter 11 transform MCA obligations into a more manageable repayment structure? >> And this is really the core of Chapter 11 is to manage those pre-petition debts. And one of the fundamental ways of doing that is to stretch out your debt payment. So, where you you may owe an MCA an MCA lender $100,000 and on their normal payment schedule that was under your contract with them, maybe you had to pay that back in 3 months. Maybe you had to pay that back in 12 weekly installments over 3 months. In a Chapter 11 plan you you could pay that amount over monthly installments over 4 years. It's possible to stretch that out. And not only that, unlike the APR that you had pre-petition, which the APR on these facilities could easily be 100% or more. Sometimes we've seen 200 250% APR on uh merchant cash advance facilities, is that on a post-petition basis? Not only are you stretching it out and possibly paying it over multiple years, you're also paying it at an interest rate that's a normal interest rate. You're talking about a prime plus 1 to 3% if it's considered a secured debt. So, you're making it a much more manageable financial obligation to be dealt with and paid over time under a Chapter 11 plan. >> The other thing that happens in Chapter 11, it gives you a form to challenge the integrity of the loan itself, whether it's the usurious or whether it is in fact just a purchase agreement. Or or in most cases where the litigation is going around the country with respect to these, is they're reading through the documents and calling them usurious loans. And these usurious loans carry with them punishments. For example, you may lose your ability to collect the loan. You may have be subject to personal liability. In some states, you may be subject to criminal liability for the amount of interest charged when it's turned determined to be a loan and not a purchase. That's why they're purchase agreements. Their agreements say, "This is a purchase agreement. This is not a loan." They do everything they can to say, "This is not a loan." But courts, when challenged, are looking closely at these and the scrutiny is coming out more and more that these are loans and they're usurious loans and they're subjecting the FC lenders to serious consequences because of that. And it gives you as bankrupt you the form to challenge that very vigorously. >> And another means of challenging it, which is um separate and apart from being a usurious loan and trying to recognize it as a loan, is that there's there's an action that's very common in bankruptcy called a fraudulent transfer action. Uh and the specific one called a constructive fraudulent transfer action, which is a transfer for less than a reasonably equivalent value. For instance, if a company was to give a car away to a relative of an owner, that might be clawed back as a transfer for no value to the entity. In a similar way, if the these facilities have been challenged on the basis that they're they are not reasonably equivalent value, that they're giving too much value away and there's a possibility of clawing some of that amount back into the bankruptcy estate as well. So, there's many ways of uh attacking these facilities after you're in a bankruptcy case either by trying to characterize it as a loan that's a usurious loan or alternatively, you know, clawing back some of the funds as being less than reasonably equivalent value. >> Charles, here's where I want to wrap this up today. Uh what should business owners be evaluating if MCA obligations are creating significant financial pressure for them? >> Well, certainly uh as a bankruptcy lawyer I would say you need to be evaluating, you know, your your bankruptcy options and you know, chapter 11 you you don't have to be insolvent to use chapter 11. That's incredibly important. You just have to have a financial issue that chapter 11 can solve. So, you know, that it that course of action uh needs to be considered for for business owners who are in the situation and can look out a month or two on the horizon and see, you know, maybe I don't have a liquidity problem right now, but we're this is snowballing into a liquidity problem. So, um that's one thing that business owners should be concerned about. And just as a more general matter, you know, we've seen merchant cash advance facilities go from really uh industries where it's really mom and pop businesses, smaller businesses that are getting facilities for 100, 200, 300,000 short-term facilities and we've seen these really penetrate the middle market now where we started to see million-dollar, two-million-dollar MCAs that are going to more substantial businesses. So, you know, it's not just the mom and pops that are looking at this. It's even the smaller businesses that may have just taken on too much of this and their expectation of why they needed that short-term liquidity actually was a longer duration and they need a a longer term solution, and chapter 11 is something that they should be evaluating. >> Right. Companies who need, for example, a million dollars and can find an MCA lender who'll do it. If you're borrowing a million dollars at an excess of probably 30% interest. And and it's coming right out of your bank account, and you realize all of a sudden then if your business is not generating the kind of revenue you expected, you are burdened by a tremendous draw on cash flow. And therefore, you have to decide how you stop that draw on cash flow and run your business successfully. And chapter 11 offers that alternative to basically run your business successfully and pay off the debt over time. And challenge the integrity of the debt. Maybe you'll get a deal where the debt goes down by virtue of the challenge against the integrity of the debt, and you'll have less debt to pay in the aggregate over time in a chapter 11 plan. But the goal is to go in, do a chapter 11 plan, a payout program for the creditor, and the right and venue and form to challenge the debt in order to reconcile it to a right amount. >> Lenny, Charles, thank you so much for your insights and walking us through this process and how it can support business owners in moving forward. That's it for today's episode of The Business Restructuring Podcast with Parkins and Rubio. If you'd like to learn more about Leonard Parkins and Charles Rubio, you can visit their website at parkinsrubio.com. Thank you so much for listening, and be sure to like, leave a review, and subscribe so you don't miss a future episodes. We'll see you there. >> Thanks for watching. Be sure to hit that like and subscribe button, [music] and leave us a review in the comments.

There are also going to be other disclosures as far as how interest rates are stated on contracts and what brokers have to do and what funders and lenders have to do. So, this doesn't just affect MCA or revenue-based financing or sales-based financing. It does include factoring and asset-based lending. The Financial Technology Association includes Block, Amazon Pay, PayPal, SoFi who just got into business loans, WebBank, Intuit who does, you know, financing through QuickBooks and its marketplace, and the RBFC. metadata.title: 3 Shifts Reshaping Commercial Lending That Most Brokers Are Missing
metadata.author: Commercial Loan Broker Institute
metadata.shortDescription:
Commercial lending trends are reshaping how brokers win deals over the next 3 to 5 years.

Shane Walton, co-founder of the Commercial Loan Broker Institute, explains where we are in the credit cycle and what the commercial real estate maturity wall means for refinance demand. S&P Global Market Intelligence projects that wall peaking near $1.26 trillion in 2027. Shane then covers the three structural shifts most brokers are missing: a lender mix where banks are more selective and private credit has gone institutional, technology that compresses approval timelines, and selective capital that rewards fewer, better deals.

You'll also see the specialization paths that build lender and borrower trust. Then come the four things smart brokers are doing now to gain market share instead of competing on price.

4:40 Shift 2: Technology, AI, Digital Workflows, and Faster Approvals

metadata.title: How do Commercial Loan Brokers get Paid?
metadata.author: Commercial Loan Broker Institute
metadata.shortDescription:
How do commercial loan brokers actually get paid, and where does the money come from?

Learn the two most common commission structures in commercial finance: the client-facing (front-end) commission the borrower agrees to and knows about, and the lender-facing (back-end) commission, often called yield spread. 

You'll see how each one is structured, how points and engagement fees work, how you can earn one or both on a single deal, and how these commissions actually get paid at and after closing.

Watch next: Learn the Broker Commission Mechanics (Fee and Split Numbers)
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7OHPVFeEmD4

Want to see if brokering fits you?  Take the free personality quiz:  https://commercialloanbrokerinstitute.com/loan-broker-personality-test/

CLBI creates educational content for people who want to start, operate, and grow a commercial loan brokerage. Subscribe for weekly training on the business.

Disclosure: This video is for educational and informational purposes only and is not financial, legal, or investment advice. It does not guarantee or imply any specific earnings or results; individual outcomes depend on effort, experience, market conditions, and other factors, and many participants earn less or nothing at all.

#CommercialLoanBroker #CommercialFinance #YieldSpread

I'm Gloria Leduc here on the CU
compliance connection by league info
site bringing you a brief overview of
FinCEN's new rule for customer or member
due diligence requirements for financial
institutions compliance with these new
rules is required on May 11th of this
year and with multiple frequently asked
questions issued by fencin we thought it
would be a good idea to provide a
high-level summary and overview back in
2016 FinCEN or the Financial Crimes
enforcement Network issued new rules
under the Bank Secrecy Act or BSA to
clarify and strengthen customer due
diligence requirements for financial
institutions these new rules created a
new requirement for credit unions to
identify and verify the identity of
beneficial owners of legal entity
customers or members there were also
changes to anti money laundering or AML
program requirements which will require
credit unions to implement and maintain
appropriate risk-based procedures for
conducting ongoing member due diligence
for all members which includes first
understanding the nature and purpose of
the customer or member relationship and
to conducting ongoing monitoring to
identify and report suspicious
transactions and on a risk basis to
maintain an update member or customer
information therefore in order to comply
with new rules which is required on or
before May 11th
credit unions need to make sure their
member or customer due diligence program
is updated to include the requirement to
identify and verify the beneficial
owners of legal entities and update
their overall AML program to include
risk-based procedures for conducting
that ongoing due diligence for all
members so how will these changes impact
the credit unions existing processes
first after May 11th when legal entity
members come in to open a new account
the credit union will need to obtain
certain information from them in order
to identify those beneficial owners now
the credit union can obtain
that required information by either
having the legal entity member fill out
the certification form that is included
within Appendix A of the regulation or
through another method if the credit
union is using an alternative method
they need to ensure they're capturing
the same data at a minimum that's
included in the certification form in
Appendix A additionally if using an
alternative method the credit union will
still need to obtain certification from
the individual who's providing the
information of its accuracy for purposes
of our review today we will consistently
refer to the use of the certification
form but viewers should know as we just
explained that doesn't necessarily mean
they have to use this form the
alternative method we just described is
also permissible this information can be
obtained from the individual seeking to
open a new account at the credit union
on behalf of the legal entity member so
that may be an authorized signer for

metadata.title: What Brokers Get Wrong About Commercial Financing | Sua Truong
metadata.author: CFM™ (Commercial Financing Mastery™)
metadata.shortDescription:
🎁 FREE DOWNLOAD - The COI Playbook + SBL/SBA Deal Screener + Workshop Invite
Get all three here: https://cfmcapitalacademy.com/deal-system-yt

What are mortgage brokers getting wrong about the market right now, and where is the business actually moving?

In this CFM™ FAQ episode, Desmond Soon asks Sua Truong, Founder and CEO of Commercial Financing Mastery™, why waiting for the residential market to get better is the wrong play. Sua explains who the foreign buyer ban change really helps, why small multifamily (triplexes and fourplexes) is getting special treatment from CMHC, and why business insolvencies are trending differently from personal ones. He walks through the commercial options residential files cannot offer: working capital, receivables financing, buying the building through a holding company, and leasing to your own operating company. He also covers why brokerages avoid commercial files, why E&O coverage matters, and who really funds the trades when building starts again.

Want the CMHC special training Desmond mentions? Get on the waiting list at CommercialFinancingMastery.com

Learn more at CommercialFinancingMastery.com

CHAPTERS
0:00 Who funds the trades? We do.
0:11 Welcome to the FAQ series
1:30 Waiting for it to get better
1:45 Who the foreign buyer ban change helps
3:02 Stay in your lane, watch where the ball moves
4:57 CMHC 10% down on triplexes and fourplexes
5:55 Insolvencies: personal versus business
7:50 Commercial options residential cannot offer
10:34 Same footprint, residential versus commercial
12:35 Why brokerages avoid commercial files
16:58 Outlook for the months ahead
19:27 Who funds the trades, and programs owners miss

HOSTS
Sua Truong, Founder and CEO, CFM™ (Commercial Financing Mastery™)
Desmond Soon, Co-Founder and Chief Revenue Officer, CFM™

Educational purposes only. Not financial advice. No income guarantees. Results vary. Always confirm rules with your regulator, your brokerage and your CPA.

#CommercialFinancing #MortgageBroker #CMHC

metadata.title: Why the Bank Declined His 8th Subway Loan: Lender Capacity Explained | Sua Truong
metadata.author: CFM™ (Commercial Financing Mastery™)
metadata.shortDescription:
FREE WORKSHOP for mortgage brokers moving into commercial financing. Get the CFM™ Deal System here:
https://cfmcapitalacademy.com/deal-system-yt?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=organic_social&utm_campaign=sneak-peek-ep06-nov18&utm_content=261118-yt-cfm-desc-x

Why would a bank decline the 8th Subway loan after funding the first seven? This is a sneak peek inside a live CFM™ cohort mentorship session.

Sua Truong, Founder and CEO of Commercial Financing Mastery™, explains lender capacity: why banks do not want certain commercial files on the portfolio, how mortgage-backed securities and thin spreads drive that call, and how a broker finds out where the money really is. He tells the story of a client who did seven Subway franchises at one institution, then got declined on the eighth, and shows why a weekly call to your commercial managers is how you learn a lender's appetite. He also explains why what got you here on the residential side will not get you there in commercial financing, and why a decline is not the end of the file if you can restructure it.

Learn more at CommercialFinancingMastery.com

CHAPTERS
0:00 The bank declined the 8th Subway
0:25 Why lenders don't want this on the portfolio
2:57 Make friends at the retail channel
3:38 Why the 8th Subway was declined
4:24 How do you know when a lender has no appetite?
6:16 Why banks refer you their deals
8:17 What got you here won't get you there
8:40 Fail forward: a decline is not a bad thing
10:25 Join the complimentary CFM™ workshop

HOSTS
Sua Truong, Founder and CEO, CFM™ (Commercial Financing Mastery™)

This is a sneak peek from a live CFM™ cohort mentorship session, not a masterclass.

Educational purposes only. Not financial advice. Results vary.

#CommercialFinancing #CommercialLending #LenderCapacity #MortgageBroker #CFM

metadata.title: TIL/RESPA Final Rule on Integrated Mortgage Disclosures
metadata.author: CLA (CliftonLarsonAllen LLP)
metadata.shortDescription:
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) released one of its most significant regulatory changes to date — the integration of Truth in Lending (TIL) and Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act (RESPA) mortgage disclosures.
 
Beginning August 1, 2015, all financial institutions will start using entirely new forms for mortgage applications and closings. A change of this magnitude requires financial institutions to begin the implementation process far in advance.
 
This webinar discussed:
 •Current TIL/RESPA disclosure requirements
 •New loan estimate and closing disclosure content
 •Timing requirements of new disclosures

segments.text: Welcome to module one introduction to
supply chain
finance. Let's begin by understanding
the broader context of supply chains
specifically the difference between the
physical and financial supply
chain. The physical supply chain refers
to the actual movement of goods from raw
materials through
manufacturing to final delivery to the
customer. It includes all the logistics,
warehousing and transportation
activities that ensure products get
where they need to be when they need to
be there. The financial supply chain on
the other hand is the flow of funds and
related financial processes that support
these physical
movements. This includes payments,
credit, invoicing and financing
arrangements. While the physical supply
chain ensures goods are delivered, the
financial supply chain ensures that
payments are made efficiently and
working capital is optimized for all
parties
involved. Historically, these two flows
have often been managed separately, but
integrating them is now recognized as
key to unlocking working capital,
reducing costs, and increasing overall
supply chain resilience. Supply chain
finance, SCF, bridges these two worlds.
It is a set of financial solutions
enabled by both legal structures and
technology that allows buyers and
suppliers to optimize working capital
and cash flow. Crucially, SCF relies on
the irrevocable payment undertaking IPU
from the buyer, a binding commitment
that gives financeers the confidence to
advance funds to suppliers. We'll
explore the IPO in detail later in this
course. Let's compare SCF with
traditional trade
finance. Traditional trade finance tools
such as letters of credit and export
credit insurance are designed to
mitigate risks like non-payment or
political
instability. These instruments are often
complex, involve many parties and may
require collateral.
SEF in contrast focuses on optimizing
payment terms and working capital
between buyers and
suppliers. The key differentiator is the
buyer's irrevocable payment undertaking
which assures financiers of payment and
allows suppliers to receive early
payment at a lower cost leveraging the
buyer's typically stronger credit
profile.
SEF is increasingly delivered via
digital platforms, but it's the legal
and financial structure that makes it
effective. Remember, SEF is not just
about
digitalization. It's about integrating
financial flows with physical flows
using the buyer's payment undertaking as
the
foundation. Why does SCF matter so much
in today's global trade environment?
Global supply chains are under constant
pressure from disruptions, be it
geopolitical events, pandemics, or
logistical bottlenecks. The coid9
pandemic, for example, exposed
vulnerabilities in both the physical and
financial supply chains. Many companies
struggled to source materials on time,
while others faced severe cash flow
crunches as payments were delayed or
demand fluctuated.
SCF has proven to be a vital tool for
resilience. For example, during the
pandemic, large buyers with robust SCF
programs were able to support their
suppliers with faster payments, ensuring
that production continued even as
markets shifted. Suppliers in turn could
access much needed liquidity without
resorting to expensive borrowing,
keeping their operations running and
safeguarding jobs.
A real world example in the automotive
industry, several major manufacturers
used SCF to support their tier 1 and
tier 2 suppliers during the pandemic. By
advancing payments through SCF
platforms, they prevented supply chain
breakdowns and maintained production
schedules, demonstrating how financial
and physical supply chain resilience go
hand in hand. This shift is also
reflected in supply chain strategy.
Companies are moving from a just in time
model which minimizes inventory and
relies on perfect timing to a just in
case approach which emphasizes
resilience, buffer stocks and flexible
financing. SF supports this transition
by freeing up working capital and
enabling companies to invest in
inventory and risk mitigation
strategies.
Let's look at the main players in the
SCF
ecosystem. Buyers, usually large
corporations with strong credit ratings.
Their financial strength is central to
SCF as their irrevocable payment
undertaking underpins the entire program
and allows suppliers to benefit from
lowerc cost financing.
Suppliers, businesses that provide goods
or services to the buyer. They benefit
from early payment and improved
liquidity. Financial
institutions. Hash Fintex provide the
funding and manage digital platforms
facilitating seamless
transactions. Logistics providers
support the physical movement of goods
and can share valuable data to enhance
integration.
Technology
partners enable the digital
infrastructure that links physical and
financial
flows, regulators and government
agencies. Set the legal and compliance
framework for SCF
programs. Collaboration and information
sharing among these stakeholders are
crucial for maximizing the benefits of
SCF and ensuring both physical and
financial supply chain resilience.
Now let's highlight the key benefits of
SCF for both buyers and suppliers. For
buyers, SCF enables extended payment
terms, optimizes working capital, and
strengthens supplier relationships by
supporting suppliers financially. Buyers
also reduce the risk of supply chain
disruptions and improve the reliability
of their operations.
For suppliers, SCF provides early access
to cash, often at a lower cost than
traditional financing, thanks to the
buyer's strong credit. This improves
liquidity, allows for better cash flow
management, and enables investment in
growth and resilience.
In summary, SEF is a win-win solution
that integrates the physical and
financial supply chains, unlocking
working capital, reducing risk, and
enhancing resilience for all parties
involved. In the next module, we'll
explore the core techniques and
instruments used in supply chain finance
and take a closer look at how the
irrevocable payment undertaking works in
practice.
