These instruments are often complex, involve many parties and may require collateral. SEF in contrast focuses on optimizing payment terms and working capital between buyers and suppliers. The key differentiator is the buyer's irrevocable payment undertaking which assures financiers of payment and allows suppliers to receive early payment at a lower cost leveraging the buyer's typically stronger credit profile. SEF is increasingly delivered via digital platforms, but it's the legal and financial structure that makes it effective. Remember, SEF is not just about digitalization. It's about integrating financial flows with physical flows using the buyer's payment undertaking as the foundation. Why does SCF matter so much in today's global trade environment? Global supply chains are under constant pressure from disruptions, be it geopolitical events, pandemics, or logistical bottlenecks. The coid9 pandemic, for example, exposed vulnerabilities in both the physical and financial supply chains. Many companies struggled to source materials on time, while others faced severe cash flow crunches as payments were delayed or demand fluctuated. SCF has proven to be a vital tool for resilience. For example, during the pandemic, large buyers with robust SCF programs were able to support their suppliers with faster payments, ensuring that production continued even as markets shifted. Suppliers in turn could access much needed liquidity without resorting to expensive borrowing, keeping their operations running and safeguarding jobs. A real world example in the automotive industry, several major manufacturers used SCF to support their tier 1 and tier 2 suppliers during the pandemic. By advancing payments through SCF platforms, they prevented supply chain breakdowns and maintained production schedules, demonstrating how financial and physical supply chain resilience go hand in hand. This shift is also reflected in supply chain strategy. Companies are moving from a just in time model which minimizes inventory and relies on perfect timing to a just in case approach which emphasizes resilience, buffer stocks and flexible financing. SF supports this transition by freeing up working capital and enabling companies to invest in inventory and risk mitigation strategies. Let's look at the main players in the SCF ecosystem. Buyers, usually large corporations with strong credit ratings. Their financial strength is central to SCF as their irrevocable payment undertaking underpins the entire program and allows suppliers to benefit from lowerc cost financing. Suppliers, businesses that provide goods or services to the buyer. They benefit from early payment and improved liquidity. Financial institutions. Hash Fintex provide the funding and manage digital platforms facilitating seamless transactions. Logistics providers support the physical movement of goods and can share valuable data to enhance integration. Technology partners enable the digital infrastructure that links physical and financial flows, regulators and government agencies. Set the legal and compliance framework for SCF programs. Collaboration and information sharing among these stakeholders are crucial for maximizing the benefits of SCF and ensuring both physical and financial supply chain resilience. Now let's highlight the key benefits of SCF for both buyers and suppliers. For buyers, SCF enables extended payment terms, optimizes working capital, and strengthens supplier relationships by supporting suppliers financially. Buyers also reduce the risk of supply chain disruptions and improve the reliability of their operations. For suppliers, SCF provides early access to cash, often at a lower cost than traditional financing, thanks to the buyer's strong credit. This improves liquidity, allows for better cash flow management, and enables investment in growth and resilience. In summary, SEF is a win-win solution that integrates the physical and financial supply chains, unlocking working capital, reducing risk, and enhancing resilience for all parties involved. In the next module, we'll explore the core techniques and instruments used in supply chain finance and take a closer look at how the irrevocable payment undertaking works in practice.

metadata.title: Trade Finance vs. Supply Chain Finance: Key Differences Explained (With Real Examples)
metadata.author: Vanijja | Trade Insights
metadata.shortDescription:
Are Trade Finance and Supply Chain Finance just two different names for the same bank loan? No—and confusing them can cost your business thousands in trapped working capital. 

With a global trade finance gap exceeding $1.5 trillion, understanding how cross-border commerce gets funded is essential for exporters, importers, bankers, and supply chain professionals. Using a real-world scenario between a Vietnamese furniture manufacturer and a Parisian department store, we break down the exact legal mechanics, timing, risk assessments, and financial instruments behind both disciplines.

🔑 Key Takeaways from This Video:
• The Core Difference: Traditional Trade Finance acts like a strict escrow agent focused on single shipments and physical documents, while Supply Chain Finance (SCF) acts like a digital logistics dashboard unlocking liquidity across continuous open account invoices.
• Solving Open Account Cash Starvation: How SCF eliminates 90-day payment delays for suppliers without requiring traditional physical collateral.
• Pre-Shipment vs. Post-Shipment Timing: Why Trade Finance can fund raw material purchases before goods exist, whereas SCF triggers after invoice approval.
• Credit Arbitrage in Action: How small suppliers bypass high local interest rates (e.g., 12%) by leveraging a large corporate buyer’s pristine credit rating (e.g., 2%).
• The Daily Toolkit: When to use a Letter of Credit (LC) for ironclad payment security versus Payables Finance (Reverse Factoring) for fast working capital.

💬 Join the Discussion:
If you were running a growing manufacturing business expanding into global export markets, which would you prioritize first—the ironclad payment security of a Letter of Credit, or the frictionless liquidity of an open account Supply Chain Finance program? Drop your thoughts in the comments below!

🔔 Subscribe to Vanijja | Trade Insights for clear, practical breakdowns of international banking, trade finance instruments, and global commerce mechanics.

chair order from a highly profitable
Parisian department store.

looking at physical collateral. They

themselves. If the buyer defaults on
payment, the bank retains the legal
right to seize the cargo or claim the
shipping insurance.

supply chain finance, we have to look at
how banks treat different borrowers.

high 12% interest rate for bank loans.

department store on the right. Because
they are a huge, highly profitable
corporation, banks view them as
incredibly safe borrowers, rewarding

When that connecting bridge forms, we
see a clever financial swap in action.
Think of it like a financially
rock-solid parent co-signing a car loan
so a teenager can get a cheaper deal.
The small supplier bypasses their own
weak credit entirely.
Once they submit an approved invoice,

on the giant French store's excellent
credit rating.
Supply chain finance serves a highly
specific purpose. It directly transfers
the financial benefits of institutional

of credit to safely purchase their raw

final invoice from the French department
store.
This comparison matrix lines up the

physical paper and single, isolated
shipments. Supply chain finance relies
on digital data and a continuous flow of
approved business.

metadata.title: Cash Flow Problems? Here's How Supply Chain Finance Provides the Solution
metadata.author: Vanijja | Trade Insights
metadata.shortDescription:
Ready to unlock hidden financial power in your business? This video is your comprehensive guide to understanding and leveraging supply chain finance (SCF) to optimize cash flow and boost your company's performance. We break down the complex world of working capital and show you how a strategic approach to SCF can be a game-changer for your bottom line.

​What you will learn:
- ​The Working Capital Puzzle: Discover how a long cash conversion cycle can create cash flow problems, even for profitable businesses.
- ​What is Supply Chain Finance?: Get a clear definition of SCF and how it makes cash flow between a buyer and supplier more efficient.
- ​The SCF Financial Toolkit: Explore the two main categories of SCF solutions: receivables purchase and loan-based solutions.
- ​A Buyer-Supplier Win-Win: Learn how SCF benefits both buyers (extending payment terms) and suppliers (getting paid faster).
- ​The Big Picture Impact: Understand how SCF can improve your free cash flow and Return on Capital Employed (ROCE).

​Ready to dive deeper?
For more insights into business, finance, and logistics, visit our blogs and connect with us on social media!

But honestly, the key thing to remember is that the timing of when that cash comes in versus what it has to go out, well, that's everything. And that timing gap has a name. It's called the cash conversion cycle or CCC for short. Let's make this super simple. Imagine you run a business that makes t-shirts. Okay, so first you have to buy the cotton, right? You pay your supplier for that. Then you have to pay your workers to actually make the shirts. All that money is out the door, but you haven't been paid by your customer yet. The time between you paying for all your supplies and you finally getting cash back from selling the t-shirt, that entire period is your cash conversion cycle. And you can probably guess the longer that cycle is, the more of your own cash is just stuck trapped in the system. Okay, so now that we have a really good grasp on the problem, this cash conversion cycle that ties up all our money, let's move on to the solution. And this is where supply chain finance or SCF comes in. It's kind of the hero of our story today. So what exactly is supply chain finance? At its core, it's a whole set of financial solutions designed to do one thing really, really well. optimize a company's working capital. It's all about making the flow of cash between a buyer and its suppliers way more efficient. Basically, it's a direct attack on shortening that cash conversion cycle we just talked about. Yep. And this right here is the main goal. The entire purpose of SCF is to bridge that cash gap we've been talking about, the one between paying your suppliers and getting paid by your customers. Now, I know what you're thinking. How can it help a supplier get paid faster while at the same time allowing the buyer to pay later? It sounds like some kind of financial magic trick, right? But it's not magic. It's just really clever finance. So, let's pull back the curtain and see how it actually works. All right, let's jump into our third section. It's time to open up the SCF financial toolkit and look at the actual nuts and bolts, the specific techniques that make this whole thing possible. Okay, so generally all of these SCF solutions fall into two main categories. On one side, you have what's called receivables purchase. This is where a seller or a supplier literally sells its unpaid invoices, you know, the money its customers owe them to a bank or financeier. Why? To get cash right now. A huge advantage here is that this is offbalance sheet, meaning it doesn't look like debt. On the other side, you've got loan-based solutions, and these are a lot more straightforward. This is when a company just takes out a loan using its assets like its inventory or those same receivables as collateral. So the big difference to remember is are you selling an asset or are you borrowing money? Now if we look closer at that first bucket, the receivables purchase one, you're going to hear a bunch of different terms thrown around like receivables discounting for fetting or factoring. Honestly, they're all just different flavors of the same idea. Selling an invoice to get paid early. But there's one I really want you to focus on here. Payables Finance. This one is a little different because it's a program that's actually set up by the buyer to help out their suppliers. And that's a real gamecher. And then on the loanbased side, it's pretty much what it sounds like. We're talking about a loan or an advance against your receivables or maybe against your inventory. These are direct traditional loans. And because they're loans, they show up as debt on the company's balance sheet. Pretty straightforward. So now we've seen the tools in the toolkit, but here's what makes supply chain finance and especially that payables finance. we mentioned so incredibly powerful. It's not about one company winning in another's expense. It's not a zero- sum game. It's specifically designed to create shared value. It is a genuine win-win for both the buyer and the supplier. Let's take a look at how that's even possible. Okay, first let's put ourselves in the shoes of the buyer, the big company that's purchasing all the stuff. You might be wondering, why would they bother setting up this whole complex financial program just to help their suppliers? Well, the benefits for them are massive. The big one is that the buyer can extend their payment terms. So, instead of paying their bills in 30 days, maybe they now pay in 60 or 90 or even 120 days. That means they get to hold on to their cash for a lot longer, which is great for their working capital. This improves a key metric called days payables outstanding or DPO. But it's not just about hoarding cash. By making sure their suppliers are financially healthy and not struggling, they build a much stronger, more reliable supply chain. And of course, all that cash they're holding on to can now be used for other important things like investing in new projects. Okay, that all sounds fantastic for the buyer, but hang on a second. What about the supplier? They're the ones being told, "Hey, you're now going to have to wait 90 days to get paid instead of 30." On the surface, that sounds like a terrible deal for them, right? And it would be, except this is where that win-win magic really happens. So, here's the brilliant part. Even though the buyer isn't going to pay for say 90 days, the supplier has the option to get paid by a bank on day one or day two whenever they want. This dramatically improves their key metric, days sales outstanding or DSO. But here's the absolute best part. The interest rate or the fee for getting that money early isn't based on the small supplers's credit risk. It's based on the giant supercreditworthy buyer's credit rating. This means the supplier gets access to cash at a much much lower cost than they could ever get on their own. It's fast, it's cheap, and it lets them grow their business without taking on a bunch of expensive debt. So, we've seen how this helps both sides operationally. But now, let's zoom out for our last section and look at the really big picture. Why do the folks in the seauite, especially the chief financial officer, get so excited about this? It's because SCF doesn't just make things run smoother. It fundamentally transforms some of the most important numbers that measure a company's health. The first big one is free cash flow or FCF. You'll often hear investors call this the king of all financial metrics. And for good reason. It's the actual hard cash a company has left over after paying all its bills and investing in its future. This is the money that's used for everything that makes shareholders happy. Paying dividends, buying back stock, paying down debt, or making big innovative bets. And as you can imagine, SCF gives a huge direct boost to free cash flow. The second metric is called return on capital employed or ROCE. This one sounds a bit complicated, but the idea is simple. It basically measures how good a company is at using its money to make more money. Think of it as the financial bang for your buck. Obviously, a higher ROCE is always better, and SCF can make this number look a whole lot better, too. And this table really says it all. This shows the before and after impact and the numbers are just staggering. Just look at the buyer. Their free cash flow more than triples, jumping from 20 million to 70 million. And then look at the supplier. Their cash flow goes up by more than six times. And both of their ROC numbers get a healthy boost. I mean, these aren't just small incremental improvements. This is a total gamecher for both companies. This is the proof right here in the numbers of that win-win we've been talking about. So, let's wrap this all up. We started with the working capital puzzle, that big cash gap that can trip up even profitable companies. And we saw how supply chain finance provides the perfect solution. It's this incredible toolkit that creates a genuine win-win. Buyers get to hold on to their cash longer, suppliers get access to cheap early payments, and the most important financial metrics for everyone involved get a massive boost. So, that really leaves us with one final big question to think about. Is a company's supply chain just another cost center to be minimized? Or is it actually a hidden source of financial power just waiting to be unlocked? What do you think? I'd love to hear your thoughts, so please leave a comment down below. If you found this explanation helpful, a like on the video would be amazing, and make sure you subscribe for more deep dives just like this one. Thanks so much for watching.

metadata.title: PO Financing for Manufacturers and Fabricators
metadata.author: Mobilization Funding
metadata.shortDescription:
Purchase Order Financing, or PO Financing, is a type of commercial financing that leverages the purchase order from your customer as collateral for the loan.

Purchase Order Financing offers you cash before the work starts, which makes it an attractive option for manufacturers with tight cash flow. PO financing is based on your purchase order, your customer’s credit, and your supplier’s reputation. A lender will charge an interest rate on the advance, usually somewhere between 1 to 6 percent per month.

Learn more here: https://mobilizationfunding.com/2020/09/18/po-financing-manufacturers/

Like what you just watched? Subscribe to our newsletter: https://mobilizationfunding.com/newsletter-subscriptions/

metadata.title: 25 years of supply chain finance  A journey to unlock liquidity
metadata.author: Trade Finance Global
metadata.shortDescription: Supply chain finance has always been crucial in creating working capital solutions for companies. However, as established supply chains are buffeted by events such as COVID-19 or structural shifts caused by the impact of US tariffs, supply chain finance will play an increasingly crucial role in facilitating negotiations and enabling trade.

segments.text: Hello, and welcome to Trade Finance Talks.
I'm Mahika Ravi Shankar, deputy editor at Trade Finance Global,
and we're coming to you from the 51st annual ITFA conference in Singapore.
I'm joined today by Natasha Condon from JPMorgan, and we're going to talk about
the last quarter-century in and around supply chain finance.
Natasha, thank you so much for joining me today.
Thank you for having me.
We'll start with a few introductions.
Just tell me a bit about your background and your role within JPMorgan, and also
what brings you to ITFA this year.
I'm Natasha Condon.
I run sales globally for JPMorgan trade and working capital,
which means I get to work with the best corporates
and the best banks in the world.
And I have been about 20 years in the industry,
in which I have had the privilege of learning an enormous amount from a lot
of people who are here today, actually, at this conference.
JPMorgan is platinum sponsor for ITFA and has been for a number of years.
It's been a fantastic tool for us to get to know our clients
and good partners in the industry.
I come here whenever I can to learn about what's changing,
what's coming down the pipe, and what I need to think about the following year.
Good, I'm going to start with
a question on something that's been really prevalent and always
ubiquitous during this conference, which is the theme
of volatility and uncertainty.
How does supply chain finance help businesses remain resilient
through these times?
I mean, look, supply chain finance and all forms of working capital finance are
a way to benefit both parties.
Fundamentally, you're solving a very simple problem in that somebody wants
to pay as late as possible and somebody wants to get paid as quick as possible.
Fundamentally, you know, supply chain finance in particular,
obviously, at its best provides a very significant
benefit to typically a smaller supplier who might not be able to access that kind
of funding, certainly not at that price against their own bank lines.
Historically, you see it used for working capital purposes.
You see it used in commercial negotiations.
That is particularly critical this year when there is significant disruption
in a whole bunch of very well established supply chains.
And we see people using that now as a tool to help them with those negotiations.
So in some small way, it is helping the wheels of commerce
to turn in difficult times.
You talk about the changes that have happened this year,
but I wonder if there's been anything learned from the supply chain
disruptions which happened during COVID.
Do you see any lessons carried over?
It's an interesting question.
I certainly think, COVID was a different kind of shock.
It was time-limited.
This is, I think, more structural, and in some ways, the lessons learned are
more, I think it's some in some ways more useful
to look back at things like the Global Financial Crisis in 2008.
You can see very much that corporates learned a lesson during that time around
access to liquidity, around making sure they've got a working capital buffer.
And I think you can very clearly see that lesson playing out right now.
People are making sure they've got a bit of extra cash in their pocket so that if
something changes overnight, they're ready to cope with it.
Thanks, I wanna pivot a little bit now
to another massive trend of this conference,
which is on tech and digitalisation.
How have you seen these trends shaping the supply chain finance industry?
It's a very interesting question because when we talk about digitalisation
in trade, you often go very quickly into traditional trade and kind of how can
I convert millions of pieces of paper into electronic documents,
and that leads you into the generative AI direction, which is obviously
a massive strength for JPMorgan,
but when you look at supply chain finance and working capital financing,
that stuff has generally been quite digitised from the start.
To me, the really interesting developments on that side are very much
around bringing down barriers to entry, making it easier
for people to use the product.
What I'm really excited about, we have this huge partnership with Oracle.
For example, we have an integrated solution in Oracle Fusion, which is
their newest version of their ERP.
If you're a corporate now, and you have that particular version of Oracle,
you already have my supply chain finance solution.
You just haven't switched it on yet.
And that is a real change.
I think we are all going to… I already have the partnership
with SAP Twilio, and I have a really advanced SAP integrator.
I think these kinds of integrated solutions are very interesting
development in that space.
The other one that we've barely scratched the surface of yet is tokenization.
Tokenization of, one of the big sort of buzzwords I've been
buzz phrases I've been hearing it for this year is tokenization of real world assets.
I think that is super interesting because we can all see that.
JPMorgan has a huge third party distribution arm.
We work with hundreds of banks to bring in funding for our programs.
If there are ways that I can use our technology advantage to bring in
more funding partners to collaborate better with the banks who are at this
conference among others to provide a better solution to my corporate clients,
that's a win for everybody involved.
Now to bring together your previous two answers,
you mentioned you've been in the industry for about 20 years.
What is the single biggest change that you've seen?
That's a really interesting question.
I was talking to you in the previous question about collaboration.
Maybe it is really about how the industry works together because, obviously,
we all compete fiercely every day for every transaction,
and that's how it should be.
But I think more and more, the trade finance industry,
it is expensive to be a trade finance bank.
You have to be very international.
There are compliance costs.
There are regulatory costs.
There are complexities that are getting greater every day.
You need deep pockets to make sure you are keeping up with the pace of innovation
and the tech spend that is required.
I think trade finance historically is
quite a fragmented industry.
There are a lot of banks in there.
It's not consolidated in the way some other branches of finance are.
I think there is a very clear macro pressure towards consolidation.
I wonder whether in future we are heading towards an industry structure
where you have these incredibly strong local and regional banks with deep, deep
relationships with their corporates in specific markets,
but without necessarily wanting to maintain an expensive
international network.
Then you have me and the banks who choose to be…
Who've got the ability to run that kind of international network,
who work with those partners to connect them to the other end
of the trade transaction.
And together, we both win a deal that we would not have been able
to win individually.
So I think that consolidation pressure creates a lot of really interesting
opportunities for the industry to work together, and I don't think
that was the case when I started out.
That's a really unique answer.
I haven't really heard that aspect before.
I feel people will always jump to tech.
Or to geopolitics, but you covered both of those already.
So I guess you had to say something new.
It's more fundamental.
Geopolitics is geopolitics, and we all swim in the water together.
Tech is obviously revolutionary, but particularly when you're talking about
the working capital products, I say they were born digital.
And we're going to find interesting ways to make them more innovative and more
exciting and easier for our clients to use, but those are incremental gains.
This change in the industry, I think, is going to change the way we all work
together, and that's really interesting to me.
To close off,
looking forward and on that note, what do you think will be the next biggest
change if we're conducting this interview in 2050?
I hope I will be happily retired on a beach in 2050.
I hope if we have this conversation in 2050, or you have it with one
of my brilliant juniors who will have taken over the world by then.
I hope if we have this conversation in 2050,
we will be living in a world in which trade finance looks a little bit
more like cash in terms of being smooth, digital, embedded, integrated,
tokenized, liquid, and you will be looking at solutions
that our clients use as easily as you use your own online banking in your
life as a consumer, which let's face it, is not something we have achieved
yet in trade finance.
You will get all of the advantages of the qualities of the solutions
we're offering today.
Maybe you'll see a bit of breadth across the working capital cycle
that we haven't seen up till now.
So we have payable solutions on the supply chain finance side.
We have obviously receivable solutions.
The industry is starting to think about inventory finance and JPMorgan's
pioneering some solutions in that space.
Maybe you will see a really flexible, integrated,
smooth, digital solution set that can help a corporate all the way along the working
capital cycle, and I really hope that's the future.
To think about something like that being as simple and easy to use as features like
mobile banking, which we're now so used to it's definitely an interesting prospect.
-That's it. -Tasha, thank you so much for joining me.
-Thank you so much. -Enjoy the rest of the conference.
Thank you.

metadata.title: Unlock the Lucrative World of Supply Chain Financing
metadata.author: Commercial Loan Broker Institute
metadata.shortDescription:
Are you ready to move into a market where your skills can unlock real growth for businesses - and your own career? Most people think supply chains stall because of trucks, ports, or labor shortages. The truth is far simpler (and more profitable for those who understand it): cash timing is the real bottleneck.

In my latest video, I break down exactly how supply chain financing  - works and why it’s one of the most lucrative, high-demand niches for commercial loan brokers and finance professionals right now.

Here’s what you’ll discover:
- The “Cash Clock” Framework: Learn how to pinpoint the exact moment cash gets stuck in a supply chain - and how to use the right financing tool to get things moving again.

- Three Flows, Three Solutions: Understand the three flows every supply chain runs on (goods, agreements, cash) and how to match purchase order financing, working capital lines, or invoice factoring to each cash gap.

- A Repeatable Broker Playbook: Get a step-by-step process to diagnose, package, and fund deals - no salesy scripts, just real advisory value that manufacturers, distributors, and logistics companies need.

If you’re serious about entering a market where your expertise is in demand and your impact is measurable, this is the video you can’t afford to miss.

0:00 Why Supply Chains Really Stall - It's a Cash Timing Problem
0:32 What You'll Learn - Diagnosing Cash Choke Points & Matching Financing Tools
1:12 How a Supply Chain Works - From Materials to Customer & the Weakest Link
2:02 The 3 Flows of Every Supply Chain: Goods, Agreements & Cash
3:29 The Cash Clock Explained - Why Capital Timing Kills Good Businesses
5:15 How Cash Gets Stuck in Transit & Why Financing Tools Are Logistics Tools
6:00 Mapping Financing Tools to Each Stage: Front, Mid & Back of Chain
8:12 Invoice Financing & Factoring — Accelerating Cash After Delivery
11:24 The Broker Playbook — 4 Steps to Identify Cash Gaps to Lead with Diagnosis

WATCH NEXT: 
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ctWaQk2YDgE&t=7s
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rG7b0xOxFxc

Drop your biggest question about supply chain financing in the comments - I read every one. And if you know someone ready to make a move into this space, share this post!

#SupplyChainFinancing #CommercialLoanBroker #BusinessFinancing

segments.text: A supply chain doesn't break. It stalls.
Most people blame trucks or factories or
ports or labor shortages, but the real
reason supply chain stall, especially
for growing businesses, is often much
simpler.
The cash timing doesn't support the next
step in the chain.
And once you understand that, financing
tools stop looking like debt and start
looking more like logistics, ways to
move cash to the right link in the chain
at the right time.
And in this video, you're going to learn
how to diagnose the cash choke point
inside a supply chain, and match it to
the right financing tools so the chain
keeps moving.
I'm Shane Walton, co-founder of the
Commercial Loan Broker Institute. And
we've helped launch and support over 400
brokerages nationwide, and we maintain
an active lender network that's used by
brokers placing deals with hundreds of
lenders. So, what I'm about to walk
through is the pattern that we see over
and over in the supply chain. Businesses
don't stall because the opportunity
isn't real, they stall because there's
timing gaps in the funding.
So, basics first. A supply chain is
moving materials to manufacturing, to
logistics, to distribution, to sale to
the customer, and
along the way, it's really a chain of
dependencies.
And it only moves as fast as the weakest
link.
If the materials don't arrive, nothing
gets built. If the equipment goes down,
production stops. If warehousing isn't
ready, then shipping is going to back
up. And if retailing can't receive yet,
the inventory piles up. That's the
physical side.
And most businesses don't stall out
because they can't move a pallet, they
stall because they can't fund the next
step in the chain.
And there are three separate flows that
underlie every supply chain. This is a
simple model that every supply chain
runs on. Flow one is physical goods.
That's what I was just talking about.
It's stuff, physical stuff moving
through the chain.
Flow two though is agreements.
And the supply chain is not just a
movement of goods, it's a sequence of
agreements that authorize each of those
movements.
Contracts, purchase orders, invoices,
delivery confirmation, payment terms,
these agreements are the permission
slips that say
you can produce now. You can ship now.
You can invoice now. You'll get paid
later. Here's the paper that says it.
And then you have flow number three, and
that's cash. This is the capital, the
fuel. And when cash is missing,
the chain isn't just slowing down, it
waits for the cash to arrive.
So next, we're going to walk through why
cash timing, not demand from the
client side, from customers, is often
the constraint for a huge number of
businesses. And the exact questions that
brokers can use to spot that restriction
really quickly.
So capital is this input across each of
the different steps. And timing of that
is the choke point that stops the
process. Capital buys everything that is
creating the motion. It's buying the
materials, the labor, the equipment, the
fuel, the inventory, the floor space,
the repairs, the freight, everything
along the way.
So here's the real world situation that
you've seen a thousand times.
A business lands a big contract, and the
opportunity is real. It's in their
hands. And the margins can even be
great.
But the business can't front the
necessary inputs.
A contract or an opportunity can be
highly profitable
and still be impossible for that
business
if the inputs can't be funded.
That's supply chain financing in one
sentence.
This is why you'll meet businesses that
look healthy on paper, but they still
can't take the next job. It's not
because they're failing, but because
their cash timing is wrong. Let's think
of this like a clock. All right, we'll
call it the cash clock or the cash in
transit clock. And here's what that
clock is measuring. You, as a business
owner, pay cash out and then you wait to
get your cash back.
Your cash clock is counting down how
long it is between spending and
collecting your cash. Cash goes out to
suppliers for labor, for shipping, for
inventory, and then cash comes back when
your customer pays based on terms.
So, the cash clock is simply how long is
cash tied up between sending it or
spending it and collecting. And the
longer that cash clock is running for,
the more working capital a business
needs just to keep operations rolling.
You can have demand, you can have profit
margins, you can have good operations,

The video is about DSCR loans for commercial real estate. The host, Beau Eckstein, explains that while DSCR loans are commonly used for one to four unit non-owner occupied properties, they can also work for commercial properties with five units and above. However, the availability and terms of the loan may depend on the specific situation.

Eckstein notes that DSCR loans are typically used for properties with 5 to 20 units. While the loan is available for larger properties, he suggests that other types of loans, such as bank debt or agency debt, may be more appropriate for properties in the multi-million dollar range. The occupancy level of the property may also affect the loan options available.

In conclusion, while DSCR loans are an option for commercial real estate with 5 to 20 units, the suitability of this loan depends on the specifics of the situation. It's essential to consider other loan options, such as bank debt or agency debt, for larger properties.

segments.text: What is a bridge loan in commercial real estate? Do you need fast capital
to close a property that you're acquiring? Well, a bridge loan may be the best option
for you. In this video, I want to talk about what a bridge loan is,
what to look out for when getting a bridge loan, when not to get a bridge loan, and
ultimately what terms should be expected when buying real estate with a bridge loan.
If you're buying value-add real estate or investment property,
then a bridge loan may be the best option for you. I'm going to break down all of the
details of what a bridge loan is. We're going to dive right into it.
Have you ever wondered how real estate investors get capital for a property when
the property’s not stabilized or it has a lot of damage? Well, the answer is bridge financing.
So, what is bridge financing? A bridge loan is short-term financing that bridges
the gap between acquiring a property and getting conventional financing and
stabilizing the property with long-term debt. A bridge loan
means it's temporary—typically 6 months to 24 months in duration.
The purpose of a bridge loan is it helps investors move quickly. That is the key. When there's a
great value-add opportunity or a building that a business needs to acquire in order to operate
their company out of, and they need to do it quickly, a bridge loan can be the right financing
tool. It allows you to close and execute quickly, even if there are challenges with the property.
So, what scenarios would you use a commercial real estate bridge
loan? I'm going to list five of them right here:
Buying value-add property that needs a lot of capital, deferred maintenance, and renovations.
Acquiring a property with low occupancy or unstable income,
meaning that the tenants are leaving or their leases are almost expired.
Closing fast, where you need a 30- to 60-day closing period.
When you need to close but you're waiting for final loan approval from a conventional bank.
Refinancing out of a maturing loan where your loan that is coming due needs to be paid off.
A bridge loan can help you bridge that gap and pay off that loan before you find long-term financing.
So, what are the key features of a bridge loan? Well, like I said, the loan term is
six to 24 months in duration. The interest rate can range anywhere between 7% and 12%,
depending on the source of funds coming from the lender. The loan-to-value or the
leverage on the property ranges between 65% to 80% of the appraised value.
The speed of the loan can be as fast as 5 days up to 60 days, depending on the
bridge loan source. Amortization on the loan? Well, it's typically interest-only because it's
such a short-term loan. There's not a 30- or 40-year amortization. It's interest payments.
Costs can be more expensive. There can be a 1% origination fee up to 3% or 4% origination fees,
depending on how risky the loan is in the lender's eyes.
Prepayment penalty? Not typically. There may be a minimum period of 3 months of interest,
or some lenders do require you to fulfill the entire loan obligation of 6 to 24 months,
but overall that's pretty rare. There's typically no prepayment for a bridge loan.
Now, a key tip here is knowing your exit strategy before you enter the loan. The
bridge loan lender is going to want to know this as well. They want to know the exit strategy:
How am I going to get paid off, and what is the timeline around that? The last thing a bridge
lender wants to do is extend the loan out longer in the terms. And if you can't pay off the loan,
they can call the loan in default and take the property back. So, knowing the exit
strategy upfront—finding a conventional lender, a private investor, or a source of funds that can
pay off the bridge financing—is critical before entering a bridge loan agreement.
So, let's compare bridge loans to permanent or conventional loans.
Bridge loans: Short-term.
Permanent loans: Long-term, with a 5-year to 30-year maturity date.
Bridge loans have a lot more flexibility in underwriting. They may not require income from the
property or stabilization. Permanent loans have strict debt coverage ratio requirements.
They need to know that the property generates enough income in order to pay the interest,
which is typically a 1.2 to 1.3 debt coverage ratio. This means that there's at least $120 to
$130 of NOI (net profits) coming in from the property before you pay debt. That margin
makes the lender secure that there's enough income to support the loan debt payments.
Bridge loans have higher interest. They typically have a 300- to 600-point spread above the index,
meaning their interest rate could be 2%, 3%, or 4% higher than a conventional loan.
Permanent loans have lower interest. The more stable the property, the better the market,
the lower the leverage—the lower the interest rate, because there’s less risk to the lender.
Bridge loans can close very fast. As long as the lender has a reputation for executing,
they can typically close the loan within 30 days. Permanent loans need to go through
underwriting and committee review. This is a long process, which could take 60, 90, even 120+ days.
Bridge loans are used for value-add or non-stabilized asset use,
possibly even partial developments or lease-up projects. Permanent loans are
used for stabilized properties or owner-user properties where there's
consistency in the income and occupancy. That’s more comfortable for the lender.
The bottom line: You're going to use bridge loans for speed and flexibility. It's not a
long-term solution. It's a short-term solution for getting a property under your control,
owning it, making the improvements, and then getting a permanent loan.
So, who are the permanent lenders? They’re the regional banks and credit unions,
the Wells Fargos, the Bank of Americas, the Chase Banks. These are CMBS loans and life
insurance companies. They're permanent loans used for stabilized properties.
So, who are the bridge lenders? I highly recommend that you work with a loan broker to help you find
the right bridge lenders. When I'm buying a value-add property, I work with a handful of
private lenders or bridge lenders that allow me to close quickly. We buy mobile home parks,
self-storage facilities, and small-bay industrial at my firm, Patriot Holdings. And my loan broker
is critical in sourcing capital for me. The loan broker sources that capital by having
that database of all the bridge lenders. These can consist of credit unions. They can consist
of debt funds. They can consist of family office sources of capital where the family office lends
capital. Also, non-bank lenders. These are private lenders where individuals will pool together money
and lend those on commercial properties. And then lastly, there are certain banks
that like to lend on bridge products because of the higher interest rate and short-term payoff.
So, check in the comments below. I'm going to leave links to the commercial brokers
that I work with. If you're looking for a bridge loan, give them a call.
They do a great job for me, and their goal is to create competition amongst lenders
so you get the best bridge loan possible that supports your real estate project.
So, wrapping it up—risks and considerations to evaluate when looking at a bridge lender. First,
I think you should be experienced in commercial real estate or have counsel or advisory from
a legal professional who can help you look at the loan docs. Bridge lenders range in a wide
variety of character. There are some bridge lenders that lend to take the property back,
and the provisions in the loan documents are very restrictive, or there are hidden
provisions that would default the loan so they can call it due and take the asset. You do not
want to work with these types of bridge lenders, and some bridge lenders are very unforgiving.
They have a short timeline. If you cannot stabilize the property and find an exit
strategy for another source of funds, then you could put yourself in a precarious position
because that lender will want to be paid on time. You want to work with a lender that's going to be
flexible with you, or have that source of funds teed up where you're going to be able to pay
off the loan in that 6- to 24-month period. Remember, bridge lending is a high cost. So,
the project itself must be successful. The real estate investment must have the opportunity to
generate high yields to justify the cost of multiple origination points
charged by the lender. Plus, if you're using a broker, there's another origination point,
and then you have the high interest along the way. Be sure that you can create enough
value to justify all the costs of taking on a bridge loan. Bridge loans are not for beginners.
I highly recommend professional counsel to review it. I want to reinforce the fact that you should
get an attorney that evaluates commercial real estate loans and have them redline the documents.
A lesson that was new to me 15 years ago, when I was beginning my commercial real estate career,
is that I didn’t know commercial loan docs could be edited. My attorney would redline the documents
and change some of the provisions of the loan. This is typical. There are normal negotiations
between the lender and the borrower, and the borrower should be using professional counsel
to protect their interests. There’s compromise. Some lenders are going to say “take it or leave
it,” but the majority of times lenders will compromise and work with you to help get the right
loan terms where they're not egregious in some of the asks in the documents. If you don’t edit them,
then you are stuck with what's in writing. Be very careful before you sign your loan docs.
And lastly, the biggest risk is the exit pressure. From the beginning,
the clock is ticking. Be sure upfront that you know you can pay off that loan in time. One
final caveat with your bridge loan: you can ask for construction improvements, repairs,
or additional capital expenditures that they possibly can fund. If you don’t ask,
you don’t get it. If you need additional funds to create value in the property, ask for it upfront.
You can also ask for an interest reserve where you borrow 12 months of interest payment in the loan
amount that you can draw on to help make payments. It sounds counterintuitive, but you're borrowing
more money to be able to pay interest back to the lender. That is how commercial real estate
bridge loans can work. It helps you preserve your liquidity so you can use your equity to
buy the property and make improvements. You're not spending so much cash on interest payments while
stabilizing the property when there's no income or minimal income that isn’t covering the debt.
So, now that you know what a bridge loan is, how to get a bridge loan, and when to get a bridge
loan—in this next video, I'm going to look at the Big Beautiful Bill. This is very important for
real estate investors. If you're a real estate investor and you need tax benefits, and you're
going to be buying more commercial property or making property investments, watch this next
video on the Big Beautiful Bill. You will know everything you need to be the best real estate
investor possible, maximize the value of your portfolio, and make great investment decisions.

There's typically no prepayment for a bridge loan. Now, a key tip here is knowing your exit strategy before you enter the loan. The bridge loan lender is going to want to know this as well. They want to know the exit strategy: How am I going to get paid off, and what is the timeline around that? The last thing a bridge lender wants to do is extend the loan out longer in the terms. And if you can't pay off the loan, they can call the loan in default and take the property back. So, knowing the exit strategy upfront—finding a conventional lender, a private investor, or a source of funds that can pay off the bridge financing—is critical before entering a bridge loan agreement. So, let's compare bridge loans to permanent or conventional loans. Bridge loans: Short-term. Permanent loans: Long-term, with a 5-year to 30-year maturity date. Bridge loans have a lot more flexibility in underwriting. They may not require income from the property or stabilization. Permanent loans have strict debt coverage ratio requirements. They need to know that the property generates enough income in order to pay the interest, which is typically a 1.2 to 1.3 debt coverage ratio. This means that there's at least $120 to $130 of NOI (net profits) coming in from the property before you pay debt. That margin makes the lender secure that there's enough income to support the loan debt payments. Bridge loans have higher interest. They typically have a 300- to 600-point spread above the index, meaning their interest rate could be 2%, 3%, or 4% higher than a conventional loan. Permanent loans have lower interest. The more stable the property, the better the market, the lower the leverage—the lower the interest rate, because there’s less risk to the lender. Bridge loans can close very fast. As long as the lender has a reputation for executing, they can typically close the loan within 30 days. Permanent loans need to go through underwriting and committee review. This is a long process, which could take 60, 90, even 120+ days. Bridge loans are used for value-add or non-stabilized asset use, possibly even partial developments or lease-up projects. Permanent loans are used for stabilized properties or owner-user properties where there's consistency in the income and occupancy. That’s more comfortable for the lender. The bottom line: You're going to use bridge loans for speed and flexibility. It's not a long-term solution. It's a short-term solution for getting a property under your control, owning it, making the improvements, and then getting a permanent loan. So, who are the permanent lenders? They’re the regional banks and credit unions, the Wells Fargos, the Bank of Americas, the Chase Banks. These are CMBS loans and life insurance companies. They're permanent loans used for stabilized properties. So, who are the bridge lenders? I highly recommend that you work with a loan broker to help you find the right bridge lenders. When I'm buying a value-add property, I work with a handful of private lenders or bridge lenders that allow me to close quickly. We buy mobile home parks, self-storage facilities, and small-bay industrial at my firm, Patriot Holdings. And my loan broker is critical in sourcing capital for me. The loan broker sources that capital by having that database of all the bridge lenders. These can consist of credit unions. They can consist of debt funds. They can consist of family office sources of capital where the family office lends capital. Also, non-bank lenders. These are private lenders where individuals will pool together money and lend those on commercial properties. And then lastly, there are certain banks that like to lend on bridge products because of the higher interest rate and short-term payoff. So, check in the comments below. I'm going to leave links to the commercial brokers that I work with. If you're looking for a bridge loan, give them a call. They do a great job for me, and their goal is to create competition amongst lenders so you get the best bridge loan possible that supports your real estate project. So, wrapping it up—risks and considerations to evaluate when looking at a bridge lender. First, I think you should be experienced in commercial real estate or have counsel or advisory from a legal professional who can help you look at the loan docs. Bridge lenders range in a wide variety of character. There are some bridge lenders that lend to take the property back, and the provisions in the loan documents are very restrictive, or there are hidden provisions that would default the loan so they can call it due and take the asset. You do not want to work with these types of bridge lenders, and some bridge lenders are very unforgiving. They have a short timeline. If you cannot stabilize the property and find an exit strategy for another source of funds, then you could put yourself in a precarious position because that lender will want to be paid on time. You want to work with a lender that's going to be flexible with you, or have that source of funds teed up where you're going to be able to pay off the loan in that 6- to 24-month period. Remember, bridge lending is a high cost. So, the project itself must be successful. The real estate investment must have the opportunity to generate high yields to justify the cost of multiple origination points charged by the lender. Plus, if you're using a broker, there's another origination point, and then you have the high interest along the way. Be sure that you can create enough value to justify all the costs of taking on a bridge loan. Bridge loans are not for beginners. I highly recommend professional counsel to review it. I want to reinforce the fact that you should get an attorney that evaluates commercial real estate loans and have them redline the documents. A lesson that was new to me 15 years ago, when I was beginning my commercial real estate career, is that I didn’t know commercial loan docs could be edited. My attorney would redline the documents and change some of the provisions of the loan. This is typical. There are normal negotiations between the lender and the borrower, and the borrower should be using professional counsel to protect their interests. There’s compromise. Some lenders are going to say “take it or leave it,” but the majority of times lenders will compromise and work with you to help get the right loan terms where they're not egregious in some of the asks in the documents. If you don’t edit them, then you are stuck with what's in writing. Be very careful before you sign your loan docs. And lastly, the biggest risk is the exit pressure. From the beginning, the clock is ticking. Be sure upfront that you know you can pay off that loan in time. One final caveat with your bridge loan: you can ask for construction improvements, repairs, or additional capital expenditures that they possibly can fund. If you don’t ask, you don’t get it. If you need additional funds to create value in the property, ask for it upfront. You can also ask for an interest reserve where you borrow 12 months of interest payment in the loan amount that you can draw on to help make payments. It sounds counterintuitive, but you're borrowing more money to be able to pay interest back to the lender. That is how commercial real estate bridge loans can work. It helps you preserve your liquidity so you can use your equity to buy the property and make improvements. You're not spending so much cash on interest payments while stabilizing the property when there's no income or minimal income that isn’t covering the debt. So, now that you know what a bridge loan is, how to get a bridge loan, and when to get a bridge loan—in this next video, I'm going to look at the Big Beautiful Bill. This is very important for real estate investors. If you're a real estate investor and you need tax benefits, and you're going to be buying more commercial property or making property investments, watch this next video on the Big Beautiful Bill. You will know everything you need to be the best real estate investor possible, maximize the value of your portfolio, and make great investment decisions.

metadata.title: Debt Yield vs. DSCR: The Metric Every Commercial Mortgage Broker Needs to Understand
metadata.author: Academy For Commercial Lending
metadata.shortDescription:
Debt Yield and DSCR are two of the most important underwriting metrics in commercial real estate finance, but they answer very different questions. In this video, I explain why lenders evaluate both and why understanding the difference can help you structure stronger loan requests and avoid deals that fail during underwriting.

We also examine today's commercial real estate maturity wall and why Debt Yield, not DSCR, has become one of the primary metrics lenders use when refinancing maturing loans. With nearly $800 billion in commercial mortgages maturing this year and another $677 billion next year, refinance risk has become one of the defining issues in commercial lending.

In this video you'll learn:

What Debt Yield measures and how to calculate it
How DSCR differs from Debt Yield
Why Debt Yield is unaffected by interest rate changes
Why loans with acceptable DSCR can still fail refinance
Typical Debt Yield expectations by asset class
Why multifamily and owner-occupied properties have different Debt Yield requirements
Practical underwriting tips every commercial mortgage originator should know

Whether you're a commercial mortgage broker, residential loan officer expanding into commercial lending, investor, or commercial real estate professional, understanding Debt Yield will make you a stronger originator and help you anticipate lender decisions before submitting a deal.

Learn more about commercial lending education:
https://academyforcommerciallending.com

Subscribe for weekly videos covering:

Commercial Lending
Commercial Real Estate Finance
Commercial Underwriting
Multifamily Lending
SBA Lending
DSCR Loans
Commercial Appraisals
Loan Packaging
Small Balance Commercial Real Estate

Source: Trepp Inc., The CRE Rundown

segments.text: One of the biggest mistakes new
commercial originators make is assuming
that debt yield and DSCR measure the
same thing. They don't. DSCR measures
the borrower's ability to make the loan
payment.
It compares the property's net operating
income to its annual debt service.
Because debt service changes with
interest rates, DSCR can improve or
deteriorate even when the property's
income never changes.
Debt yield measures something entirely
different.
It compares net operating income to the
loan balance.
Since it ignores the interest rate and
amortization, it's a pure measure of
lender risk and collateral protection.
That's why lenders rely on it so heavily
when refinancing maturing loans or
evaluating leverage.
The simplest way to remember the
difference is this.
DSCR asks,
"Can the borrower make the payment?"
Debt yield asks,
"If this loan defaults, how much equity
cushion does the lender have?"
Strong commercial underwriters evaluate
both because a loan can have an
acceptable DSCR but still have a weak
debt yield if leverage is too high.
Roughly 15% of the outstanding
commercial mortgage universe comes due
this year. CREP puts the number at
billion. With another $676.9
billion or 13.45%
of the total following in 2027.
Within the CMBS market alone, $76.6
billion
faces hard maturity this year and the
bulk of it is back loaded into the
fourth quarter. Nearly $30 billion or
39% of the cohort
one metric consistently separated the
loans that refinanced cleanly from those
that struggled.
Debt yield.
Why this maturity wall looks different.
Many of the CMBS loans maturing this
year were originated in 2016,
when the 10-year Treasury averaged 1.84%
and the 5-year averaged 1.33%.
Coupons on those loans likely sit in the
to 4% range.
Loans written today generally start at
6% and up.
That gap between legacy coupon and
current market rate is the whole story
behind refinance risk this cycle,
and it shows up cleanly in the payoff
data.
billion of CMBS loans hit their hard
maturity.
Only 56% paid off on time.
Another 11% paid off late,
and 12.3 billion dollars remained
outstanding past maturity.
billion dollars matured.
70% paid off on time,
and 11.4 billion dollars still went
unpaid.
Trepp's data shows a consistent pattern
behind both years.
Loans that paid off on schedule carried
debt yields of 13.3%
at maturity.
Loans that didn't were sitting at
sub-10%
debt yields.
DSCR wasn't the variable separating
those two groups.
Debt yield was.
What debt yield actually measures.
Debt yield is net operating income
divided by loan amount.
That's it.
No interest rate in the formula.
No amortization schedule.
No assumption about what refinance terms
will look like 5 years from now.
It's a pure leverage check.
If a lender had to foreclose on the loan
today and hold the note, what yield
would that NOI represent against the
balance owed?
DSCR measures something different. It's
NOI divided by debt service, and debt
service is a function of the interest
rate and amortization at the time the
loan is written.
That makes DSCR sensitive to the rate
environment in a way debt yield is not.
A loan written in 2016 at a 3.75%
coupon could clear a comfortable 1.35x
DSCR at origination while carrying a
debt yield well under 10%
because the low rate kept debt service
manageable even against a large loan
balance relative to NOI.
That's the trap.
The loan looked perfectly healthy when
it was originated because low interest
rates produced an acceptable DSCR.
But debt yield never changed.
When rates reset at refinancing,
DSCR deteriorated while debt yield
revealed the leverage that had been
there all along.
Why the debt yield threshold moves by
asset class. Lenders don't apply one
debt yield number across every property
type.
Multifamily generally carries the lowest
debt yield requirement in the market,
often in the 8% to 9% range depending on
the lender and execution.
Special purpose and owner-occupied
assets run meaningfully higher,
frequently 11% to 13% or more.
The gap reflects how a lender thinks
about the workout scenario,
not just the income scenario.
Multifamily has deep, liquid exit
markets, agency execution through Fannie
Mae, Freddie Mac, and HUD,
and cash flow that spread across dozens
or hundreds of units, rather than
concentrated in one tenant or one use.
Owner-occupied and special purpose
properties carry more single point of
failure risk.
If the operating business fails or the
specific use becomes obsolete, the
lender is holding a harder asset to
release or sell.
The higher debt yield requirement is the
lender's way of building in more cushion
against that scenario before the loan is
ever written.
What this means for originators,
I always underwrite to both DSCR and
debt yield, not just the one the
borrower's income statement makes look
best.
A property can clear DSCR comfortably
and still fail a lender's debt yield
requirement.
And that gap widens the most in a lower
interest rate environment,
exactly the environment a lot of the
current maturity wall was originated in.
If I'm only screening on DSCR,
I can miss a deal that's thinly
capitalized on a pure leverage basis and
won't refinance cleanly when rates are
higher at maturity than they were at
origination.
For anyone originating today, the
practical takeaway is to run debt yield
alongside DSCR from the start, and to
know that the debt yield bar moves with
asset class.
A multi-family deal and a single-tenant
owner-occupied deal with identical DSCR
profiles can sit on very different
footing once debt yield enters the
underwriting.
DSCR tells you whether today's loan
payment works.
Debt yield tells you how much leverage
the property is really carrying.
In a refinancing market defined by
higher interest rates, lenders are
increasingly relying on the second
question to answer the first.
Source:
Trepp Inc., The CRE Rundown.

Because debt service changes with interest rates, DSCR can improve or deteriorate even when the property's income never changes. Debt yield measures something entirely different. It compares net operating income to the loan balance. Since it ignores the interest rate and amortization, it's a pure measure of lender risk and collateral protection. That's why lenders rely on it so heavily when refinancing maturing loans or evaluating leverage. The simplest way to remember the difference is this. DSCR asks, "Can the borrower make the payment?" Debt yield asks, "If this loan defaults, how much equity cushion does the lender have?" Strong commercial underwriters evaluate both because a loan can have an acceptable DSCR but still have a weak debt yield if leverage is too high. Roughly 15% of the outstanding commercial mortgage universe comes due this year. CREP puts the number at $797.1 billion. With another $676.9 billion or 13.45% of the total following in 2027. Within the CMBS market alone, $76.6 billion faces hard maturity this year and the bulk of it is back loaded into the fourth quarter. Nearly $30 billion or 39% of the cohort one metric consistently separated the loans that refinanced cleanly from those that struggled. Debt yield. Why this maturity wall looks different. Many of the CMBS loans maturing this year were originated in 2016, when the 10-year Treasury averaged 1.84% and the 5-year averaged 1.33%. Coupons on those loans likely sit in the 3.5% to 4% range. Loans written today generally start at 6% and up. That gap between legacy coupon and current market rate is the whole story behind refinance risk this cycle, and it shows up cleanly in the payoff data. In 2024, 37.6 billion of CMBS loans hit their hard maturity. Only 56% paid off on time. Another 11% paid off late, and 12.3 billion dollars remained outstanding past maturity. In 2025, 44.2 billion dollars matured. 70% paid off on time, and 11.4 billion dollars still went unpaid. Trepp's data shows a consistent pattern behind both years. Loans that paid off on schedule carried debt yields of 13.3% to 14.4% at maturity. Loans that didn't were sitting at sub-10% debt yields. DSCR wasn't the variable separating those two groups. Debt yield was. What debt yield actually measures. Debt yield is net operating income divided by loan amount. That's it. No interest rate in the formula. No amortization schedule. No assumption about what refinance terms will look like 5 years from now. It's a pure leverage check. If a lender had to foreclose on the loan today and hold the note, what yield would that NOI represent against the balance owed? DSCR measures something different. It's NOI divided by debt service, and debt service is a function of the interest rate and amortization at the time the loan is written. That makes DSCR sensitive to the rate environment in a way debt yield is not. A loan written in 2016 at a 3.75% coupon could clear a comfortable 1.35x DSCR at origination while carrying a debt yield well under 10% because the low rate kept debt service manageable even against a large loan balance relative to NOI. That's the trap. The loan looked perfectly healthy when it was originated because low interest rates produced an acceptable DSCR. But debt yield never changed. When rates reset at refinancing, DSCR deteriorated while debt yield revealed the leverage that had been there all along. Why the debt yield threshold moves by asset class. Lenders don't apply one debt yield number across every property type. Multifamily generally carries the lowest debt yield requirement in the market, often in the 8% to 9% range depending on the lender and execution. Special purpose and owner-occupied assets run meaningfully higher, frequently 11% to 13% or more. The gap reflects how a lender thinks about the workout scenario, not just the income scenario. Multifamily has deep, liquid exit markets, agency execution through Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and HUD, and cash flow that spread across dozens or hundreds of units, rather than concentrated in one tenant or one use. Owner-occupied and special purpose properties carry more single point of failure risk. If the operating business fails or the specific use becomes obsolete, the lender is holding a harder asset to release or sell. The higher debt yield requirement is the lender's way of building in more cushion against that scenario before the loan is ever written. What this means for originators, I always underwrite to both DSCR and debt yield, not just the one the borrower's income statement makes look best. A property can clear DSCR comfortably and still fail a lender's debt yield requirement. And that gap widens the most in a lower interest rate environment, exactly the environment a lot of the current maturity wall was originated in. If I'm only screening on DSCR, I can miss a deal that's thinly capitalized on a pure leverage basis and won't refinance cleanly when rates are higher at maturity than they were at origination. For anyone originating today, the practical takeaway is to run debt yield alongside DSCR from the start, and to know that the debt yield bar moves with asset class. A multi-family deal and a single-tenant owner-occupied deal with identical DSCR profiles can sit on very different footing once debt yield enters the underwriting. DSCR tells you whether today's loan payment works. Debt yield tells you how much leverage the property is really carrying. In a refinancing market defined by higher interest rates, lenders are increasingly relying on the second question to answer the first. Source: Trepp Inc., The CRE Rundown.

Download my FREE DSCR Cheat Sheet. 📥

Here’s the truth: most investors are playing Monopoly with their own money — and losing. 

Meanwhile, smart investors are using DSCR (Debt Service Coverage Ratio) loans to buy properties like they’re scooping up Boardwalk and Park Place.

The dumbest thing in real estate? Having cash in the bank, finding a property that pays for itself, and still getting denied because your tax returns make you look broke. Conventional lenders want pay stubs, W-2s, and clean tax returns. 

DSCR lenders? They only ask one thing: Does the rent cover the mortgage? If yes, you’re good. Write off your car, your dog, even your cousin’s Netflix account — it doesn’t matter.

I’ve helped investors who were told they needed co-signers, extra reserves, or that they “couldn’t buy more property.” With DSCR loans, I got them pre-approved for almost anything they wanted. No pay stubs. No tax returns. No underwriter grilling you about why you bought a new boiler last year. 

Just market rent versus the mortgage. That’s it. It’s that simple.

I’m Andrew Russell, a licensed Mortgage Loan Officer (15+ years) and Regional Executive Vice President at CrossCountry Mortgage. This channel is your mortgage FAQ hub, with a big focus on self-employed buyers and real estate investors. 

Drop your questions 👇 I turn them into videos.

metadata.shortDescription:
FREE Financial Analysis Fundamentals Course: https://www.realestatefinanceacademy.com/finance-prerequisite
Free Commercial Loan Document Kit: https://www.realestatefinanceacademy.com/commercial-loan-document-kit/

---
Debt service coverage ratio determines the maximum LOAN PAYMENT and LOAN AMOUNT that can be placed on a property, based on the property's income... In this video, I show you how it works.

DSCR FORMULAS:
1. Debt Service Coverage Ratio  = NOI / Debt Service
2. Maximum Annual Debt Service = NOI / DSCR
  
Debt Service Coverage Ratio - DSCR is an underwriting term used by lenders that effectively sets a minimum for the amount of net operating income available to cover the debt service. The ratio is often set right around 1.25, sometimes it's 1.2, sometimes it is 1.3, depends on the industry, the market, the market timing, and the product type.

Debt Service Coverage Ratio tells us how much extra cushion we need to have in our net operating income over the debt service or the annual loan payments. In this case, a 1.25 debt service coverage ratio means that the NOI needs to be 125%, or 1.25 times the amount of the annual loan payments. Debt service coverage ratio sets a limit on how much risk the lender's going to take in terms of what they loan compared to the cash flow on the property. They don't want to put borrowers in a position where they have barely enough net income to cover the debt service or, even worse, not enough net income, so the debt service coverage ratio builds in the amount of cushion that they want. Lenders can adjust this for competitive reasons, or market reasons, but it typically is about .25 over the debt service amount.

Example: $100,000 NOI / 1.25 DSCR = $80,000 Max Debt Service

metadata.shortDescription:
I once walked into a bank with a GREAT real estate deal.

The numbers worked. The cash flow looked incredible. The bank manager was impressed.

And then she rejected me.

Not because the deal was bad. Because I didn't have a job, and my debt-to-income ratio was too high.

I actually ended up WORKING at that bank just to qualify for the loan. But today, there's a much better option for real estate investors who want to scale: the DSCR loan.

In this video:

The term DSCR stands for “Debt Service Coverage Ratio.”  It is a financial metric used to evaluate a property's ability to generate enough income to cover its debt payments and to assess the risk and feasibility of a real estate investment. 

While it is one of the more obscure metrics, it’s definitely one that you should become familiar with if you’re going to be dealing with any commercial and non-owner occupied loans for your rental properties.

Here's how it works:

In order to calculate the DSCR, you'll need to divide the property's net operating income (NOI) by its total debt service (TDS). 

The NOI is the property's income from rent and other sources, minus all of its operating expenses.  Operating expenses do not include TDS and TDS is all principal and interest payments owed to a lender for that particular property.  

When doing this calculation, you would typically calculate it on a monthly basis, but it comes out to the same ratio on an annual basis as well.

segments.text: Maybe you heard someone mention DSCR
when talking about their latest real
estate investment. Or maybe you heard it
from a mortgage broker when referencing
the minimum requirements for a loan, and
you wondered, "What does that mean
exactly?" Well, you came to the right
place because in this installment of my
chalkboard real estate investing series,
I will explain what DSCR stands for and
how investors calculate and use it.
Let's get right into it. The term DSCR
stands for debt service coverage ratio.
It is a financial metric used to
evaluate a property's ability to
generate enough income to cover its debt
payments and to assess the risk and
feasibility of a real estate investment.
While it is one of the more obscure
metrics, it's definitely one that you
should become familiar with if you're
going to be dealing with any commercial
and non-owner occupied loans for your
rental properties. Here's how it works.
In order to calculate the DSCR, you'll
need to divide the property's net
operating income, NOI, by its total debt
service, TDS. The NOI is the property's
income from rent and other sources minus
all of its operating expenses. Operating
expenses include everything except for
TDS, and TDS is all principal and
interest payments owed to a lender for
that particular property. When doing
this calculation, you would typically
calculate it on a monthly basis, but it
comes out to the same ratio on an annual
basis as well. Let's take a look at a
quick example so you can get a better
idea of what I mean. Let's say that
you're looking at a 4-unit rental
property with a twocar garage. The
apartments combined rent for $4,000 per
month and the garage rents for another
$200 per month. So, the total gross
monthly income for this property is
$4,200. Let's say that the property's
owner paid expenses such as taxes,
insurance, utilities, maintenance,
repairs, capital expenditures, and
vacancy combined come to approximately
$2,200 per month. In order to figure out
the NOI, we would subtract $2,200 from
$4,200, and the resulting number in this
case would come to $2,000 per month.
Let's say you're looking to finance or
refinance this property and need a
$360,000 loan. At a 25-year amortization
and a 6% interest rate, your monthly
mortgage principle and interest would
come to
$2,319. This would be your TDS in this
example. Applying the DSCR formula, we
would divide the monthly NOI by the
monthly TDS, which is 2000 /
$2319, resulting in a DSCR of
0.86. Now, you don't need to be
particularly experienced in real estate
to know that this is not a very good
outcome from a pure cash flow
perspective, as you would have a monthly
deficit of
$319. And in fact, assuming these
numbers are correct, there is zero
chance you're getting a loan for
$360,000 from a bank on this property.
This is because in order for a property
to break even and cover all of its
expenses, including the debt service,
the DSCR has to equal at least
1.0. But that's just to break even. Most
banks will want to see a healthy cushion
in your monthly cash flow over and above
this number. Typically, the banks will
ask for a minimum DSCR of 1.2 or 1.2.
25. So in this example, it would mean
that if the bank's minimum DSCR
requirement was 1.2, the most that it
would be willing to lend on this
property would be about
$258,000. The way I figured that out is
by taking the $2,000 net operating
income, and dividing it by the bank's
minimum DSCR of 1.2. This equals
$1,666, which is the maximum principal
and interest payment, the TDS, that the
bank would allow you to have in this
case. Once I have the maximum monthly
mortgage payment, and I know that the
loan terms are 6% and a 25-year
amortization, it's just a matter of
plugging the numbers into a loan
calculator like the one on bankrate.com
and playing around with different loan
amounts until the monthly payment
matches $1,666.
The actual numbers for the NOI and the
TDS will vary from deal to deal. But
what's important is that you understand
how to use them in calculating the DSCR.
Also important is the fact that you
really never want your DSCR to be lower
than 1.0. If it is, it means that the
property is going to be cash flow
negative and also that you will not be
able to get a bank mortgage on it unless
you reduce the loan amount to the point
where the DSCR increases to the bank's
preferred minimum threshold. Obviously,
as the amount of money you can borrow
from the bank goes down, the amount of
money you have to come up with out of
pocket if you're trying to buy the
property goes up. Similarly, if you're
trying to do a cash out refinance, as
with the burr strategy, a lower loan
amount also means that you may not be
able to get all of the money you
initially invested back out. Speaking of
the burst strategy, if you want to learn
how you can make an infinite return
using this strategy and how I have been
able to grow from nine rental units to
120 rental units in just 5 years, click
or tap on this video on the screen and
I'll see you there.

metadata.title: Debt Service Coverage Ratio (DSCR) Explained
metadata.author: REtipster
metadata.shortDescription:
Full article:https://retipster.com/terms/dscr?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=terms&utm_content=7sx67OQUmsM

Debt Service Coverage Ratio (DSCR) measures the net operating income available to cover debt service (principal and interest) in a given operating period.

Debt Service Coverage Ratio (DSCR) is useful for analyzing financial statements and estimating cash flow for a business or investment property. Commercial lenders commonly use the debt service coverage ratio to establish creditworthiness and determine the size of the loan.

DSCR expresses the net operating income divided by the total debt service for a particular property.

For example, if the net operating income (NOI) is $100,000 and the total debt service is $80,000, the DSCR would be 1.25, often notated as 1.25x. This means that the property’s NOI covers debt 1.25 times.

Aside from getting insight into financing options, the debt service coverage ratio is a useful metric for real estate investors to use when comparing properties to add to their portfolios. DSCR provides a good cash flow estimate for prospective properties and can help an investor determine an offer amount.
