segments.text: What exactly is the debt service coverage ratio?
And why is it such an important number for real estate investors and their lenders?
In order to understand the debt service coverage ratio or DSCR for short
it's best to start by defining debt service in the first place,
simply put debt service is the amount of money needed
to cover the regular reoccurring loan payment
A.K.A both the principle and the interest for an outstanding loan.
The term is often used by bankers, accountants, investors, and other financial professionals,
because it can be used to refer to all of the borrowers outstanding loan payments.
For example, when a loan officer asks what's the monthly debt service on this loan,
they're referring to the total amount of monthly loan payment or payments a borrower is obligated to pay.
This can be for one loan, or it can be for several,
depending on how many loans a borrower has.
Lenders use this number in conjunction with the total income generated by a property
or in the case of financing a personal residence,
the net income a borrower makes from their job
to determine the debt service coverage ratio.
So what is the debt service coverage ratio?
In essence, it's a ratio that compares a loan applicant's net income
to their debt service obligation during a set period of time.
Here's an example.
If a business generates $500,000 in net operating income and the annual debt service is $400,000,
the debt service coverage ratio would be 1.25.
Again, that's $500,000 in net operating income divided by $400,000 in debt service
and that gets you a 1.25 DSCR.
In other words, for every $1 of debt service, the business will have 1.25 available to pay it.
To determine the debt service coverage ratio
you're simply dividing the NOI of a specific time period,
whether it's a month or a full year by the debt service amount for that same period of time.
Now you might be asking yourself what is considered a good DSCR?
A debt service coverage ratio of 1.0 is the break-even point.
So if the analysis shows that a business or investment opportunity is coming in below 1.0,
meaning 0.99 or lower,
they are officially operating at a loss and want to be able to afford the loan payments.
So anything above 1.0 shows positive cashflow,
however, a lender is typically going to want some kind of cushion in place
just in case of business or individual has a sudden drop in income.
Now, the exact amount of cushion depends on the type of business,
the risk appetite of the lender,
the condition of the market, and a whole lot of other factors.
So there isn't one correct amount that applies to all borrowers,
but generally speaking,
most asset based lenders want to see a DSCR of 1.2 or higher.
A business or investment opportunity with a DSCR of 1.5 or higher is normally perceived as really good
and may have a case for obtaining better rates on their loan,
depending on what the lender is willing to offer.
Now, be aware that DSCR requirements aren't set in stone.
Each lender has its own guidelines on
what's acceptable for any given property, industry and loan type.
Ultimately, the debt service coverage ratio
is a useful formula that real estate investors can use to compare different properties
and see how they fit into their investment strategy and portfolio.

metadata.title: The Solar Tax Credit Explained
metadata.author: Transform Solar
metadata.shortDescription:
Get an Instant Solar Estimate Today: https://gosolar.transform.solar/

Included in the Inflation Reduction Act was a strengthening of the existing Federal Solar Tax Credit (ITC). This federal tax incentive is a vehicle that promotes the affordable adoption of solar energy for a home or business.

The ITC is now available for homeowners that invest in solar energy at a rate of 30% of the project cost, until 2032. In 2033, the tax credit will step down to 26% of the project cost, and 22% in 2034 before expiring in 2035.

metadata.title: What is Solar Tax Equity Financing?
metadata.author: Rob Freeman | Insuring The Built Environment
metadata.shortDescription:
https://robfreeman.com/what-solar-tax-equity-financing/ - Solar project development is often financed with solar tax equity. The term refers to pairing a solar project that qualifies for tax incentives, but can’t use them, with an equity investor who has a tax liability and wants to invest in solar energy. 

A tax equity investor will usually invest 40% of the equity in a solar project in return for 100% of the tax benefits, plus additional cash proceeds, over a period of around 5 years. 

The result is reduced tax liabilities and a nice return on investment for the tax equity investor, a profitable solar project generating renewable energy for a customer who buys it from the solar developer.

metadata.title: The 30% Solar Tax Credit Didn't Disappear. It Moved.
metadata.author: The Money Side
metadata.shortDescription:
Last year, the government paid for 30% of your solar panels. This year, the pitch is "the panels are free." Both come from the same tax break. What changed is who gets it.

Since January 1, 2026, homeowners who buy panels no longer get the 30% federal credit. But the company that owns the panels on your roof can still claim one, and that's why leases, PPAs and $0-down offers are suddenly everywhere. In this video we follow the money in a $0-down solar deal: what one system really costs, what the company gets back, and the four lines in the contract that decide whether it's a good deal for you.

If someone is pitching you solar right now, or you already signed, this is the checklist to read first.

Chapters
00:00 - Intro
01:17 - Why the Pitch Changed
03:22 - What One System Really Costs
05:36 - Line One, the Escalator
08:03 - What the Company Gets Back
10:28 - Lines Two, Three and Four
13:31 - If You Take a Loan
15:43 - When Renting Wins
17:43 - Ending

About the numbers
The $150-a-month lease with a 2.99% yearly escalator (about $304 a month in year 25, about $65,500 in total) and the $40,000 loan with a 30% dealer fee are illustrations calculated by this channel from the sources below, not real quotes. The roughly $13,000 company tax break is a rough calculation: Sunrun's reported average credit rate applied to a median-priced system. Your prices, rates and state rules will differ.

Sources
IRS, FAQs on Public Law 119-21 changes to the residential clean energy credit (25D)
SEIA and Wood Mackenzie, US Solar Market Insight Q3 2026 (September 2026)
EnergySage Marketplace Report, first half of 2026 (October 2026)
Sunrun, Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results (November 4, 2026)
Sunrun, $267 million securitization press release (August 4, 2026)
SEIA, One Big Beautiful Bill Act fact sheet (July 2025)
U.S. Energy Information Administration, Short-Term Energy Outlook (November 2026)
Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, Issue Spotlight: Solar Financing (August 7, 2024)
Federal Trade Commission, Solar Power for Your Home; Cooling-Off Rule
Canary Media, Sunnova and Mosaic bankruptcies (June 11, 2025)
Solar Power World, court approves sale of Sunnova (August 1, 2025)
Canary Media, California cuts payments to new rooftop solar customers (December 2022)
Solar.com, Solar PPA rates in 2026 (January 2026)

This video is for education only and is not financial, legal or tax advice. Rules differ by state; check your own contract and local laws.

metadata.title: Transferrable tax credits can offset passive income tax liability with Jason Prince
metadata.author: Tax Alpha Insider
metadata.shortDescription:
The Inflation Reduction Act (2022) made it easier than ever to transfer tax credits, but most investors don't know anything about how this works.


Jason Prince of Giraffe Financial takes us through buying tax credits at a discount and applying them against a passive income tax liability.

videos.full_text: The value proposition is, you can purchase $1 of tax credits which offset $1 of your tax liability, but you can buy that dollar of tax credit at less than a dollar. Call it something like 85 cents. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act did cause a lot of anxiety. The good news, however, was despite a lot of headlines that the sky is falling, the tax credit transferability mechanism was preserved. What we've actually seen in practice is that the market is growing. >> [music] >> I'm Brett Sullivan. This is The Albatross, a show about concentrated asset risk and tax management, and I hope to see you at my conference, Basis Points Seattle. That's November 18th, 3 to 6 p.m. at Stoop Brewing, Capitol Hill. A tax credit reduces a tax liability dollar for dollar. Congress incentivizes developments like solar, wind, nuclear, and other energy projects with tax credits, and since 2023, they're transferable more easily than ever. Today I speak with someone who facilitates tax credit compliance and transfer. >> My name is Jason Prince. I'm the founder and CEO of Giraffe Financial. Our company has the letters IRA for the Inflation Reduction Act in the name, and we're a facilitator of tax credit transfer. The origin story of Giraffe really relates to our name. It's the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, and that's the reason why most people probably haven't heard of transferability because before the Inflation Reduction Act, transferability was not a mechanism that people took advantage of. It just didn't exist. The Inflation Reduction Act created this rule, the Internal Revenue Code Section 6418, which allows third parties to buy and sell tax credits. Energy tax credits have been around for decades, but before the Inflation Reduction Act, the only way to monetize them was through complex traditional tax equity structures. That's my background. worked in energy finance for 15 years under that old paradigm. In traditional tax equity, the entity that wanted to take advantage of the tax credit had to form a partnership to actually own the eligible energy property. So practical example, someone wants to take advantage of the tax credits. They're an investor. They actually form a partnership with a solar project owner. That partnership then takes advantage of the tax credits and distributes out proportionally cash and tax credits. So that's how it always used to work for decades and then the Inflation Reduction Act made it so that it's much easier for a third party to just buy credits and not have to form a partnership to be an owner. >> So this is like a fascinating development with the Inflation Reduction Act. So I think like most folks, I mean like the investors who are like listening to this and the allocators will be aware of something like the the partnership rules called an anti-mixing bowl. And that's where the seven-year kind of hold period for the partnership comes from. And essentially, and Jason, you can elaborate on this, but the idea is that like you have a party that's taxable, that has capital, and then you have traditionally a low tax or a no tax entity. And the way that the the way that Congress is incentivizing certain behavior is to grant tax credits. And oftentimes the no or low tax entity has no use for them and they need capital. And so these partnerships form to be able to transfer the tax credits to the taxable entity. >> Yes, you're you're spot on. It's really a symbiotic relationship where the synergy is you have one party that has a tax credit that they can't do anything with. And you have another party that wants the tax credit. Once we hit the Inflation Reduction Act and this new transferability mechanism took off, it absolutely boomed and has blossomed to become about a 60 billion dollar a year market. Here's how you can reduce your tax liability
by 30% or more of your total solar installation costs.
So Dale, a lot has changed in terms of the ITC.
the investment tax credit,
for residential and commercial entities.
Why don't we take a dive in and let's talk about,
first of all, the residential tax credit
and what that looks like right now.
- Sure, so it's richer than it had been.
- Yeah. - So we're back to 30%.
We've been there for years and then it gradually come down.
But we're back to 30% through 2032.
So it's a nice, long span of increased tax credits
for residential customers.
The tax credit for residential is under Section 25
and under Commercial Section 48.
And the rules are very different.
And one of the things we've seen with the IRA bill
that was passed was that changing even more drastically.
- [Warren] Right. - I mean, for years and years
it seemed like they were kind of viewed as the same thing,
even though they never were,
but they functioned pretty much the same way
and now we're seeing that change.
- Correct, and so one of the things you can't do
with the residential is you can't sell to sell the tax trade
like you can in the commercial.
- Correct. Correct.
Yeah, and there's a number of things
worn around the commercial.
There are add-ons for different things,
energy communities, low income, domestic content.
None of that applies to residential.
I actually had a call about that the other day
from one of our consultants asking about the transferability
of residential, and I said, "No, that's not gonna work."
So the residential is pretty much functional the same way
as it was because Section 25 was not really addressed
very much in the IRA except to move it to 30%.
- So let's talk about the ability to use the tax credit
in the current year if you have the liability,
and then the possibility of carrying it forward.
I know you can't go backwards, but if you could give
some details on carrying it forward.
- Yeah, and even here we have differences
between residential and commercial.
So with residential you can roll it forward
to the following year if you can't use it.
Under both of these, you have to owe the tax
to take advantage of the credit.
So under residential you can roll it forward
to the next year.
If you can't use it all this year,
you can roll it forward.
That's fine. You cannot roll it backward.
- [Warren] Okay. Yep.
- With the commercial, you can roll it backwards three years
and you can roll it forward for up to 22 years.
So you've got a much longer span.
Residential as far as how far you can roll it forward,
it's not really defined and it's not been defined
for years, even before the IRA bill.
There was confusion around that, but certainly as long
as the tax credit is in place, at least through 2032,
you'd be able to use it. - Okay.
So just in summary, for the tax,
for the residential component,
the tax credit is 30%, it's good through 2032.
And if you can't use it all of the tax credit
in the first year, you can carry it forward up until 2032,
is our understanding as of right now, at least.
So now let's talk about specifically commercial
and AG projects, and what that looks like.
And I know thanks to IRA Bill, there are more requirements
for larger projects that really are one megawatt AC
or larger, which are very large projects,
very little of what we do.
And then there are different guidelines
for projects that are under one megawatt AC.
Can you talk about those differences?
- Yeah, so the biggest difference between the two
is that if you go over a megawatt on the AC side,
you're gonna be required to get the 30% base tax credit.
You're gonna be required to have pay prevailing wage
for that area.
And you're gonna have to have an apprenticeship program
in place.
And to be really honest, a lot of solar companies
did not have that in place.
So that's a challenge for companies like ourselves
and others right now, is to develop
that apprenticeship program.
Under a megawatt, none of that's required.
So that's the biggest difference
between over and under megawatt.
- Right.
And we talked about in the residential section
with the commercial tax credit that's currently at 30%
as the base credit you can go back three years now,
it used to be two years.
You can now go back three years
and you can carry it forward for 22 years.
- Right.
- That's just for the base tax credit.
Now there are additional adders thanks to the IRA.
Talk about each one of those briefly.
- Yeah, so there's a varying amounts of detail that we know.
So let's start with the low-income community adder.
That's 10%. - Right.
- So if you're in that area, a designated area,
that meets that requirement, you can go
through an application process and it's actually twofold.
You have to apply with the EPA
and you have to apply with the IRS.
And you're gonna get scored.
At the first step of the EPA, you get scored
on whether how's that gonna rank against other projects.
Because there's a limit
to how much they're going to award here.
And it's based on the size, not on the dollars.
So it's 1.8 gigawatts that's gonna be available
under the low-income category.
- In that first part of the process,
the EPA is making a recommendation to the IRS
on whether or not to actually approve it.
And it's up to the IRS.
Just because you got approved in part one,
you may not get actually approved for it in part two.
- Yeah, because what's gonna happen is
it's gonna be oversubscribed probably.
So they're gonna have more than 1.8 gigawatts
and they're gonna have this scoring system
and they're gonna know how many people applied
and does your score get you anywhere close?
And they're gonna give you that recommendation.
- All right.
So that's where the first 10% adder is.
Now let's talk about the energy communities.
- Energy community is a little bit simpler.
They've already published a map.
You can go online and find that map,
and basically it's based on census track.
So if you had a coal mine that closed or a fossil fuel plant
that closed, I think it's around 2000 or 1999,
something like that.
If it closed since then, then that census tract qualifies.
And any census track that's touching it is also qualifying.
And then they have what they call the MSAs,
which is something that's gonna be adjusted each year.
And that's a little metropolitan statistical area,
I think it's called.
And those areas, depending on some employment statistics
and things that they track, will determine
whether those census tracks qualify as well.
But there's significant areas that are qualifying,
particularly in some of our market area up here at Paradise,
Western PA, Eastern Ohio, all of West Virginia,
and a band across Northern PA as well.
Significant areas that qualify.
- And you can qualify for more than one 10% add
or you can qualify for the low-income
as well as the energy communities.
And potentially the domestic and so on and so forth.
So you could stack these up. - Right.
- So if you're interested in learning more about
or whether or not finding out whether or not
you're in an energy community,
the map is on the IRS's website?
- It is. - Okay. Great.
So now let's talk about the domestic content adder.
- Yes. Okay.
This one's an interesting,
a lot of uncertainty around this one.
It's split structural steel
on iron and manufactured products on systems.
So let's say you did a ground mount,
the posts would be structural steel
and that has to be 100% US-made to qualify for this.
And then any manufactured products,
it has to be 40% US-made. - [Warren] Right.
- And that gets really... The whole calculation,
I think that's a whole separate video.
And I think we've done one, but that whole calculation
around how you arrive at that 40% is really messy.
And it's gonna require a lot of information
for people like ourselves, like Paradise,
to receive from the manufacturers to say,
"Here's the components in our inverter or in our modules,
and what components are US-made
and what percentage of the cost of that product is it."
- Correct, so we're waiting on really the manufacturers
at this point to be able to attest to the fact that X amount
of their components are made in the United States.
And whether or not it actually qualifies for it.
- Right.
- So those are the three adders,
the 10% for the low-energy areas 10% for the low-income.
I'm sorry, 10% for the low-income,
10% for the energy communities,
and 10% for the domestic content.
What about for nonprofits?
- Nonprofits are in a new position.
They used to have to use power purchase agreements
for the most part, or some type of lease arrangement.
And now they qualify for direct pay.
They also use the word elective pay.
But basically a non-tax paying entity,
municipalities, nonprofits can now qualify
to receive a refund, to receive payment for the ITC,
for the tax credit.
And that would include any adders.
So if they were to qualify for an energy community
and nothing else and they had the tax credit,
they would qualify for 40%,
and that money would be paid to the entity.
- But the requirements for that are changing
over the next few years.
So currently in 2023, you don't have to worry
about the domestic content or any other at requirements.
What's happening starting next year?
- Well, next year they're gonna start to bring in
the domestic content piece into it.
So 2023 is the best year to do this, actually.
So 2024 you have to have domestic content on the project.
You have to meet those requirements
the same as everybody else.
Or if you don't, you only get 90% of your tax credit.
- Right.
- The following year it's 85%, 2025.
And the following year, 2026, it's zero.
So it will not be refunded to these nonprofits after 1/1/26,
if they're not meeting the domestic content requirement.
- Great.
And then we created a video on this as well,
the transferability, which is new.
The ability to sell or transfer the tax credit.
Really briefly sum that up for us.
- Yeah, so basically what it does is allows people
who can't use that tax piece, this tax credit,
which is not refundable, what they can do is sell it.
And there's gonna have to be brokerages,
there's gonna have to be platforms
that develop to enable you to do this.
And there's more guidance needed as to the exact
how it will work, the details around that.
But what we know is you're gonna have
to register your system, and then you'll be able
to sell your tax credit to somebody else
who wants that tax credit.
- Right.
And then there's multiple parts
to the investment tax credit.
One of them...
Well, there's the investment tax credit to the Section 48.
There's the investment tax credit,
there's a production tax credit.
How do they compare? What's the difference between those?
- Yeah, those are the two that apply to solar.
There's other tax credits in Section 48
that do not apply to solar, but the PTC,
production tax credit, is different in that it is paid
on the output of the system.
And it's a per kilowatt hour number,
and that number can be adjusted
for inflation or as the IRS sees fit.
But you can take that.
If you don't take the investment tax credit,
you can take the production tax credit for 10 years
on the system.
Where we see this being the most functional, Warren,
and I've looked at numbers on this,
usually for our clients that Paradise works with,
the non-utility scale market it's ITC.
- [Warren] Yeah. - That's what makes sense.
You get into some of the really big utility scale,
where you've got possibly real high outputs
in certain regions of the country
and some real low cost because of the scope
of the sheer size of the project.
Then the PTC may make more sense.
And in addition, whoever owns that system in that year
can take the tax credit,
so you don't have to take it all.
If I'm part of ownership for three years,
I get three years worth of the PTC,
and then the next owner gets the next seven years,
if they hold it that long.
- All right, Dale, so it seems like there's a lot of clarity
that's missing on these different pieces.
When do you think we'll have more guidance on this?
- Yeah, I think we're gonna be staring at third
and fourth quarter guidance coming out.
I think hopefully by the end of the year
we'll have most of it.
Energy community is pretty clear. They've got the map.
So I think we're pretty clear on that.
You just file it with your tax return.
The other one is low income community.
We need the process to be defined more tightly.
Domestic content, we need manufacturers
to provide information as to what's gonna get us there.
And as far as transferability and the direct pay,
there's still some details needed around that.
So yeah, the IRS has a lot of work out of it.
- Yeah.
So in summary with the commercial projects,
there's quite a bit that's changed
and some new guidance coming out that impacts
whether or not you're gonna get
or how all the adders will work.
There's also a additional requirements
if your project is over one megawatt AC.
Very large projects will be required to pay prevailing wage
as well as have apprenticeship program.
So know that we don't have complete clarity
on any of the adders yet.
Hopefully we will by the end of the year.
And when it comes to the solar tax credit,
the investment tax credit for businesses,
remember you can roll back and go back three years,
use it in the current year, roll back three years,
and then carry it forward for 22 years.
For the most part, the investment tax credit
seems to make more sense than the production tax credit
for smaller systems.
And then finally, if you're a nonprofit or a municipality,
you now have the ability to get a direct payment
from the Treasury Department or the IRS, as opposed
to not being able to take the tax credit as well.
Thank you so much for watching.
We hope you found this valuable.
Please leave a comment in the comment section below,
if you liked this video.
Even if you didn't like the video, leave a comment,
but let us know why, and thanks for watching.

segments.text: Hello, I'm Jeremy from TurboTax with important news for taxpayers who are interested in making energy efficient home renovations.
Typical home renovations can be very expensive, especially when you can't deduct their cost.
However, two tax credits are available if you make certain energy efficient and environmentally friendly improvements.
The 2010 Nonbusiness Energy Property Credit allows you to reduce your tax bill
by up to 1,500 dollars, or 30 percent of your renovation costs.
by up to $1,500, or 30 percent of your renovation costs.
This includes the price you paid in 2010 to purchase new exterior doors, windows and skylights
for your main home, that reduce energy consumption.
This credit is reduced to ten percent of your renovation costs for 2011 purchases.
When you go to the store to purchase energy efficient items, make sure they have the Energy Star label,
otherwise, they will not qualify for the credit.
If you install electric heat pumps, water heaters and boilers,
or even a stove that runs on biomass fuel, you can also qualify for the credit.
But for these items, you can include the cost of installation, in addition to the purchase price.
The Federal Government is focused on generating cleaner energy using solar power.
This why it also offers what can be a very substantial residential energy efficient property tax Credit.
for purchasing and installing solar panels and other solar powered equipment in your main home.
There is no maximum credit you can claim, so the sky is the limit.
Remember though, you must file Form 5695 to claim either of the credits.
TurboTax can help you determine whether you qualify for these credits, and will fill in all the right forms for you.
For more tax tips and guidance, visit TurboTax.com.

metadata.title: Introduction to Commercial Litigation Finance
metadata.author: The National Law Review
metadata.shortDescription:
This webinar provides an essential introduction to commercial litigation funding, specifically tailored for attorneys seeking to leverage funding to support their clients and practice. Whether you represent plaintiffs in high-stakes litigation or are exploring funding options for your firm, this episode breaks down the key aspects of litigation finance and how it can be a strategic tool for legal professionals.

Attorneys will gain insights into how litigation funding can help manage financial risk, improve access to justice, and provide the necessary resources to pursue meritorious claims without upfront costs. The session will also address ethical considerations and best practices to ensure compliance while maximizing the benefits of third-party funding.

Specific topics covered include:

Introduction to Litigation Funding
Types of Cases Funded
Key Stakeholders
How Funding is Structured
Legal and Ethical Considerations
Benefits of Litigation Funding
Risks and Challenges
Application and Approval Process

Learning Objectives:
Understand the Fundamentals of Commercial Litigation Funding:
Define commercial litigation funding and explain why it is typically not categorized as a "loan"
Gain a general overview of the litigation funding industry, including its scope and purpose
Identify Key Components of Litigation Funding:
Recognize the types of cases eligible for funding
Identify the key stakeholders involved in litigation finance and their respective roles
Comprehend the Structure and Processes of Litigation Funding:
Explain how litigation funding agreements are structured
Outline the application and approval process for securing funding
Analyze Legal and Ethical Implications:
Explore the legal and ethical considerations surrounding litigation finance
Discuss how these considerations influence industry practices
Evaluate the Benefits and Risks:
Identify the primary advantages of utilizing litigation funding
Assess potential risks and challenges associated with the practice

metadata.shortDescription:
**What is litigation finance, and why are investors exploring it as an alternative investment?**

In this recorded educational webinar, Richard Lowe, Founder & CEO of Turn-key Investments, joins our Litigation Finance and Law Partners to explore how litigation finance works, where potential investment returns come from, and the risks investors should understand.

**What you'll learn:**

✅ What litigation finance is and how it works

✅ How investors can participate in litigation finance

✅ Where potential investment returns come from

✅ How litigation finance differs from traditional investments such as property, equities and bonds

✅ An introduction to UK motor finance claims

✅ Key investment risks, structures and investor considerations

✅ Questions and answers with our Litigation Finance and Law Partners

**About Turn-key Investments**

Turn-key Investments helps investors explore carefully researched opportunities across international property, private financing, private credit and alternative investments.

Our approach is educational and consultative, helping investors understand opportunities before making investment decisions.

🌐 **Website:** https://turn-keyinvestments.com/

📩 **Interested in learning more?**

Visit our website to explore our investment opportunities or arrange a discussion with our team.

**Important Disclaimer**

This webinar is provided for general educational and informational purposes only. It does not constitute financial, legal or investment advice, or an offer to invest. All investments involve risks, including potential loss of capital. Any projected or targeted returns are not guaranteed. Investors should conduct their own due diligence and seek independent professional advice before making investment decisions.

---

**Recorded:** October 2026  
**Presented by:** Turn-key Investments and Litigation Finance and Law Partners

#LitigationFinance #AlternativeInvestments #InvestmentEducation #PrivateCredit #TurnKeyInvestments

metadata.title: Introduction to Commercial Litigation Finance
metadata.author: The National Law Review
metadata.shortDescription:
This webinar provides an essential introduction to commercial litigation funding, specifically tailored for attorneys seeking to leverage funding to support their clients and practice. Whether you represent plaintiffs in high-stakes litigation or are exploring funding options for your firm, this episode breaks down the key aspects of litigation finance and how it can be a strategic tool for legal professionals.

Attorneys will gain insights into how litigation funding can help manage financial risk, improve access to justice, and provide the necessary resources to pursue meritorious claims without upfront costs. The session will also address ethical considerations and best practices to ensure compliance while maximizing the benefits of third-party funding.
Download the slide deck (PDF) - https://financial-poise-video-webinars.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/2026/COMMERCIAL_LITIGATION_FUNDING_-101/1+Introduction+to+Commercial+Litigation+Finance/1+Introduction+to+Commercial+Litigation+Finance.pdf

And and prefer cases with with strong, experienced counsel who themselves have a strong track record and ideally have a track record of taking risk. Other things that funders look at will be the venue, the the trier of fact if you know it. I've long said you can kind of take the same set of facts and law and swap in and out the lawyer and get a very different result, and swap in and out the the judge or the trier of fact and get a very different result. So, if the case has gone on a little bit, you know who that is, that's an important thing that we're we're looking at. Um and then, you know, finally, you want you want a healthy you want a healthy enough return to account for the risk. I sort of mentioned this at at the outset of this of this piece that depending on the risk profile, a funder might be looking to earn a 2x, or they might be looking to earn a 3x or 4x depending on on how risky they perceive the case to be. And sometimes and the way that the returns are actually structured there's a myriad of different ways. Sometimes it's a multiple of what's been committed or deployed. Sometimes it's a percentage of the proceeds and and sometimes it's a combination there of. >> Got it. And and we'll get into some of those details in our second episode where we talk a little bit more about the specifics of a transaction and and sort of uh some of the documentation details and specifics. But So, Stewart, Dave talked a little bit about some of these factors. Um and I know you know, anecdotally that there are some courts that might have different rules about disclosure and um you know, judges have reputations. Uh so are there I was going to frame this as are the courts you stay away from, but let me just ask it slightly less directly. How much does a specific court or specific judge or is it a jury trial versus a bench trial or even a specific state versus federal, you know you know, factor into your analysis? If there are rules of particular court that you just find unappealing just non-starters? I mean, how does that all fit together? >> So, you know, there a couple ways of to go that question. I think you know, one just on the kind of bench trial versus a jury trial versus an arbitration. I mean, that's certainly one we think about. I mean, to to Dave's point, we always underwrite cases as if they're going to go to trial and and this comes from our own practicing days where, you know, from from day one we're thinking about what the opening and closing statements are going to look like in a case. And you know, that's going to depend on who the ultimate decider is whether you're doing that to a jury or to a a judge or an arbitration panel. So, I think you know, those are all factors. None None of them are dispositive of whether we will, you know, finance a case or not, but certainly factor in to our analysis as to, you know, the venue and and kind of other kind of larger kind of regulatory disclosure issues. I mean, there's a there is a patchwork of of rules out there around whether litigation funding has to be disclosed in some form, whether that's kind of mandatory or whether it can just be part of the standard discovery process. Um as well as whether discussions or communications with a funder are confidential and protected from discovery. And I think just taking that that first category of disclosure, you know, we are and I'll speak from Satera's perspective, we're not going to get involved with a case that we're not willing to be known as the funder on it. Um, you know, we're we're happy to for our involvement to be on the front page of the New York Times or the Wall Street Journal. But it's relevant if, you know, our funding agreement has to be disclosed in the litigation because of certain court rules or or state rules, that is relevant. And it's again, not because we're worried about our funding agreement being disclosed or our role being disclosed, but that can give a defendant certain strategic advantages if they know the litigation budget of a plaintiff in a case. Um and I think, you know, what a lot of these disclosure rules come down to, I think it's just exactly what has to be disclosed. You know, if you're just talking, does a plaintiff have to certify whether they have funding, whether the funder, you know, certify the funder doesn't have control, and kind of who the funder is, you know, that's you know, that's one thing. But again, if you're talking about disclosing the funding agreement in its entirety, you know, that's a that's a different thing to think about um from a a funder's perspective, but also from a plaintiff's perspective. Um and again, that's that's something that really varies by by court and jurisdiction. You know, there's some jurisdictions like the District of New Jersey has a has a pretty high level of disclosure rule that's you know, kind of whether there's funding, the name of the funder, certifying lack of control, and that's generally the end of the matter. There are other jurisdictions like Wisconsin where it's a much more robust disclosure obligation. You've got to it's basically part of initial disclosures. You've got to hand over your funding agreement to to the other side. >> So, we have about 15 minutes left, but I just want to follow this to one more uh question that just popped into my head and I guess I'll I'll throw it out to Nick at or just a quick comment. When we talk about non-recourse financing, so obviously the fundee wants to win, right? But um if they know that they're getting financing that's non-recourse from a behavioral perspective, you know, does that make them more aggressive or how do you how do you manage their risk profile since now they basically have this money that they might not have to pay back? >> Yeah, great question. Um and um I I'll I'll say that it is certainly something we think about and the way it is usually addressed is to structure the economics of a deal in a way that the incentives of the funder and the plaintiff are aligned because as as Dave mentioned as as Stewart mentioned, we don't control litigation. We can't make uh our counterparties settle cases um and and oftentimes we we we disclaim uh control. And so, the the plaintiff has to have adequate incentives to to see the case through or to accept a reasonable settlement on their own without involvement of the funder. Um and the the way to do that, right, a lot of it has to do with the sizing that we we talked about before. Um where they the plaintiff can use litigation funding as a tool to to move a case forward and get it into a good spot to settle for an amount where the funder can receive its return, the attorneys can receive any contingency fee that they're entitled to, and the plaintiff still feels like they're getting good value for this case. Um and without um that appropriate sizing, you're right, you can end up with a situation where um you know, a plaintiff will maybe maybe incentivized to take the case to trial and take a big swing. And this is this is something that we think about at the front end. And when I talked about, you know, why why do we see so many cases and fund so few, we really have to be comfortable uh that there's going to be uh coverage for the investment um for this reason. Um so that plaintiffs and funders and their attorneys are all aligned uh in their incentives. >> I just want to add, you know, there's also notwithstanding the the non-recourse nature of of these transactions, there's an exception there are bad boy guarantees in most of these documents. Um and there's also other contractual provisions that permit a funder to stop funding if uh certain, you know, based on particularized egregious behavior occurs. >> So, I'm familiar with bad boy provisions from sort of more you know, lending situations, you know, um misuse of proceeds or fraud or mis- breach of representation. Are are they are they similar in this context, or Jonathan, or are there other more litigation funding specific bad boy provisions? >> Um sure, there there there the former and and the latter. Um you know, for example, um, if the plaintiff uh, does something to affirmatively, negatively impact the litigation, uh, it's not stated as broadly. I mean, there's there's a an artful and lawyerly way to to write it, but, um, i- if if, uh, the plaintiff goes completely off the reservation, that that can be an example of, um, a right to stop funding. >> Well, we're not quite ready for the speed round, but I'm going to >> [clears throat] >> push us along. Um, back to you, Stewart. Um, what's sort of the opportune time for litigants, you know, parties to seek funding? You know, is there a a too early question? Is it a too late? Um, you know, pre-filing, pre-summary judgment, post-summary judgment, or are there different products to sort of fund in different situations? >> The short answer is really anytime is a potential time to seek funding. Certain funders may have different kind of risk parameters around when they like to get into a case. I know some funders may only come in kind of after motion to dismiss and, you know, key legal issues have been resolved, but I think a lot of funders will come in pre-complaint, you know, when the case is is very early, they'll come in, you know, after motion to dismiss, you know, on the eve of discovery or, you know, after summary judgment, in the lead-up to trial, or even after a judgment, you know, when you've got a judgment in hand and you're preparing for appeal. It really just depends on when the client needs financing in better circumstances. Um, you know, each each each kind of time presents different issues for a funder to consider, you know, the earlier you come in, the more unknowns there are in a case um, in terms of kind of getting through motion to dismiss or or summary judgment. Um And I think, you know, the the key thing is that there's enough information available at any given time to make an underwriting decision both in terms of the merits, damages, and collectibility of the defendant as well as the other factors that Macon and and Dave and Jonathan have touched on. And then, you know, where you come in it may affect kind of the funders, you know, return or how they structure the investment um whether, you know, on appeal, you know, oftentimes clients are seeking monetization. They want to take some chips off the table. They've gotten a really great judgment. You know, generally speaking appeals aren't that expensive. And so, kind of a monetization is a way to try to, you know, move forward a recovery that's otherwise might be 12 to 18 months away. You know, we see a good number of situations where a client has survived summary judgment and they've got trial coming up in a few months and they want to bring in additional trial counsel to help actually try the case, but that's a whole 'nother set of expenses. And, you know, they want they need funding to kind of help bring in that trial counsel. Um you know, but it's also very standard to come in kind of pre-complaint or right around the filing of a complaint when, you know, a a client just needs significant resources to retain the lawyers they want to be able to retain to pursue the case successfully. >> And uh perhaps just real quickly since I I don't imagine that um you know, you look up litigation funders in the yellow pages, which I don't even know if they still make the the yellow pages, but you got the gist. Um And Jonathan had mentioned brokers and intermediaries earlier in the presentation. So, Dave, I I need litigation funding. How do I find you? Like, what's the How do I start the process? >> Sure. I mean, my my my my suggestion is to reach out reach out to your your friendly neighborhood funder as as as as soon as you can. Um they're you know, most funders these days are kind of uh or or some of their professionals are are out and about in the legal market talking to to lawyers all day long and and I you know, active on LinkedIn and at various conferences. So, most of the funding opportunities I see you come from sort of trusted law firm legal or legal adjacent connections or um sometimes from from bankers and certainly sometimes from from brokers as well. But, um oftentimes it'll be the lawyer who has a client who has a great case who just, you know, can't afford them or wants to share the risk or wants to incentivize the lawyer to take on a hybrid arrangement and and needs a funder to come in. And so, then the the lawyer will will often direct them to, you know, funders that they have worked with and and and trust, you know, before. And and as far as like sort of starting off, the the best the gold standard, the best thing we can get to quickly analyze a situation and see if it's something that we think we could fund into and think we could put out a term sheet on is is to is to get a short memo that sets out uh what the what the case is about, uh what what the strengths and weaknesses very important to kind of put up front what the weaknesses are. It's something we're going to figure out eventually in the in the and the you know, the quicker we can get to those points and figure out if they're risks that we want to bear, the better for everyone. Uh so, set out what those strengths and weaknesses are, what the budget is for the case and the commitment and what the potential damages value of the case are along with some key documents and and you know, then if that is all provided, a funder can relatively quickly make a decision if it's something they want to pursue. That said, we get opportunities in all forms. Sometimes we just get someone calling up and and talking to us for an hour about what a case is about. Sometimes we get a data room with a million documents in it and say, "Hey, here's a great case. Fund it." Neither of those two extremes are really perfect, but you know, we're happy to take in information about about good cases however we can get it. Ideally, it'll be kind of packaged together to let us get to a decision quicker. >> Great. So, Jonathan, I'm going to sort of give you uh two questions back-to-back. Um the first thing >> What you know what is the form of litigation financing, right? Is it a loan with an interest rate? Is it sort of a secure transaction? And it is it a um an assignment of a claim, you know what is the typical form or sort of And again, I I don't want to go too deep into this cuz it's mostly for the next episode, but just high-level what is the form of this transaction? >> Are you going to tell tell me the second question now, too, or should I take this one and then you'll regale us with your second question? >> So, the first question to the answer, you know, we should be looking at slides 33 and 35, some of which I've had up on the screen. The next question, just as a preview, is um there are certain ethical doctrines that, you know, we hear champerty, barratry, usury, fee splitting. I know you know, bankruptcy code has prohibitions against fee splitting. Um >> I I got you. Um so so let me preview the um the second question first and I'll come back to it if we have time if you want to hear more because the second question has a very short answer. Um modern courts recognize that commercial litigation funding serves legitimate purposes. We talked about it, you know, leveling the playing field, access to justice. It simple and they simply do not apply medieval doctrines to invalidate properly structured arrangements. That's the bottom line up front. And you know, I could talk about each of the, you know, old doctrines by by name, but let me get turned back to the more practical question, I think. Um the commercial litigation funding is most certainly generally not a loan. It's typically structured very intentionally not to be a loan. It's typically structured as a variable prepaid forward purchase agreement. Um and it in the context and you know, for shorthand, prepaid forward purchase agreement, PFPA. Um because it's less syllables. So, in a PFPA, uh the fundee agrees to sell a portion of future litigation proceeds to the funder at a price that cannot be determined at the time of the agreement. The funder pays upfront, might be paying in tranches, but not all the money is necessarily paid at closing, but the funder pays upfront and the funder receives a contingent return. Again, non-recourse is is the hallmark of these things. Um subject to So, so if the case is lost, if there's no recovery, funder walks away with nothing, loses the investment, again subject to bad boy guarantees. Um the funder does take a security interest in the litigation proceeds. Taking a security interest is not inconsistent with a sale transaction. A lot of people kind of um lumber under the false assumption that you can only take a security interest if you make a loan. The UCC does not say that. So, it's typical to understand to take a security interest in the litigation proceeds. In practice, this usually uh results in a UCC-1 uh that says it's an all asset lien even if the um, the actual security interest is only in litigation proceeds, which is permissible. Um, if you have the right to do it under the contract. Um, and the return is never, well, almost never uh, and usually should not be expressed in terms of like an interest rate. It's It's It's expressed in the term in terms of uh, multiple of invested capital, 2x, 3x. That can escalate over time. So, it's, you know, 2x if the if it's repaid within the first 12 months, it's 2.2x if if it's between the next X number and Y number of months, etc. Um, and, you know, do other structures exist? Yeah, you can have an assignment of a claim, a purchase of a claim um, uh, outright, um, but it's it's less common. Um, you could have limited recourse loans for law firm portfolios. Uh, but but the common theme the the common structure is a variable PFPA. >> Great. So, just by nodding heads um, do our funders agree with that sort of description? >> Yes. Yeah, and as I mentioned, there's all different ways you can actually state the return, but in principle that that that is a great and that's the most common what what Jonathan mentioned is also common way to do it. >> Perfect. Um, uh, so we have about 3 minutes left. Uh, want to touch on two topics very quickly. You know, one which I think because you guys are invested in the outcome of the case um, and then there's the sensitivity about, you know, privilege and non-disclosure. Um, how uh, do you navigate the privilege while making sure that you're staying informed as a in what's going on in the case that you that you're funding. Uh Dave, can you take us off on that one? >> Sure. And and we could probably spend a whole a whole seminar on this topic. Really really at a high level, I think it's important to note there's now a fairly extensive body of case law that's developed across the country that if the proper protections are in place such as a robust NDA between the funder and the client, that work product, lawyer and client work product, can be shared with the funder without having the protections that are accorded to that material waived. And it goes back to the origins of the work product doctrine. On the other hand, attorney-client privilege material is more tenuous. Some people try to protect that material by putting common interest agreements in place. There is conflicting case law on whether that works or not. And so we at least are very careful about not wanting to ask for, not wanting to retain if we accidentally get any attorney-client privileged information. We don't think we need that in order to diligence or underwrite the case. So if we accidentally get it, we'll return it or destroy it. But it is important for us to see work product and understand how the lawyers are thinking about the case. Uh and so first thing we do before we talk about anything in a case is to put in place a robust NDA with with a with a plaintiff or claimant. Um and then also we're we're pretty careful about what we end up keeping in our writing down in our files or keeping in our files. And so um you know, when when we when we end up discarding the vast majority of cases that we look at and as was touched on before, we invest in a very small percentage of the cases we look at, probably somewhere between 2 and 5% maybe a little higher for really trusted repeat kind of customer uh lawyers that we work with. But um once we're done with a case, we usually we usually get rid of the files on those cases as a matter of practice and policy. And so um I'm I'm not likely to have any materials relevant to a case when someone comes if someone happens to come looking for it, you know, a few year a few years later. >> Great. So, I know we're almost out of time. Um Nick, I just want to throw two questions two related questions to you sort of in the category of um risk management or recent developments. Um the West Field survey that I again I referred to a couple of times uh talks about the use of contingent risk insurance and and in our preparing for this panel we talked a little about co-investments. Um So, I know we're at time but maybe if you could just spend 30 seconds or so on each of those two topics Nick and sort of see how they're used. >> Sure, I'll try to keep it brief. Um so, contingent risk insurance um as as Dave said with the last topic we could we could have a whole seminar um on on contingent risk insurance but but essentially that um is a tool that can be used by by funders and litigants alike. I'll I'll speak to the funder perspective. Um you know, say that there's a a large judgment that's entered. You want to insure the value of the judgment up to a certain amount to protect um the judgment uh from reversal or modification on appeal. There there is an insurance market that looks at policies such as those. Um in terms of co-investment, the second topic you raised David, um this is what it sounds like. Um multiple funders will will uh fund each fund a portion of a commitment for a particular investment uh and and share in the proceeds from that investment. Um you know, the uh one benefit to highlight of that of course is uh that it spreads the risk um right? Uh there there may be situations where a a commitment is is sufficiently large um where uh a single funder may not want to concentrate be uh that amount of capital in a single case. Um sharing the risk between funders uh through a co-investment helps mitigate that risk. >> Great. And we'll we'll sort of uh dig into those two topics a little further in episode two which which I'll call maybe like litigation funding 201. So, we are at time. I want to thank our panelists. Um you can tell just by listening to them that they're all extremely knowledgeable, active in the industry. Um and so I encourage you if you find yourself in in the need of litigation funding to reach out to your counsel or get introductions to any of our panelists and uh you know, good luck on that uh process. So, thanks again. Thanks to West and to uh Financial Poise and I hope you enjoyed the uh the discussion. >> [music]

#BHBATV INTERVIEWS - Litigator's Corner: Hillary Johns (Owner, Lead Counsel at Hillary Johns, Trial Lawyer) interviews William C. Marra (Investment Manager, Validity Finance, LLC). A former law clerk at the United States Supreme Court, Will has been recognized as a Global Leader in Litigation Finance by Lawdragon. He is a frequent writer and speaker on litigation finance, and his article "The Shadows of Litigation Finance" was published by the Vanderbilt Law Review in April 2021. Will is responsible for sourcing investment opportunities from the country’s leading lawyers and claimholders, and he is also actively engaged in Validity’s due diligence and investment underwriting process. He offers Validity’s clients his expertise as a former commercial and constitutional litigator at Cooper & Kirk, PLLC, as well as his experience working at Bain & Company, the business consulting firm.

metadata.title: How to Reduce B2B Credit Card Processing Fees | Future Forward November 2026
metadata.author: Insightful Accountant
metadata.shortDescription:
In this Future Forward: Payments session, Sam Johnson, Partner Success Manager at PayTrace, explores how businesses and accounting professionals can reduce B2B credit card processing fees while improving payment efficiency and cash flow. Discover how interchange rates work, how Level 2 and Level 3 processing can lower the cost of accepting commercial and government credit cards, and what Visa's Commercial Enhanced Data Program (CEDP) means for merchants. The session also covers accounts receivable optimization through payment software integrations, credit card surcharging, and ACH payments, helping accountants and advisors identify opportunities to reduce transaction costs and streamline their clients' payment operations.

Speaker(s): Sam Johnson, Partner Success Manager, PayTrace

Host/Moderator: Mat, Insightful Accountant

Sponsor(s): PayTrace

Series: Future Forward: Payments


Chapters: 
0:00 Introduction and understanding processing fees
8:26 Interchange rates and Level 3 processing
14:47 Automating Level 3 data and reducing costs

metadata.title: Virtual Cards: Transforming B2B Payment Processes in 2025
metadata.author: Facilero
metadata.shortDescription:
Contact us today for a free consultation at https://facilero.com

B2B payments have come a long way, but many businesses are still stuck with outdated systems that slow them down. Virtual cards are changing that—fast. They’re digital, secure, and offer the kind of real-time control finance teams have been asking for.
 
Unlike traditional cards or manual transfers, virtual cards are issued instantly and tailored to each transaction. You can set limits, expiry dates, and assign them to specific departments, projects or suppliers. This means more control, better tracking, and less chance of unauthorised spend.
 
Security is a huge benefit. With virtual cards, each payment can have its own set of card details, so even if one gets compromised, it won’t affect the rest of your operations. Plus, you can cancel or disable a card with a click.
 
They also reduce the time your finance team spends on reconciliation. Since each card is linked to a purpose, matching transactions to invoices is quicker and more accurate. And that doesn’t just help you—it keeps your suppliers happy too.
 
With clearer spend visibility, businesses can spot trends, reduce waste, and make smarter decisions. Want to see how much a department spent last quarter? Or who your top vendors are? Virtual card platforms make those insights easy to access.
 
The best part is they fit right into your current systems. Many providers offer integrations with accounting or ERP platforms, so you don’t have to overhaul everything to modernise how you pay.
 
Virtual cards aren’t just a trend—they’re a smart move for any business looking to reduce risk, boost efficiency, and take back control over corporate spending.
 
At Facilero, we’re focused on delivering smarter, scalable solutions for modern finance teams. If your business is ready to simplify payments and gain more control over spend, visit us at https://Facilero.com to book a free consultation call today!

metadata.title: How B2B Businesses Lower Credit Card Fees (Visa Product 3 Explained)
metadata.author: Matt Dubois
metadata.shortDescription:
If you accept business, corporate, or purchasing cards, you may be paying more interchange than you need to.

In this video:
→ What Visa's Commercial Enhanced Data Program (CEDP) is
→ Why Level 3 is now called Product 3, and why Level 2 is gone
→ The invoice data Visa wants with each payment
→ What enhanced data can be worth on a real invoice
→ A live demo of the data being enhanced automatically

Missed Part 1? Watch "Where your $100 card payment actually goes" first.

Savings shown are illustrative and vary by card type, merchant category, and data quality.

I'm Matt, CEO of Chargezoom. More on enhanced data for B2B payments: https://chargezoom.com

#payments #B2Bpayments #level3 #interchange #creditcardprocessing #fintech

standard rates. That's money you could
be keeping.

metadata.title: How a Fractional CFO Helps Canadian Businesses Scale and Prepare for Sale with Robert Cinapri
metadata.author: Selling Your Canadian Business
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode of the Expert Interview Series, David Prowse of the Shaughnessy Group sits down with Robert Cinapri, founder and president of CFO Collective. They discuss the vital role of fractional CFOs in helping Canadian and U.S. businesses scale profitably.   

Robert breaks down the misconceptions between bookkeepers, controllers, and strategic fractional CFOs, explaining why growing companies need forward-looking financial leadership. 

Robert introduces the “value ladder” approach moving from compliance and cash-flow management to accurate reporting, dashboards, and strategic planning and explores the “rule of three and 10” regarding how businesses break as they triple.

Whether you are looking to fix constant cash crunches, optimize working capital, or position your enterprise for a future business exit, this conversation offers actionable insights to help you build a sale-ready organization.

About the Guest:
Robert Cinapri CPA, CA, MBA, MAcc
Email: robcinapri@cfo-collective.com
https://cfo-collective.com/

Host: David Prowse CPA, CA, CVA, CEPA, CMAA
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/velorum/
Web: https://shaughnessy.group/ 

Subscribe to The Canadian Exit Briefing for exclusive articles, guides, and reports for Canadian business owners and their advisors: https://sellingyourcanadianbusiness.com/subscribe

Check out the book Selling Your Canadian Business: A Step-by-Step Guide to Maximizing Value and Securing Your Legacy, available in English and French on Amazon.ca.
