videos.full_text: Welcome to the expert series from selling your Canadian business. Our book lays out the expert team of advisers every Canadian business owner needs in their corner. This series brings those experts into the conversation one at a time. Here is your host. >> Hello everyone. I'm David Prowse from the Shawn Group and this is another episode of the expert interview series. This is our chance to interview the experts to help people business owners grow and exit their business. Today's guest is Robert Senatore. He's he's the founder and president of CFO Collective. Robert, thanks so much for joining us. >> My pleasure. Thanks for having me, David. >> So Robert, tell us a little bit about your background and how you got to doing what you're doing today. >> So I mean the quick answer is doing all the corporate stuff. You know, I did my EY time, got my CPA doing the corporate jobs, moving up through the ladder. I'm running the aerospace finance division for Canada for Honeywell. They wanted me to move to the US due to family reasons. We just weren't able to. Eventually, I moved on. I tapped out there. I moved on from there to a couple other jobs that really weren't hitting for me. I didn't feel like I was adding the value that I really should be. So I literally just blew everything up. I took a full-time teaching role at Humber College, started doing fractional CFO work just with a few clients on the side. That was about that was almost 13 years ago now. About 6 years ago, I had to kind of make a call cuz the the teaching and this business was growing and I I wasn't able to to dedicate enough time to both. So I decided I was adding a lot of value here. So CFO Collective it is and there's uh there's seven of us right now including me. Uh Canadian and US businesses we serve. Uh and that's it. We're strategic operational fractional CFOs serving B2B owner-operated businesses. It's going great. So, Excellent. >> So, what should an owner look for if they're hiring a a fractional CFO? And and and how do you differentiate that, say, from uh a controller or a bookkeeper? Because I think there's some misconceptions out there about what what a fractional CFO is. >> Yes, it's interesting cuz over the obviously the the time I've been doing this now, I look around and at all the people sort of trying to provide this service, right? And so, a lot of bookkeepers and controllers and bookkeeping services are are offering fractional CFO services as well. And what I always say there is, a good controller is not a good CFO. And a good CFO is also not a good controller. These, you know, are not skills that necessarily cross both ways. So, if you have a good controller, that's amazing. Actually, that's really important. So, stick with that, use that, but they're not going to give you the true forward-looking CFO advice and support that we give. On the other side of it, oftentimes your external CPA, your tax preparer, even if it's someone that's doing your audit or your review, um they also believe that they're offering CFO services. The issue is they can't. They're not there enough. They're not involved enough. They don't truly understand your business at that level to be able to give that kind of support. And even worse still, sometimes, for example, I love tax preparers, they're great, they've never run a business. >> Yeah. >> So, a real fractional CFO is someone who's come out of the corporate world as a CFO, who understands how businesses run in detail, and takes all that skill and experience and applies it to your business, to you, and to your leadership team. That's where you get the real value of that service, right? So, >> Yeah. Now, do you think education about what a fractional CFO is has increased in Canada? Because I certainly know, you know, I think about the United States where I think the concept was started to be well known maybe about 10 10 or so years ago. And and here in Canada it was I I still think a bit of a a mystery. Uh so, do you think that that education and awareness of that there are fractional CFOs out there and what they can do has improved? >> I think it's improved for sure, but definitely the US is much more mature in this space. There's a lot more fractional CFO services down in the US and it's accepted a lot more readily by the business owners there. Here it's still uh you know, not that well known. Much better I tell you than it was 5 years ago, but still there's some confusion around it. And I think part of the confusion is that these business owners think they are getting this advice from their their bookkeepers and their external accountants. And like, why would I pay all this money for something else? Uh and I I think that that's unfortunate and that's part of the education process, right? Cuz when you look at a 20 30 million dollar business and when someone says to you, "Look, if you give us 100 grand a year, the ROI on that is going to blow your mind. And it's nothing you're going to get from your external CPA or your bookkeeper." >> Yeah. >> But it's that sort of education piece, bringing all these business owners along to say, "Hey, you don't have to go without." Right? You can get it and you get it for this price and the ROI is amazing. So, but yeah, education is still needed for sure. >> Yeah, and I think I think for a lot of business, especially if you're you're you're on a growth trajectory for sure and and especially if you are thinking about doing an exit the next, you know, let's say 3 to 5 years, having a fractional CFO to me is like having you know, it's like having a strategic business partner, but but but they're good at numbers. You know, I can I think I think having a good operations person is important and having a good person with numbers is important. And and you know, sometimes business owners, even if they're very good with numbers, some of them are like that, the reality is they don't really have time to slice and dice and really understand their business the way they should. So, I think that's where to me anyways where a fractional CFO can come in. >> Yeah, no, 100%. It's like you could probably do it. You wouldn't do it as well as we do it, and you would spend way more time doing it. So, why don't you focus on what you're good at? Right? Being the visionary, running your business, growing your business, and let us build that foundation that you can scale that business on profitably, right? And get yourself set up to be a sale-ready business. And well, I'm sure we'll talk about that after, but it's you're not Doesn't matter if you're selling or not. I keep saying every business owner should want to own a sale-ready business because frankly, that's a well-run business. Right? >> Yeah. >> So. >> For sure. >> [snorts and clears throat] >> Now, you um you you talk about a a value ladder approach when you when you start working with clients. Why don't you tell the audience a little bit about how that works? >> Yeah, cuz every client is different. It's It's not a one-size-fits-all, and I know there are organizations out there that do what we do, that believe there is a one-size-fits-all. It's not what we do. So, we'll go into a client, and the initial, what I call the onboarding period, we're running up that value ladder. The bottom of the value ladder is always things like compliance. Are you good with CRA, IRS? Are you good with your bank covenants? Let's make sure all that is stable. >> Mhm. >> The next thing often is cash flow, right? When we're called, it's because the business owner has had enough of the pain. They're tired. They want it fixed. And that pain often comes from the fact that they're in this constant cash flow crunch. Right? So, the next thing we usually do is set up a process to understand cash flow, monitor, and then the difference with us from say your external CPA or your bookkeeper, we'll help you execute a plan to fix your cash flows. >> Yeah. >> And that therein lies the big difference. Now, once that's all stable, we get into the next part of the ladder as we move up. >> Mhm. >> There's nothing we can do for a business owner really long-term if their data is garbage. So, the next thing is do we have timely and accurate financial reporting? >> Mhm. >> And does it have the data necessary to actually help run the business? >> Mhm. >> If it doesn't, we will actually help fix that. We don't do bookkeeping, but we will work with your team to get it right and get it working. >> Yeah. >> Once we have that, then you get into the next you know, the next level is monthly reporting with you know, your financial statements with lots of analysis, with your KPIs and dashboard. You're talking about your budgeting and forecasting. And then we continue to ratchet it up that ladder when the business owner is ready all the way up to strategic planning. And we're getting this business sale ready. Again, you're going to hear me say this over and over. Doesn't matter if they're selling. We want that business to be sale ready. It's the kind of business they should want to own. That's the ladder we run up. And we move through that ladder at different paces with different clients depending on where they are. Right? So. >> Yeah. And I think I think that's important because you can't just go into a client that fundamentally has you know, no no real foundations and then let's talk about strategic planning. Well, you could talk about it, but you won't be able to execute on it. So, I always think of it like you know, if you're building a house, I mean the first thing you got to worry about is you got to worry about the foundation. >> Right. >> So, don't worry about like the color of the stucco you're going to use on the side if if your foundation is is faulty and you're going to your house is going to crumble. So, so so I I tend to you know, I totally agree with your approach and that you know, you you you need some certain fundamentals like what I would call infrastructure really. Um and and then from there you can start to build you know, better more robust tools to help you run the business. >> Yeah, that foundation is critical, right? You want it you you right now you have a little bungalow on that foundation and it's fine. But you want to put a skyscraper on that foundation. That foundation is not going to hold that skyscraper. >> Yeah. >> Right? So, we need to build out and that infrastructure is all it's your systems, it's your people, it's your processes, it's your leadership team, it's all of it. That's the foundation that we're going to come in and help you build so that you can scale profitably. I said all the time to clients, "Do you really want to be 50 million and making 3 million when you were 20 million and making 3 million? Just so you can tell your friends that you have a $50 that's the case. It's a lot easier and a lot simpler, right?" 50 million at 3 million, you didn't build that foundation. >> Yeah. >> So, >> Yeah, unfortunately we see a lot of that, too. >> Sure, of course. >> Yeah, and you know, I think I always think, you know, from an M&A perspective, uh if you're business looking to sell, I always feel like you should have the ability to do some some type of budgeting or forecasting. You know, some some ability to talk about at least the next 12 months. Like, what do you think's going to happen? And unfortunately, you know, most of the most of the business owners I run into, they it's probably sitting up in their head, but that's not good enough, you know, you need to be able to like put it down on paper and and and be able to justify like why why you think that's going to happen and and hopefully it's going to be some some degree of accuracy behind it. >> Sure, yeah, you have to justify it. You have to be able to stress test it. Cuz a buyer has to have I'm preaching to the choir here, but a buyer has to have confidence in what they're looking at it that they'll be able to continue to enjoy cash flow from this business going forward, right? So, >> Now, you've talked a bit about the the rule of a three and 10. So, why don't you tell us a little bit about that and, you know, why why is that something that's for someone who's maybe thinking about growth, what why is that rule important? >> Yeah, so I I think one of our differentiators, we have a few differentiators, one of them is that in building CFO Collective on a vision, and that vision is based on the rule of three and 10. And the simplest way to explain that rule is just to say, "Look, in general, every time a business triples in size, it breaks." >> Mhm. >> The [clears throat] systems, processes, team all start breaking. Okay? If you're you're a $3 million business and you're rocking it. You get up to a nine million, but let's call it 10, right? So, I I like to do the the three and 10 kind of thing that way. It just makes it easier to explain. You're 10 million, you're running the business the same way, and the wheels are falling off, and you can't understand why. >> Yeah. >> Okay? So, you get that cleaned up, you get that working. You get up to 20, 25, 30 million, the same pattern starts happening again. The wheels start coming off again. And it's completely natural because for most business owners, and I say most, there are exceptions, most business owners, this is all they know. They started this business business when they were 24, 25 years old. They might not have ever worked at a large company that had best practices. So, they don't know what a 10, 30, 50 million dollar business should look like. >> Mhm. >> So, they keep thinking as long as they work harder and just keep doing more of the same thing, it's going to grow and scale in a profitable way. It generally doesn't happen. Which is why as they grow, their profits go flat, cash flow becomes a problem, the owner starts burning out. So, we love our clients that are growing and suffering because they're growing, cuz those are the things we fix, right? >> Yeah. Yeah, and I think I think it's important to understand that, you know, when you're tripling in size, the the complexity of the business is is more than tripling, you know, like it's it's an exponential function, it's not linear. So, uh you know, you and and you're right, you when you see a business that's at three million, a lot of times you're still at that level where the business owner's wearing, you know, 10 different hats, and they can get away with it, and and it's working just fine. And you start to get to 10 million, all of a sudden now, well, you know, things are getting lost in the shuffle somehow. You know, the the communications, the the the knowledge, the data. And and that's where you you really start to have to build like a management team. And and and once you start to build a management team, all of a sudden now the complexity of the organization becomes, you know, it goes goes through the roof in terms of like how how how do you effectively run it? So, you know, I totally agree with you know, your your supposition about you know, how you know, you we get getting back to like that foundation. You have to apply a new a new foundation to support that that bigger size of organization. >> Yeah, and and I'll tell you, I've seen the movie before, right? So, you're getting it exactly right. At 10 million all of a sudden now they need some help on a leadership team, but they're still running on QuickBooks, they're still using a lot of spreadsheets. At 30 million, if you're not on a full ERP system, there's no way you can actually have the data you need to know that you're pricing things properly, that your jobs are are are profitable, that your customers aren't bleeding you dry. You just you'll have your spreadsheets won't work anymore. QuickBooks isn't enough. We have to have some other systems there to support that leadership team. And often the leadership team may not be able to grow into that new complexity. So, all of this has to be monitored and evolved as you grow, right? So. >> So, what are the warning signs uh that a business has outgrown its uh its ability to handle its finances? >> So, there there's three simple warning signs for me. And I say this to people all the time. If you're speaking to business owners and you hear any combination of these three things, you know they're hitting the rule of three and 10 problems. Again, your top line is growing, your profit isn't. Right? So, you're scaling your sales, but you're not making more money than you did before. The second being one is the cash flow issues become constant. You are always in a state of crisis. You don't have the working capital you need to support that growth. And the last one is the business owner. They are burning out because they continue to wear too many hats and too many things go across their desk. They're working harder than they ever have and it's not getting better and they don't understand why. So for me, those are the simple external signals that tell you that they've hit those gates and that something has to change. >> So what can an owner do to address those problems? >> Well, we've been talking about. It's about building that foundation. And it's not about building that foundation catching up after it's a problem. Right? It's about continually evolving the business and putting new police pieces in place as you grow, right? Not waiting till everything falls apart. Right? So this is where having someone like us involved through the journey is where the value is really added because we know at this point where the investments have to be made, where the processes have to change, where the systems have to change. And we're not looking to bleed owners dry of all these investments they have to make. Our job is to manage that pace and make sure it's there as they grow. If they tried on their own, the issue is they they often don't know. They don't know what they don't know. So they don't know what piece of that foundation needs to be reinforced or improved in order to support that scalability, right? >> Yeah, so again and getting into strategy right now, you know, you know, Jim Collins came up with the whole the whole idea of, you know, putting the right people in the right places. Um you know, and so you you might get involved with that as as a fractional CFO as well. What are What are your thoughts on that in terms of, you know, how a business owner should approach that? >> Yes, I mean some of our clients run on the entrepreneurial operating system EOS. >> Mhm. >> It's a great system. Uh it requires a certain type organization, one that's really disciplined, dedicated, and wants to invest heavily in that. But, a lot of those tools in there are ones that we use with our a lot of our our clients as we need to. We pull them out, we use them, uh, we bring in other partners where it makes sense. But, on that path right away you start seeing in early days that concept of what got you here won't get you there. That is very much a way of time about the rule of three and 10, right? So, what got you to the three million isn't going to get you to 10, isn't going to get you to 30, right? And a lot of that discussion wraps around people. And it's the right seats and the right people in those seats. And often times business owners will you know, they're dedicated to those people have come along with them on that journey. The issue is that at a certain point those people simply may no longer be appropriate for the business and for that journey. And you're doing a disservice to the company and to those people by forcing them through when they no longer fit. So, all a big part of that is managing the leadership team and the key managers in [clears throat] the organization to make sure they are the appropriate people in the appropriate seats so that you can scale properly. >> Yeah, I think that's probably one of the more complicated aspects of growth is is coming to that realization that, you know, like you said what what what got you here won't get you there. And and so who you know, the the the team that you've built to get, you know, to get to that three million dollar company could be could have could have been perfect, but, you know, if you want to if you want to be a 10 10 million dollar company or or larger it's going to look a lot different. >> And and I and it is David, 100% the one of the biggest challenges I see because there's a lot of loyalty and dedication and care in both directions. So, it's a very difficult thing to manage, but what I use often times with my clients is that concept of get it, want it, capable of it. Right? So, GWC and we apply that all the time. I say when you're looking at someone in a role as they evolve, do they get it? Do they understand the importance of why they have to change and why they have to grow into this role? Even if they get it, do they even want it? Often times, a long-term employee will step back and say, "I'm not interested in that level of responsibility. I'd like to remain in this kind of role. I don't want it." So, there's no point in forcing someone into a role when they don't want it. Finally, even if they get it and they want it, they simply might not be capable of it. They might not have the skill set and the acumen to actually execute the job. So, you need all three of these things as you evolve your leadership team and your management structure so that you can again scale profitably and be sale ready. It There's no option if that's what you want to do. So. >> Now, one of the things that I've I've always found is that for businesses that they struggle with is having a an understanding about you know, really analyzing the business, having an understanding about like where they're making money and where they're not making money. And sometimes, you know, I I they worry too much about I think top line growth. And you know, maybe they find out you know, maybe if you really analyze the business, you find out that those products or services, some of them, don't actually make you money. Um So, what are your thoughts on that in terms of you know, going in like I guess we call it financial planning and analysis, but just trying to sort of understand you know, what what's actually really making you money and and and you know, and then you know, using that information I guess to sort of figure out well, is if we're not making a lot of money here, is there's just strategic reason like this is some sort of loss leader, we're going to keep it anyways, or maybe maybe we should pair this out because it's it's just you know, it's not creating any value. >> That's I love that concept actually. Look, we just have to go in with eyes wide open. We know [clears throat] that these certain products or services may not be making a lot of money, but they are you know, they're the loss leader. They're they're the milk at the back of the grocery store that makes you walk through the potato chip aisle to get to it, right? You know, you don't want to make a lot of money in that milk cuz you want people showing up for that, then you want them buying other things while they're there. Okay? So, these are the same kind of concepts, but if we go back to the value ladder, it starts with data. You have to have accurate data so we can truly understand what's happening. Let's assume we fixed the data, we understand that the data is working and giving us what we need, then it's a matter of actually understanding your costing, and this is a big thing where often times your external auditor, CPA, tax person isn't involved enough to really understand what a fully loaded cost is for your different products or services, right? That's something we spend a lot of time building for our clients so that they can understand, based on their current pricing structure, what's making money, what isn't, and we look at customer profitability, too. And I I every business owner, their head might be exploding right now because they know there is those customers out there, those small ones that are high maintenance. They think they're bad customers. When we put the numbers in front of them, they're blown away. And the answers are really fast. It's either we're increasing the prices for these customers or we're cutting them off because it's not worth having them. So, all of this ability to understand the costing in a really fullsome way leads us then to looking at pricing. And you may decide not to change something, but at least you're doing it with eyes wide open. Right? You're not just sort of hoping on a wing and a prayer. So. >> Yeah, and it's probably illuminating once you start to do that analysis. >> Al- always. There's always surprises that come out of that analysis cuz they really don't understand, especially when you look at their overheads and their indirect costs, how all of those impact the different services or products. They just don't know. When they get a look at it, they're like, "Oh my gosh, I didn't realize." Right? So. >> And one of one of the other areas, too, is also, you know, managing working capital. I think that's something that's that many businesses like struggle struggle with. I think business owners sort of implicitly understand, well, you know, if we have too too too much receivables, that's that's not good, but I don't really see a lot of active management until, you know, we we bring in people like yourself. So, what are your thoughts there on working capital? >> Well, it's the whole cash cash process, right? From beginning to end that they really don't understand. And it it's a matter of, okay, who's paying attention to your receivables? Which customers of yours are stringing you out, causing you problems? Okay, let's back up from that. When you're buying your supplies, which vendors are being cooperative in trying to allow you to match your terms on your receivables with what you pay to them? And then in the middle is your inventory, right? >> Yeah. >> Where do you get your inventory from? How long does it have to be ordered in advance? How long does it have to sit around? That's a huge piece of that cash flow process that they don't think about it holistically, right? We really want to understand the entire cash flow entity and really try to manage all the pieces. And then you layer on top of that, what are we doing with your bank to make sure that they're making sure you have the buffer you need to deal with seasonality, to deal with spikes in cost, to deal with long-term shipping issues from the other side of the world, whatever it is. So, it's it's managing the business itself and then working with your lender to make sure they have what they need to support you, so you have the buffers you need when when those times of the year come up. So. [clears throat] >> One final question, if you uh got a business owner who's 3 to 5 years away from a potential business exit, >> Yeah. >> what should they start thinking about today? >> So, if they haven't already, it's those external things, sitting down with their wealth advisor, making sure they understand what they need to retire. It's sitting down with their external CPA and making sure they have the tax structure set up so that when they do exit, they're keeping as much of that money as possible. And setting up these family trusts and all these complex structures require time. In the US and Canada, they're different so you need a qualified person who understands these rules well. We don't do that piece of it, we understand it. For example, in Canada, if your family trust is not in place for two years or more, it's not going to be useful to you. The CRA won't accept it. A lot of business owners don't even understand this. That's the external piece. Get your you get your house set up your in order outside of the business. Then it's getting the business set up. And again, preaching to the choir. You have huge risks around customer concentration, vendor concentration, you have huge risks around reliance on the owner, around the lack of leadership team depth. You have huge risks around poor financial and corporate information. If you're not able to provide reliable data to a potential buyer, their level of confidence drops and they either walk away or they're your price drops significantly. So you may have some idea of what you think your business is worth, but we can come in and give you a good idea of what that looks like realistically. And all of those factors matter. In an ideal situation, your business may be worth X, but given all the things happening inside your business, that valuation gets ratcheted down. So what can we do in a three to five-year time frame to address a lot of those things impacting value so that you get closer to your goal. And that's the idea, right? But it takes time. It can't be done in six months or nine months. It needs at least three years if not five years or more. And if you're 10 years out, you should start thinking about it now. Honestly. >> And I and I think one of the other things that's important is that the investment in a fractional professional like yourself for those fractional CFOs, fractional operation people, uh sales and marketing, those those are investments that you're making, but the reality is is that by improving your business, your valuation goes up, the multiple goes up, and and ideally you're going to grow. So, the reality is is that, you know, you should get a very good ROI from those investments at the end of the day. >> The way I put it is, look, if a business owner at a minimum gets visibility into their business and gets more comfortable with their business so that they can make proper decisions and they sleep better at night, that ROI is priceless. Then you layer on top of it the real ROI, the hard ROI, which comes back to increasing the scalability of your business, your profits, what you take home, and then having a stronger value when the time comes that you will exit. And we're all exiting. We're going to exit at some point or another. Right? Wha- And whether you're transitioning to family members or employees or you're selling, the answer is the same. And by the way, the reason you want to get your business sale ready as soon as poss- possible is because you never know if something happens. Knock on wood. Let's all hope that's not the case, but sometimes life has other ideas in mind. So, you want to be ready, right? So. >> Robert, thank you so much for joining us. This has been a very enlightening conversation, so I really appreciate it. And to our audience, thank you for joining us. If you want to contact Robert, we'll provide some of [clears throat] the information down below, and we'll catch you on the next episode. Thanks very much. >> Thanks, David. Loved it. >> That concludes this episode of the expert series from Selling Your Canadian Business. This conversation is for educational purposes only and is not professional advice. Always consult qualified professionals. Click on any of the additional resources on screen or visit sellingyourcanadianbusiness.ca. Thank you for joining us.

metadata.title: Don't Act as a Broker-Dealer
metadata.author: Trowbridge Law Group
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, Gene Trowbridge Esq. CCIM explains why you should never act as an unregistered broker-dealer. 

Acting as an unregistered broker-dealer is a violation of rules promulgated under the 1934 Exchange Act. Not only may you face lawsuits from investors, you may also suffer severe penalties from the SEC, including losing the ability to deal in securities ever again. Don't risk it! 

Watch the video to learn what activities are considered violations under the '34 act, what penalties you may face for such violations, and how to sell securities without running afoul of the law.

metadata.title: Broker dealer exclusions (NASAA Series 63, 65, 66)
metadata.author: Achievable
metadata.shortDescription:
Along with the rules and regulations related to broker dealers on the NASAA Series 63, 65, and 66 exams, you will also need to know the key exceptions to those rules. In this video, we explore what the key exclusions are to being forced to register as a broker dealer, and then do a Series 63/65/66 practice question on the topic together. 

--

Brandon Rith is the co-founder of FINRA tutoring firm Basic Wisdom (https://basicwisdom.net) and a former 8x-awarded Licensing Instructor at Fidelity Investments.

Achievable’s FINRA courses are the most modern and effective on the market. We leverage data analytics and learning science to create a personalized study program for you, on your phone, tablet, or computer. Follow it, and we guarantee that you’ll pass.

Best of all, it’s free to try - visit https://achievable.me/?utm_source=basicwisdom to see why more students are switching to Achievable.

--

https://www.financialregulationcourses.com/dictionary/f/form-u4
Form U4 is one of the most important regulatory documents in the securities industry. Officially known as the Uniform Application for Securities Industry Registration or Transfer, Form U4 serves as the primary registration document for individuals seeking to become registered representatives, investment adviser representatives, securities agents, and other regulated financial professionals.

In this Finance Dictionary episode from Financial Regulation Courses, we examine the purpose of Form U4, registration requirements, disclosure obligations, reportable events, amendments, disciplinary disclosures, employment history reporting, and the ongoing compliance responsibilities associated with securities industry registration.

Understanding Form U4 is essential for candidates pursuing careers in wealth management, broker-dealer firms, investment advisory services, financial planning, compliance, and securities regulation.

Key Concepts Covered

• Form U4 Explained
• Uniform Application for Securities Industry Registration
• FINRA Registration Process
• Broker-Dealer Registration Requirements
• Investment Adviser Representative Registration
• Disclosure Obligations
• Reportable Events
• Disciplinary Disclosures
• Employment History Reporting
• Regulatory Compliance Requirements
• Continuing Disclosure Responsibilities
• Securities Industry Registration Fundamentals
• FINRA and State Registration Systems
• Financial Services Compliance

This topic is highly relevant for individuals preparing for the Securities Industry Essentials (SIE) Exam, Series 6, Series 7, Series 63, Series 65, and Series 66 examinations, as well as professionals pursuing careers in financial services and investment management.

Whether you are entering the securities industry, preparing for registration examinations, or seeking a deeper understanding of compliance obligations, Form U4 represents a foundational component of financial services regulation.

Who Should Watch?

✔ Aspiring Financial Advisers
✔ Investment Adviser Representatives
✔ Registered Representatives
✔ Wealth Management Professionals
✔ Compliance Officers
✔ Broker-Dealer Personnel
✔ Finance Students & Graduates
✔ SIE, Series 7, Series 63, Series 65 & Series 66 Candidates

About Financial Regulation Courses (FRC)

Financial Regulation Courses (FRC) is a professional education provider specializing in financial regulation, compliance, risk management, banking, financial markets, fintech, and financial services education.

Our educational content is designed for finance professionals, compliance practitioners, students, graduates, and organizations seeking practical knowledge across global regulatory frameworks, including the United States, United Kingdom, Singapore, the United Arab Emirates, India, and other major international financial jurisdictions.

www.financialregulationcourses.com

Financial Regulation Courses (FRC) produces educational content developed through human research, editorial review, and subject matter expertise. Our educational materials are researched, structured, written, and reviewed by finance, regulatory, compliance, and financial services professionals. Artificial intelligence technologies may be used to assist with video presentation, narration, visual production, content formatting, and educational delivery; however, AI does not independently create, verify, or approve the educational content presented.

verified, and approved by compliance
professionals. Form U4, the Uniform
Application for Securities Industry
Registration, is the foundational
document for individuals seeking
registration with FINRA and state
regulators. Governed by FINRA rules 1010
and 1210, it establishes identity,
tracks employment history, and serves as
the primary source for the BrokerCheck
database. Accurate, timely filing is a
fundamental compliance obligation for
every professional in the US securities
industry. Form U4 is organized into
critical numbered sections designed to
capture a comprehensive professional
profile.
>> [music]
>> The identifying sections collect legal
names, residential history, and social
security numbers to facilitate mandatory
[music] background investigations. The
employment section requires a complete
10-year history of all professional
activities, including non-securities
roles, to identify gaps or potential
conflicts. Furthermore, the registration
and examination section specifies the
sought-after licenses and the sponsoring
member firm. The most scrutinized
component of the entire filing is
section 14, the disclosure questions.
This section utilizes comprehensive yes
or no triggers regarding criminal,
regulatory, and financial history.
Affirmative responses immediately
mandate a disclosure reporting page,
providing granular details to the
Central Registration [music] Depository.
Disclosure requirements are categorized
into seven primary event types designed
to surface fitness for registration.
Criminal disclosures include any felony
charge or conviction within 10 [music]
years or investment-related
misdemeanors. Regulatory actions involve
findings or suspensions by the [music]
SEC, FINRA, or state agencies. Civil
judicial actions cover injunctions,
while customer complaints require
[music] reporting for allegations
exceeding specific monetary thresholds.
Financial matters, such as bankruptcies
filed within 10 years or outstanding
liens, must be disclosed to mitigate
risk. Beyond initial filing, the
continuing amendment obligation is
paramount for all registered persons.
Most changes, such as residential
address or non-securities employment,
must be updated within 30 calendar days.
However, certain criminal matters
require an accelerated 10 business day
filing window to maintain regulatory
standing. Member firms are responsible
for submissions and must integrate
[music] Form U4 updates into their
written supervisory procedures. Failure
to maintain accurate records often
results in severe disciplinary action
against both firms and individuals. The
information flows directly into FINRA's
BrokerCheck, allowing public oversight
of a representative's record. Under Rule
[music] 2267, firms must annually inform
customers about BrokerCheck
accessibility and the hotline number.
This ensures that the regulatory record
remains transparent, serving as a
critical mechanism for investor [music]
protection. In summary, Form U4 is a
living document. Key takeaways for exams
include the 10-year lookback and the
30-day amendment rule. Remember the
10-day rule for specific criminal events
and that accurate reporting is always
non-negotiable. Visit
financialregulationcourses.com
for finance resources, professional
development, and Series 7 preparation to
advance your career in the financial
markets.

metadata.shortDescription:
This episode clarifies the statutory exclusions from the broker-dealer definition under the Uniform Securities Act (USA), focusing on specific conditions for agents, issuers, banks, and out-of-state entities, and distinguishing exclusions from exemptions.

Full transcript & study notes: https://voraprep.com/audio/series63-s632-concept-series63-s632-lesson-003
Practice questions & study guides: https://voraprep.com/series63

segments.text: Hey, welcome to Vor Prepp Audio. Glad
you could join me. So, let's picture
this exam question because you'll
definitely see something like it. A
small community bank decides it wants to
offer mutual funds to its customers. The
bank tellers start handing out some
brochures, answering a few basic
questions, and if someone's really
interested, they point them to a
registered professional. Suddenly, the
state administrator gets a complaint.
The bank is acting as an unregistered
broker-dealer. The bank says, "No, we're
a bank. We're excluded." So, who's
right? That's exactly what we're talking
about today. The line can get blurry,
and the exam loves to test you on who
needs to register as a broker-dealer
and, just as important, who doesn't.
Under the Uniform Securities Act, the
definition of a broker-dealer is really
broad. It's basically any person, which
can mean a firm, in the business of
buying and selling securities, either
for their customers' accounts or for
their own. But, the law then carves out
some specific exceptions. These are
called exclusions. Think of it like
this. Imagine a fancy club with a strict
dress code and a bouncer. Most people
have to meet the dress code to get in.
That's like needing to register. But, an
exclusion is like being the club staff.
You're not a guest, so the guest dress
code doesn't even apply to you. You're
just not in that category. That's
different from an exemption, which would
be like a VIP guest who gets to skip the
line. The people we're talking about
today are the staff. They're excluded
from the definition entirely. So, who
gets this special status? The USA names
a few key players. First, you have
agents. An agent is an individual, a
person.
They work for a broker-dealer or for an
issuer. Because they're already defined
as agents and have their own
registration rules, they are
specifically excluded from the
definition of a broker-dealer. It makes
sense, right?
A broker-dealer is the firm, the
company. The agent is the person who
works at the firm. So, Sarah, who works
at a big brokerage house, is an agent.
Her firm is the broker-dealer. Sarah
herself is not a broker-dealer. Then you
have issuers.
An issuer is just the entity that
creates or issues the security in the
first place. A corporation selling its
own new stock is an issuer. The law says
that when a company is just selling its
own securities to raise capital, it's
not acting as a broker-dealer. It's just
selling its own stuff. Here's a quick
example to make that stick. Let's say a
company, Tech Innovations Incorporated,
wants to raise money. It decides to sell
shares of its own common stock directly
to the public from its website. That's
it. It's not selling Apple stock or
anything else. In this case, Tech
Innovations is an issuer selling its own
securities. It's excluded. It doesn't
need to register as a broker-dealer.
Now, if Tech Innovations suddenly
started a side business selling shares
of other tech companies, well, then it
would be acting as a broker-dealer and
would have to register. Okay, next up
are banks, savings institutions, and
trust companies. This brings us back to
our opening story. These institutions
are generally excluded from the
broker-dealer definition. Why? Because
they're already heavily regulated by
banking authorities. The law wants to
avoid piling on duplicate regulations.
But, and this is a big but for the exam,
this exclusion isn't a free pass to do
anything. It applies when the bank is
acting like a bank. You know,
traditional banking services. If a bank
sets up a whole [snorts] separate
division that just does securities
trading for the public, or if its
employees are actively soliciting
trades, that's crossing the line. The
bank as an institution might be
excluded, but the employee acting like a
stock broker would likely need to
register as an agent, and the bank might
have to register that separate division
as a broker-dealer. The key is whether
the activity is a normal part of
banking, or if they've basically set up
a brokerage firm inside the bank. And
there's one more group, a firm that has
no place of business in the state. Let's
say there's a brokerage firm based in
New York. It doesn't have an office, a
mailbox, or even a sign on a door
anywhere in, say, Texas. That New York
firm can do business with certain people
in Texas without registering in Texas.
Who can they talk to? Big, sophisticated
players. The rule calls them
institutional buyers, other
broker-dealers, banks, insurance
companies, pension funds. Basically, the
pros. They can also keep serving one of
their existing clients who happens to be
traveling or temporarily living in
Texas. But the moment that New York firm
opens an office in Dallas or starts cold
calling regular retail investors in
Houston, it has to register. So, let's
put this into a simple decision-making
process. When you see a question, first,
identify the entity. Is it a person? A
company selling its own stock? A bank?
If it's an individual working for a
brokerage firm, they're probably an
agent, excluded from the broker-dealer
definition. If it's a company selling
its own shares, it's an issuer,
excluded. If it's a bank, look at what
it's doing. Are the activities part of
normal banking, like managing a trust?
Probably excluded. Are they running a
full-blown trading desk for the public?
That's getting into broker-dealer
territory. Let's try a quick scenario.
Sarah is an individual. She works for a
registered broker-dealer, and her job is
to execute trades for clients. She's
properly registered as an agent. Is
Sarah herself considered a
broker-dealer? No. She's an individual
representing her firm. She's an agent,
and agents are specifically excluded
from the broker-dealer definition. She's
staff, not a guest. Now for the exam
traps. They love to blur the lines on
this. The biggest one is the bank
employee. The question will describe a
bank teller who's really pushing a
particular stock fund on every customer
who walks in. Remember, while the bank
institution has an exclusion for its
traditional activities, that individual
employee is performing the functions of
an agent, they'd likely need to be
registered. The exclusion for the bank
doesn't automatically cover every single
thing its employees do with securities.
Another trap is confusing exclusion with
exemption. I know I mentioned it before,
but it's worth repeating. Excluded means
you don't even fit the definition.
You're not in the club. Exempt means you
fit the definition, but you're given a
special pass to not register. The four
groups we talked about today, agents,
issuers, banks, and certain out-of-state
firms are all excluded. If you're
finding this kind of step-by-step
breakdown helpful for connecting the
dots, you should check out the full app.
Vora Prep is a full exam prep app,
lessons, practice questions, and an AI
tutor in one place. You can get started
for free at voraprep.com.
So, to wrap this up, what do you
absolutely need to remember for exam
day? First, an agent is a person, a
broker-dealer is a firm. An agent is
excluded from the firm's definition.
Second, an issuer is only excluded when
selling its own securities, not anyone
else's. Third, the bank exclusion is for
the institution's traditional banking
activities, not for employees who are
essentially acting as unregistered
agents. And finally, an out-of-state
firm with no office in the state can
deal with institutions, but not the
general public. Keep those distinctions
clear, and you'll be able to spot the
right answer when you see that question
about the small-town bank. You're doing
great. Just keep putting in the time,
one concept at a time. I'll talk to you

metadata.title: Projected Investment Returns: 4 Compliance Priorities for Broker-Dealers
metadata.author: LeGaye Law Firm
metadata.shortDescription:
The SEC has approved amendments to FINRA Rule 2210, giving broker-dealers new flexibility to communicate certain projected investment performance and targeted returns. But what does this mean for compliance and supervisory responsibilities?

The changes are particularly significant for private placements, alternative investments, and investment banking. While the amendment creates new opportunities, firms must continue to meet FINRA's standards for fair, balanced, and non-misleading communications.

In this video, The LeGaye Law Firm examines four key compliance considerations:

Audience Selection:
* Ensuring projections are appropriate for intended investors.
Assumptions and Disclosures:
* Clearly communicating underlying assumptions, risks, and limitations.
Third-Party Materials:
* Reviewing issuer-prepared projections before distribution.
Supervisory Documentation:
* Maintaining required source information and documenting compliance controls.

*Important* 
SEC approval does not authorize immediate use of the new exception. The effective date has not yet been announced, and existing Rule 2210 restrictions remain in place until the amendment takes effect.

Broker-dealers should use this time to update written supervisory procedures, strengthen distribution controls, and prepare compliance teams.

At LeGaye Law we make regulations make sense. 
For regulatory updates via email subscribe at:
www.LeGayeLaw.com

Disclaimer: This video is provided for informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. Firms should consult legal counsel regarding their specific facts and circumstances.


#FINRA #FINRARule2210 #BrokerDealerCompliance #SEC #PrivatePlacements #RegulatoryCompliance

segments.text: The SEC approves changes to FINRA Rule 2210. Here’s what broker-dealers need to know.
Broker-dealers will soon have more flexibility to communicate projected investment returns.
But the SEC's approval of changes to FINRA Rule 2210 comes with important limitations,
and new supervisory responsibilities.
What’s changing? On October 15, 2026, the SEC approved amendments allowing broker-dealers
to include certain projected performance figures and targeted returns in investor communications.
This is particularly significant for private placements,
alternative investments, and investment banking.
The amendment creates a limited exception to existing restrictions,
but FINRA's requirements for fair, balanced, and non-misleading communications still apply.
There are four key compliance considerations.
First: Know your audience. Projected returns must be appropriate for
the intended investors, considering their likely financial situation and investment objectives.
Unrestricted websites and mass-market advertising will generally be unsuitable.
And accredited investor status alone doesn't establish compliance.
Second: Explain the assumptions. Firms must clearly communicate the
assumptions, risks, and limitations underlying projected returns.
For example, real estate projections may depend on occupancy rates, financing costs,
or future property values. Generic disclaimers aren't enough.
Third: Review third-party materials.
Broker-dealers remain responsible for communications they distribute—even
when projections come directly from an issuer or sponsor.
Those materials still require appropriate supervisory review.
Fourth: Document compliance. Firms must retain information
about the source of projections. Documenting audience selection,
disclosures, supervisory reviews, and approval decisions can also help demonstrate compliance.
One critical point: SEC approval does not mean the amendment is effective.
The effective date has not yet been announced. Until then,
existing Rule 2210 restrictions remain in place.
The Rule 2210 amendment creates new opportunities,
but taking advantage of them requires careful preparation.
Broker-dealers should use this time to update written supervisory procedures,
establish distribution controls, review disclosure standards, and train personnel.
At LeGaye Law we make regulations make sense. For more regulatory updates, subscribe.

demand first and that might sound obvious but the last thing you want to do is delude yourself into thinking you can easily start a company and jump through all the hoops and do all these things that you have to do to get started just to realize that you know you thought you had demand and you don't really so that's the first thing you need to make sure you have willing customers who are going to and plans and using software to help people achieve their goals investments which is getting people savings into a place where it's actually growing and helping them generate returns and building and things like that and lastly things like mortgages financing other products like that now for the sake of today i'm gonna really hone in on what it is that i do and i would say that first and foremost for me is probably investing and financial planning those are like our biggest services so i want to talk about the plumbing that's required to build a business like that once you've defined where you want to specialize you'll realize why that's so important right away because the biggest thing you need to do whether you're going to start your own business or not is have the right license and credentials whether in the u.s or you're in canada you're going to need different licenses to distribute different products if you're doing financial planning you're probably going to need some sort of planning credential like a cfp i think that's probably the one you'd want to go for if you're going to be doing investments you'll need a series 7 in the u.s or the csc in canada or other things like that and for insurance you're going to need your own provincial or state qualifying exam to actually sell and distribute insurance so once we've thought about do we have demand and we thought about what do we specialize in now you actually have to go and study and get the right credentials you see this isn't as easy as just starting a business there might be a couple of years of education you have to go through just to get the licensing for the most confusing thing of all where are we going to get distribution that's the massive question when i was an independent advisor i knew that i had this big company behind me and when we needed to do insurance or investments all the infrastructure was in place that we were connected with the stock exchange and with custodians that would allow us to buy and sell and invest and insure people on our clients behalf but then when you're on your own you're like how does all this work like this makes no sense i don't really understand what's lying underneath and i think that is where most people get stuck is they see that as the most complicated thing and they kind of stop right there and think that just must be too too mind-numbing to ever understand so i'm just not even going to give it a try if you know what your specialty is you can know exactly where you want to hone in and this is where i need you to kind of stay with me for a second and this is technical so please like leave a comment below if you'd like to know a little bit more about what i mean by these but the great thing is is that many many people have gone independent before you other people have left a big company to start their own and there are other people who have actually built a business to help you leave and start your own i think a lot of people don't understand that many businesses and even most businesses are just a collection of other people's businesses kind of recombined and repackaged and sold again so if you take a marketing agency as an example you know they're using adobe photoshop which is adobe's company and they're booking clients with calendly which is a different company and they're using g suite like gmail to do communications it's just a company that's using a bunch of other companies and when you're building a business yourself what you're finding is you're going to be leveraging a lot of what we call b2b software or b2b infrastructure you're going to be looking at other companies who are going to help you build your company if you're hoping to specialize in financial planning that is actually the most simple of all things because all you really need is a cfp and you need financial planning software that allows you to build a product for a client and in that case the product is just a plan it's a projection it's something that helps them organize their financial life and turn all the chaos into something that can resemble a plan or something they can actually take action public by going to a big investment bank and ipo and getting those shares into people's hands and it had to make its way to the stock exchange and then into people's portfolios and there's all this abstract notional stuff going on and we don't really see much of it but the great thing is is there's a business to business platform involved in helping independent advisors get linked up with the stock market and invest on behalf of their clients and these are called independent dealer networks or independent custodians and what these companies actually allow you to do is take an existing business of financial advisory clients and migrate them over to something that is more independent away from a large company and if you think for some reason that i've built all the plumbing it's like metadata.title: $100M Is Easier to Get Than $10M — Here’s Why | Taber Small
metadata.author: The Capital Alliance TV
metadata.shortDescription:
Most people think raising $10 million is easier than raising $100 million. Taber Small says they have it backwards. And once you understand why, you will never think about private capital the same way again.

Taber is the Senior Managing Partner and Founder of Prominent Strategic Capital, a private equity capital advisory firm working across venture capital, private equity, and commercial banking. He has closed hotel deals, saved transactions other advisors could not get to the table, and built a network of family offices and investors who move on the right deals fast.

What we cover:

1. Why family offices and investment banks skip deals under $20 million

2. The real difference between private equity and private credit

3. What a mezzanine structure actually looks like inside a live deal

4. How Taber saved a hotel deal that had been stuck under contract for a year

5. Why roll-ups are one of the most powerful exit strategies for business owners right now

6. The one thing wealthy people protect more than their money

Subscribe for weekly conversations on wealth, business, and building in the private markets.

Deal Makers Desk drops every other Wednesday on The Capital Alliance Network.

Subscribe to The Capital Ledger, CAN’s weekly newsletter: https://ledger.thecapitalalliancenetwork.com/

Learn more about The Capital Alliance Network: https://thecapitalalliancenetwork.com/about

#PrivateEquity #DealMakersDesk #BlackWealthBuilding #CapitalMarkets #PrivateCredit #BlackEntrepreneurs #TheCapitalAllianceNetwork

metadata.title: Revenue-Based Financing Explained (RBF vs Loans vs VC + Red Flags to Avoid)
metadata.author: Today Capital Group
metadata.shortDescription:
Revenue-Based Financing (RBF) is one of the most misunderstood funding options for founders and small business owners.

In this video, we break down exactly how RBF works, why it’s considered “non-dilutive” (you don’t give up equity), and how it compares to traditional bank loans and venture capital.

segments.text: You know this feeling, right? It's that
classic founders dilemma. You've got the
momentum, you have the vision, but man,
you need capital to pour some serious
fuel on that fire. The problem, the
traditional options out there often feel
well, they feel like a trap. So, here's
what we're going to do. First, we'll
unpack that funding dilemma. Then, we'll
get super clear on what revenue-based
financing actually is and see how it
stacks up against the usual suspects.
From there, we'll figure out if it's the
right move for your business. And this
is crucial. How to spot the red flags so
you pick a great partner. All right,
let's dive. Yep. Every single founder
who has ever tried to raise capital
knows this feeling all too well. You
feel like you're caught between these
two very different and honestly often
pretty difficult paths. And this number,
wow, this number right here tells a
massive part of the story. Right now,
traditional bank approval rates for
small business loans, they're hovering
below a pretty shocking 14%. That means
the huge majority of ambitious founders
are left looking somewhere else. So,
what are those other options? Well,
you've got the banks. It's a slow,
bureaucratic process, and they want
collateral. Sometimes they even want you
to personally guarantee the loan. Ouch.
Then on the other side, you've got
venture capital. It's fast, for sure,
but the cost is incredibly steep. you
have to sell a permanent chunk of your
company, giving up both equity and
control. Okay, so this is where a third
option comes into the picture, one that
was really designed for the modern
economy. It's this flexible model that
sits right in that sweet spot between
old school debt and giving away the
farm. So what is it exactly? Let's put
it simply. Think of it like a
partnership. A company gets a chunk of
cash upfront. To pay it back, they share
a small agreed upon percentage of their
future monthly revenue. Once they've
paid back that initial capital plus a
simple flat fee, that's called the cap,
the deal is over. That's it. Clean and
simple. Let's break that down into three
really easy steps. Step one, you get the
cash you need to invest in growth,
marketing, inventory, you name it. Step
two, you pay it back with a little slice
of your monthly revenue, usually
somewhere between 4 to 8%. Now, here's
the cool part. That payment flexes. If
you have a slow month, guess what? Your
payment is smaller. have a killer month,
it's a bit bigger and you pay off the
total faster. And finally, step three.
As soon as you hit that pre-agreed total
amount, it's done. Payments just stop.
The partnership is complete. And this
this is the real game changer. The
single biggest reason founders are
falling in love with this model is that
it is nondilutive.
Let me say that again. Non-dilutive. You
don't give up a single share. You don't
add a new voice to your board. And you
do not lose control over your company's
destiny. you keep 100% ownership.
Period. Okay, so now we get what RBF is,
but how does it really stack up against
the old guard because, you know, funding
isn't a one-izefits-all kind of thing.
It's all about picking the right tool
for the job. And this chart just lays
out the trade-offs perfectly. Let's look
at control. With a bank, you're signing
personal guarantees and these
restrictive rules called covenants that
tell you how to run your business. With
a VC, you could get a new boss on your
board. But with RBF, those restrictions
are minimal. Then there's dilution,
giving up a piece of your company. It's
zero with RBF, but it's a huge deal with
VC. And finally, flexibility. Bank
payments are totally rigid. RBF
payments, though, they move up and down
with your revenue. And for managing cash
flow, that is a massive advantage. You
want to see what dilution actually looks
like? Here it is. When you take on
venture capital, you are literally
selling a permanent slice of your
company pie. That 25% that the investor
now owns, it's gone forever. And that
slice is probably going to get smaller
with every new funding round. With RBF,
that whole pie stays 100% yours. Now, we
have to make a really critical
distinction here. RBS gets confused all
the time with its much more aggressive
cousin, the merchant cash advance or
MCA. The absolute key difference is the
payment structure. With RBF, payments
flex with your revenue. With an MCA, you
are typically paying back a fixed daily
amount that gets yanked out of your bank
account no matter how much you sold that
day. A slow week with an MCA can be
absolutely brutal. With RBF, it's
totally manageable. And this quote from
fintech analyst Jason Miller just nails
it. If your funding doesn't breathe with
your revenue, it's a liability, not an
asset. That really gets to the heart of
the problem with these old rigid payment
structures. For a modern agile business,
your funding has to adapt with you.
Otherwise, it just becomes an anchor
holding you back. And this isn't just
theory, right? Check out this real world
example. An e-commerce brand was seeing
their ads perform like crazy, but they
were burning through cash. They used RBF
to scale their ad spend. And because the
payments were tied to their revenue,
they could go allin on marketing without
that constant fear of a huge fixed
payment coming due during a slow sales
week. And the result, a 200% increase in
revenue. So, this all sounds pretty
great, but you're probably asking, "Is
it the right fit for my company?" Good
question. Let's walk through a quick
self assessment. So, the ideal RBF
candidate, they usually share a few key
traits. First, they have pretty
predictable revenue. Think about SAS
subscriptions or steady e-commerce
sales. That's because the whole model is
based on that revenue stream. They're
also usually past the idea on a napkin
stage, bringing in at least 10 grand a
month. They also need healthy gross
margins so that sharing a slice of
revenue doesn't their business.
And most importantly, they're already
growing and they have a crystal clear
plan for how this new capital is going
to kick that growth into high gear. But
here's the thing. As RBF gets more
popular, you got to know that not all
providers are created equal. It is
absolutely vital that you know how to
choose the right partner and avoid the
bad actors. So, here are six big red
flags to watch out for. Number one,
opaque terms. If you can't get a simple,
straight answer on all the costs, you
walk away. Two, unusually high fees. You
want to stick in that 4 to 8% range.
Three, they don't seem to care about
your business's health. A good partner
does their homework. Four, inflexible
terms. Five, aggressive, you have to
sign now sales tactics. And finally,
number six, a lack of knowledge about
your industry. At the end of the day, a
good provider should feel like a real
partner, not a predator. And let's just
end on this thought. It's so easy to get
paralyzed by the fear of making the
wrong funding choice. But in today's
market, you know what the biggest risk
of all is? It's doing nothing. It's
standing still while a growth
opportunity and your competitors speed
right past you. The right funding isn't
just a lifeline. It's a strategic weapon
you can use to win.

metadata.title: Debt vs Equity vs Revenue-Based Funding: Which Fits Your Business? | EIN Business Funding | EINBF
metadata.author: Enterprise Industry Network
metadata.shortDescription:
What type of business funding actually fits your company: debt, equity, or revenue-based funding?

These capital options are not the same, and choosing the right one depends on what the business needs, how repayment may work, how much control the owner wants to keep, how stable cash flow is, the growth plan, the level of risk involved, and the timing of the funding need.

Debt funding can help a business access capital while allowing the owner to retain ownership, but it creates repayment obligations and requires financial discipline. Equity funding can support growth without traditional loan payments, but it may reduce ownership and decision-making control. Revenue-based funding can offer a different repayment structure tied to business performance, but it should still be reviewed carefully for total cost, repayment speed, and cash flow impact.

For many business owners, the better question is not only whether they can get approved for capital, but which type of capital actually fits the business model and financial reality.

EIN Business Funding, part of Enterprise Industry Network, helps business owners think more clearly about funding readiness, capital structure, repayment impact, and how different financing paths may align with business goals.

metadata.title: Business Loan Broker Training: Why Lenders Ignore You
metadata.author: Commercial Loan Broker Institute
metadata.shortDescription:
Most business loan broker training misses one uncomfortable truth.
Lenders aren’t ignoring brokers because they’re new. They’re ignoring them because of signal.

In this business loan broker training video, I break down how lenders actually decide which brokers deserve attention and which ones quietly get screened out. This is not theory. It is based on repeated lender feedback and real-world exposure to how lenders behave behind the scenes.

Many brokers tell themselves:
“I need more time.”
“I need a track record.”
“I need to fund a few deals first.”

Those explanations feel logical. They are usually wrong.

Lenders don’t know your history.
They don’t know your volume.
They don’t know how long you’ve been around.
They only know what you put in front of them.

In this training, you’ll learn:
• Why lenders ignore brokers without ever saying no
• The five screens lenders use to evaluate brokers
• Why clarity matters more than experience
• How bad lender fit damages your credibility
• What packaging quality signals to lenders
• How deal viability silently kills engagement
• Why perseverance is a market screen, not a lender preference

RESOURCES 
If you want additional resources, lender connection frameworks, or direct guidance, comment “BROKER” and we’ll share the Lenders Network Guide for free.

If you want to learn more about how to become a business loan broker visit https://commercialloanbrokerinstitute.com/

CHAPTERS
0:00 – New Broker Life
1:21 – Lender Research
2:45 – Five Lender Screens
7:55 – Broker Best Practices

TOPICS

metadata.shortDescription:
Add this monthly recurring revenue stream to your lending business: 
👉 https://youtu.be/fF11Yr0Sr2o

In this training, I speak with Josh from EquipmentFinancingLeads.com about how their exclusive leads program works. 
*************************************************************************************************
More training: How to close more business loans - 4 call system:
👉 https://www.clkmg.com/leadsforlocals/bizloanmasterclass

Free Business Loan Lead Generation Masterclass:
👉 https://www.clkmg.com/leadsforlocals/bizloanmasterclass

Learn more about EliteBroker:
👉 https://www.clkmg.com/leadsforlocals/elitebrokerinfopage

Join the EliteBroker Facebook Group:
👉 https://www.clkmg.com/leadsforlocals/elitebrokerfbgroup

At EliteBroker, we're always looking for new ways for business loan brokers to generate more leads so they can run them through the powerful automations and campaigns inside of EliteBroker.
***************************************************************************************************
Time stamp:
0:00 Intro
1:50 Equipment Financing Leads background
12:45 Equipment Financing leads vs. other lead types
17:20 How the leads are generated
21:03 Lead exclusivity
23:45 When brokers start receiving leads
25:55 Lead close and contact ratio
27:33 Sending leads directly into EliteBroker
29:28 Cost and commitment
34:15 Equipment Financing Broker School
38:28 Equipment Financing Broker Reality Show
44:35 Conclusion and final thoughts

The more business owners you can get into EliteBroker, the better.

And while we have a very robust training area that teaches some very powerful business loan lead generation strategies, like Facebook ads, direct outreach group prospecting, etc., having a good source to purchase leads from can be a very valuable addition to your lead generation.

Of course, lead providers are a dime a dozen and most are unreliable.

But that's why we do trainings like this one where we interview the lead provider to get all of the information about their leads so we can make an informed decision about whether or not to try them.

I decided to interview Josh about his equipment financing leads because they ONLY provide exclusive leads to clients that are generated online, in real-time and can be delivered right into your EliteBroker account as the leads are generated.

This means the leads you get are YOUR leads and are not re-sold dozens of times.

So if you're a business loan broker looking to potentially add a steady stream of new leads into your business, this training is definitely for you.

metadata.title: Mortgage Loan Officers: The Second Commission Stream Hiding in Your Client List
metadata.author: Equipment Finance Academy
metadata.shortDescription:
Mortgage loan officers already work with self-employed borrowers who own businesses — and those businesses finance trucks, machines, and shop equipment all year long. This video explains the second commission stream hiding in that client list: how equipment finance brokering works, what the broker actually does step by step, and why documentation and lender skills from mortgage work transfer directly. It puts the opportunity in context with ELFA data ($1.51 trillion in equipment financed in 2025; 87% of companies finance their equipment), Michael Chen's verified first deal ($180K excavator, $4,200 commission, in 60 days), and Sam's own deal history.

Equipment Finance Academy teaches this process in Equipment Finance Broker Mastery — a 6-module course (25 lessons) plus the Broker CRM with lender directory, calculators, pipeline, borrower intake link, one-click lender submission, document checklists, AI Lead Finder, and renewals tools. Current launch price is $97 one time (regular $297), all sales final, for beginners in the US and Canada including those with zero finance experience.

Learn how to become an equipment finance broker at www.equipmentfinanceacademy.com
Get the weekly broker letter, The Equipment Finance Broker: https://theequipmentfinancebroker.substack.com

Disclaimer: Results vary. Commissions described in this video are one broker's experience and Sam's own deal history, not a guarantee of income or results for anyone else.

metadata.title: Equipment Financing | Learning with Business Finance Glossary
metadata.author: Biz2Credit
metadata.shortDescription:
Equipment financing is asset-based lending that helps businesses acquire essential machinery or tools without paying the full cost upfront. In this financing option, the equipment itself serves as collateral, making it a more accessible solution for businesses needing capital. 

Typically, companies provide a down payment and use business loans to cover the remaining costs, ensuring they have the resources to operate efficiently.

Want to learn more about machinery financing and other key financial concepts? The Biz2Credit Business Finance Glossary is your ultimate guide to essential small business finance terms—all in one place.

So as the transfer or the seller, you have to be able to say, well, I anticipate so much I will end up having to buy back under the recourse terms. You have to be able to reasonably estimate that. In other words, it's like estimating bad debts. Second, the the seller, the transfer says, but I'm relinquishing control. They are your receivables factor. You can do with them whatever you see fit. And third, I can't be forced to repurchase them. Now, you might look at that and go, "Wait a minute. If you cannot force a repurchase, then how the heck is it with recourse?" Well, usually it's because there's an alternative method. So, they may say, "Look, if we have certain receivables that are bad, we will give them back to you and you are then obligated to replace them with new receivables. As long as those three conditions are met, then it's treated as a sale, just like a without recourse, basically. If not, then it's recognized as a loan instead. All right, there is one last thing. Consider this more of a financially creative thing to do with it is you could securitize the receivables. In this case, you transfer a bucket of receivables to another entity. Could be to a trust, could be to a subsidiary. Then that trust that subsidiary sells stock sells a security and the security is collateralized by the receivable. Effectively investors in this securization they get paid as the receivables are collected. So in effect you could say hey investors we've got some outstanding receivables. We're going to sell them to you. we're going to collateralize or excuse me securitize them effectively collateralize them uh at 50 cents on the dollar. So you as an investor would say, hm, so if I think that more than 50% of those are collectible, I would make money because I could pay 50 cents and effectively my security will be worth more than that. More like most securities, it could go the other way. But that's securization. It's another way to leverage the value of those assets for financial benefit. So now you have an answer to what else could I do with those receivables other than just collect them or write them off. All right, we'll see you on the next one. Thanks. [Music]

metadata.shortDescription:
A Primer on Asset Based Lending (ABL) presented by SG Credit Partners
Wednesday, January 17 | 2-3 PM ET

In today's challenging fundraising environment, companies are relying more and more on debt to finance their growth. Asset-based lending (ABL) offers a unique and flexible way to borrow against company assets and fund ongoing operations.

Join Evan Waggoner from SG Credit Partners to learn about and better understand the world of ABL, including which business models are best suited for this type of lending arrangement, the mechanics of the ABL structure, and when in the growth-stage it makes sense to consider ABL as a primary source of working capital.

metadata.title: Accounts Receivable Factoring Vs Assignment (Transferring Receivables For Cash)
metadata.author: Allen Mursau
metadata.shortDescription: Accounting for the assignment of accounts receivable (as collateral) for loan (note) versus factoring accounts receivable where the holder of the accounts receivable sells the receivables to a financing institution for cash less a financing charge, the holder of accounts receivable can transfer (or assign) the receivables for cash either as (1) selling the receivables (factoring receivables) where the seller surrenders control receivables and records a sale of an asset (accounts receivable) on the balance sheet or (2) thru secured borrowing where the receivables are assigned (pledged) for for a loan (notes payable) the seller secures from a financing institution, payments received on the receivables are used to pay off the loan (notes payable), where the seller maintains control of receivables and records a liability (notes payable) on the balance sheet the example demonstrates both methods (1) factoring receivables and (2) assigning receivables to generate immediate cash on the receivables, the basic differences of the methods are demonstarted, detailed accounting example by Allen Mursau
