metadata.title: Asset Based Lending (ABL) - Business Financing Explained
metadata.author: FinanceKid
metadata.shortDescription:
Asset Based Lending (ABL) are loans made to businesses backed by a liquid asset used as collateral for the loan. Businesses that use ABLs are either highly leveraged or too small to take on more bank debt and must resort to alternative lending solutions.

These loans are used to increase the working capital of a business in order to help finance growth or operating activities. 

In this video, we cover the three categories of the ABL market:
- Recourse/nonrecourse financing
- Purchase order financing
- Inventory financing

Are ABLs a possible solution? Why is inventory financing so bad? How can an ABL help a company become more organized? We answer all of these questions in the video. 

If you have any other questions, please comment below. If you want to reach out via email, you can contact me at; 

financeekid@gmail.com 

If you are looking to sell your business and would like to learn more about Roblee Capital, please reach out to me for an introductory call. Roblee Capital is a Toronto-based M&A Investment Bank focused on serving companies with revenues between $1MM to $100MM primarily offering sell and buy-side M&A services. We work with Canadian-based business owners looking to sell their lower mid-market business. If you are a Canadian business owner looking to sell or buy, please reach out so we can connect at the link below:

https://www.robleecapital.ca/

CMA| Part 1 | Section A  | Accounts Receivable Factoring | Letslearn Global

In factoring, the business transfers its receivables to the factor, who then collects payment from the customer. The business receives an advance, often around 70% to 90% of the invoice value, and later gets the remaining balance minus fees after collection.

Costs in factoring
The main cost is the factoring fee, which is charged as a percentage of the invoice value. Fees vary based on factors such as customer credit quality, invoice volume, industry risk, days outstanding, and whether the deal is recourse or non-recourse. Some sources note that costs may range roughly from 1% to 10%, and in many cases from about 1% to 5% for standard arrangements.

Advantages
It provides quick cash flow and reduces the wait for customer payment.

It can help a business pay payroll, suppliers, or other operating expenses sooner.

It may reduce or transfer some collection risk, especially in non-recourse factoring.

It is often easier to obtain than a traditional bank loan for some businesses.

Disadvantages
It can be expensive compared with traditional financing, especially if invoices remain unpaid longer.

The business may lose control over customer collections and related communication.

In recourse factoring, the business may still be responsible if the customer does not pay.

It can affect customer relationships if customers are notified that a factor is handling collections.

Simple example
If a company has a $100,000 invoice, the factor may advance about $80,000 to $90,000 immediately, then later send the remaining amount after the customer pays, minus the factoring fee. This helps the business access cash now, but it pays for that convenience through the discount and related charges.

metadata.title: Factoring Receivable and Pledging of Receivable
metadata.author: Farhat Lectures | CPA, CMA, EA & Accounting
metadata.shortDescription:
Factoring receivables vs. pledging receivables explained for the CPA exam and financial accounting students — learn the two main ways businesses convert accounts receivable into immediate cash and how each is recorded. This lecture explains factoring (selling receivables to a factor at a discount and removing them from the books), pledging (using receivables as collateral for a loan), the difference between with-recourse and without-recourse arrangements, and the real-world significance of these distinctions, including the 2007-2008 financial crisis. Ideal for CPA candidates, CMA candidates, EA candidates, and college accounting students studying accounting for receivables.

Try it free at farhatlectures.com — interactive exercises, lectures, simulations, cases, multiple choice, and AI tools for CPA, CMA, EA and students.

Video Timeline & Key Concepts:
0:00 Introduction to converting accounts receivable into immediate cash
1:46 Factoring receivables: selling receivables to a factor at a discount and removing them from the books
5:45 Pledging receivables: using receivables as collateral for a loan disclosed in the notes
8:27 Real-world significance: why the distinction matters for financial reporting, including the 2007-2008 crisis

Frequently Asked Questions:

Q: What is factoring of receivables?

A: Factoring is the sale of a company's accounts receivable to a third party, called a factor, usually at a discount. The business gets cash immediately instead of waiting for customers to pay, and the receivables are removed from its books.

Q: How is pledging different from factoring?

A: Pledging uses accounts receivable as collateral to secure a loan rather than selling them. The receivables stay on the company's books, the company records a loan or note payable, and the pledge is disclosed in the notes to the financial statements.

Q: What is the difference between with-recourse and without-recourse factoring?

A: In a without-recourse arrangement, the factor assumes the risk of uncollectible accounts. In a with-recourse arrangement, the company retains responsibility and may have to reimburse the factor if customers do not pay, which usually results in a lower discount rate.

Q: Why does the distinction between factoring and pledging matter?

A: How a transaction is classified affects whether receivables are removed from the books and whether a liability is recorded. Misclassifying financing arrangements as sales can distort a company's financial position, an issue highlighted during the 2007-2008 financial crisis.
